Election rout creates a mandate to govern The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade. The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire. Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time. "Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said. For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?" The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality." A new generation of leaders After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver. Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition. Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".
He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.
But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".
"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
Climate talks in an age of 'overshoot'
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.
In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.
Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035
But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.
"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work,

Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back Health Nov 22, 2026 1:02 PM EST People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer's disease. But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer's, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch. Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won't even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble. WATCH: 'The Price of Exclusion' explores lasting impact of racial inequality in medicine "The community will look like, 'Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they're gonna leave us hanging,'" said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years. Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation's long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation's medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow. The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city's Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer's and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La'Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study's field coordinator. Studies are mislabeled as diversity, equity and inclusion Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer's Association. As Blair said, "You start forgetting things and you start to wonder, do you have Alzheimer's? You wonder, do you have dementia?" Then the study, which had been near completion in its fifth and final year, was stripped of funding last year by the National Institutes of Health, on the grounds that it was "not science," according to the study's researchers, despite a rigorous review and vetting from a community advisory board. "It wasn't a Black study or a DEI study," Wagner said. "It was something that was happening that was real." WATCH: Scientists sound alarm on Trump administration's dismantling of research funding Similar terminations happened all over the country. Negar Fani, a neuropsychologist at Emory University in Atlanta, was two years into a five-year, $2.9 million project on how daily experiences of racial discrimination affect the brain and body of Black Americans when NIH terminated it in July. While Fani tries to find the roughly $2.3 million she needs to complete the study, she and her team were left to try to explain the situation to participants who feel abandoned. "It takes a lot to restore trust with the Black community, who has experienced so many different betrayals," she said. Like the Pittsburgh study's funding, Fani's grant had been terminated for being "not scientific" and "subjective" — after the study had been approved and had enrolled 66 of the 220 people it. "It's simply brain science research," she said. Fewer grants awarded for multiyear studies In Pittsburgh, study lead researcher Andrea Rosso is one of numerous scientists in a recently filed lawsuit against NIH and its parent Department of Health and Human Services, one of a growing body of legal actions as the administration continues to hunt for and halt medical grants with descriptions that include the words "disparities," "minority" and "racial." Ann Cohen, a director of Pittsburgh's Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, also is part of that lawsuit after her separate, complementary study of Alzheimer's risk also was halted -- after spending $5.2 million over three years. She, too, has a troubling ethics question: What to do with blood samples collected from the participants? "You lose trust a hell of a lot faster than you build it," she said. A spokesperson for HHS said "Massive amounts of DEI grants have failed to translate into better health outcomes for minority populations. Following President Trump's directives, NIH is shifting money into rigorous research that will help Americans — including minority populations — live longer, healthier lives." WATCH: Black midwife's death highlights racial gap in maternal mortality This year, the NIH has awarded 2,000 fewer grants for multiyear studies worth a total of $200 million compared with 2025, according to an Association of American Medical Colleges report. "It's unprecedented. Many of the decisions are based on political biases and based on what politicians think is valuable rather than peer review processes, evidence-based decisions about where to invest our research dollars," said Jill Rosenthal, the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress. "We're wasting resources, we're wasting the opportunity to identify cures for diseases," she said. Researchers in Pittsburgh are especially concerned that promises made to the community will remain unfulfilled. At least three bodies have been recovered the site of a residential building that was hit by a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Services said.

4a0db0857164.text: By — Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/french-activists-demand-a-tear-gas-suspension-over-reported-menstrual-changes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes Health Nov 22, 2026 12:34 PM EST PARIS (AP) — French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection. WATCH: Why French students are leading massive protests across the country The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons. Here's what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health. Tear gas is commonly used by police to disperse crowds Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it. Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches. Women reported pain and unexpected bleeding after exposure A member of the French gendarmerie shoots a tear gas canister during a demonstration as part of a nationwide day of strikes and protests over wages, the cost of living and public services called by French labour unions, and joined by high school and university students calling for better education conditions, in Nantes, France, on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Stephane Mahe/Reuters Mélina Galland, 24, was working as an independent photographer during Oct. 17 protests in Paris that were marred by rioting and looting. She wore a double surgical mask along with a diving mask when tear gas grenades were fired. "Heading back home, I felt intense belly pain which was unusual because I never experience pain that intense at that stage of my period," she said. Chloé Baroux, 25, also a photographer, first noticed pain and irregular periods after covering protests against a security bill in 2020 and 2021. She said her menstrual cycles eventually became more regular, and she didn't think of a potential link to tear gas until she covered the recent protests, noting, "over the past two months, it's become irregular again." WATCH: French authorities impose curfews after weekend rioting Eva-Luna Tholance, a former journalist who investigated the issue six years ago, decided to found the "Lacrymos de sang" ("Tears of blood") advocacy group during the protests to raise awareness about possible effects on menstrual cycles and pregnancies. The group asked people last month to complete a questionnaire describing their exposure and symptoms. Its collection of accounts doesn't establish how common symptoms are among those who say they were exposed to tear gas, and they were not reviewed by independent doctors. Still, Tholance said, many women described pain or unexpected bleeding, and thousands are asking questions about what's happening in their bodies. "Some people experience mild cramps, but a huge number tell us about cramps that are far worse than what they normally experience during their periods," she said, adding that bleeding reports range "from spotting to extremely heavy bleeding lasting several days. Some people bleed for weeks." Others reported bleeding despite being postmenopausal or taking hormonal contraception that normally prevents menstrual bleeding, Tholance said. Investigations have yet to establish a causal link An Associated Press investigation during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests in the U.S. found there had been limited study and oversight of tear gas, though it did raise concerns about tear gas exposure in confined spaces, excessive use and canisters fired directly at people. A recent study collected accounts of symptoms reported after the BLM protests. It found a "potential relationship" between exposure and "adverse reproductive health outcomes" but did not prove cause and effect. That's in part because the study relied on self-reported information collected at one point in time — similar to the French group's questionnaire — and because people who felt most impacted may have been more likely to respond. "There's a lot of theories. We don't really 100% know," said the study's lead author, Asha Hassan of the University of Minnesota Medical School. The study calls for more research "urgently." WATCH: French students lead massive protests against education policies Hassan said much early research on tear gas involved healthy young men in military settings, which could help explain why menstrual and other reproductive health effects have gone undocumented. Alsetex and Nobel Sport, two leading suppliers of tear gas grenades to French law enforcement, did not respond to requests for comment. The Interior Ministry says no published scientific studies show that CS causes menstrual changes or miscarriages. It said other effects of tear gas generally resolve within hours, although it acknowledged that some longer-lasting symptoms affecting the skin and eyes "cannot be ruled out." 30228365a20f.text: By — Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/as-ai-detects-flaws-in-computer-systems-is-it-causing-more-tech-outages-and-disruptions Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter As AI detects flaws in computer systems, is it causing more tech outages and disruptions? Nation Nov 22, 2026 12:13 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. In the span of one week, Microsoft services went down, flights were grounded nationwide, some banks' services briefly stopped working and an internal platform for the National Security Agency went dark. It left people wondering: Is artificial intelligence the culprit? In a Fox News interview, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he asked someone in the tech industry what could be causing the outages, and that person believed it's "super intelligence," the Trump administration's preferred term for AI (they're not the same thing). "That kinda makes sense to me, because I can tell you with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack, no one's out there taking claims for it," Mullin said Nov 17. WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity In a separate Nov. 17 Fox Business interview, National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton pointed to flaws that AI detected in a programming language used in systems across the world, and he said fixing them caused unexpected problems. "The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said. Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chairman Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said some of the recent outages were "AI-related." "What's happened is that these AI tools, what they've been able to do is spot vulnerabilities in all of our existing systems," Warner said in a Nov. 18 CNBC interview. "Then all of these companies are in this mad rush to create patches because nobody wants to have their system vulnerable." High-profile AI hacks have happened this year, but there's no indication that the recent outages were the result of AI-related cyberattacks or rogue AI agents. Experts say AI is boosting companies' ability to detect weaknesses in their systems, and therefore requiring more fixes, which could lead to outages. But no evidence has shown that caused the recent string of tech disruptions. "Vulnerabilities are being discovered and exploited faster than ever before, especially with increasingly capable AI models," said Bryan Ward, a Vanderbilt University computer science assistant professor. How AI is helping detect system flaws In the past, organizations would task specialists with finding flaws in their software systems, said Stuart Madnick, an MIT Sloan School of Management information technology professor. Now, AI is often able to do this 10 to 100 times faster than humans, Madnick said. If an organization previously found four or five flaws in a year, they would now be aware of 40 to 400. "The question is: Is (it) the fixing that's causing the problem, or the fact you got 400 open windows and doors in your system that are now known that's causing a problem?" Madnick said. WATCH: Cascade of tech outages 'separate events' and 'under control,' Trump says Leading AI companies, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, have released sophisticated models that have uncovered serious vulnerabilities in software. On Nov. 17, a cybersecurity start-up using an OpenAI model found a critical software flaw in a programming language used by government agencies, banks, hospitals and the majority of Fortune 500 companies. To give a sense of the volume of fixes deployed by one major company, the cybersecurity firm Qualys reported that Microsoft addressed 1,235 vulnerabilities in November, compared to 68 in November 2025. More secure software systems must be built in the future, Ward said, but there is an immediate need to fix problems now. No evidence so far that the tech outages are connected to each other Based on what the government and affected companies have reported so far, the outages did not happen because of a common weakness. Microsoft said it had a technical issue unrelated to AI or AI agents, and the problem stemmed from a "network capacity upgrade." It hasn't given more details. The nationwide ground stop happened after a router upgrade disrupted the FAA telecommunications infrastructure, government officials said. Investigators haven't determined whether there was an installation error or a faulty router, but they have ruled out an AI system the FAA recently rolled out. WATCH: What a string of tech problems reveals about America's digital vulnerabilities JPMorganChase attributed its outage to a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems." Unintended consequences, such as services becoming unavailable, can be a trade-off when companies update their systems, said Nicholas Leiserson, president of the Center for Advancing Cybersecurity at the Institute for Security and Technology. "That's like a perennial challenge that has existed in information technology operations for a long time, and AI can potentially accelerate it," he said. Before an outage, people can protect their personal devices and information by: Keeping software updated. Using strong passwords, and not reusing them across websites. A password manager can help store passwords securely. Using multifactor authentication. Keeping a data backup. "I think recent events should be a wake-up call and the public should take the opportunity to improve their cybersecurity posture," Ward said. "Recent outages demonstrate how critical and intertwined software systems have become in our society today, and how important cybersecurity truly is." e99e0449a122.text: By — Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/mercury-gets-its-first-visitor-in-years-as-a-pair-of-spacecraft-loop-into-orbit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit Science Nov 22, 2026 11:41 AM EST CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries. The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available. BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade. NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015. Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey. WATCH: Astronauts reflect on living aboard the International Space Station Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can't wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare "unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time," he noted. Once orbiting separately, the European Space Agency's satellite and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's smaller craft will study Mercury's dense interior and exterior magnetic field, as well as everything in between: impact craters, volcanic plains, mountain ridges and peaks jutting as high as 3 miles (4 1/2 kilometers). The mercury at Mercury can hit more than 800 degrees (427 degrees Celsius), adding strain to electronic and engineering systems. Space agency officials want to keep the mission going for at least one Earth year — or the equivalent of four Mercury years. "The spacecraft and its instruments need to be kept as cool as possible, which is a huge technical challenge in itself," Jones said in an email. Despite its relative proximity to Earth, Mercury is one of the solar system's least explored planets. Only outer planets Uranus and Neptune have had fewer visitors — a lone Voyager 2 back in the 1980s. Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-climate-talks-break-down-over-bitter-disagreements-on-fossil-fuels Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels World Updated on Nov 22, 2026 3:35 PM EST — Published on Nov 22, 2026 11:30 AM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks fizzled out Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement because of disputes over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming. Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey, but impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable. Nations' negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word "disappointing" to characterize the discussions. Though the talks, called COP31, failed to reach a main agreement, known as a cover decision, the meeting had already made progress on smaller issues. The two-week session ended Sunday night, after running more than 50 hours overtime at the resort town of Antalya. READ MORE: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming This all happened as global warming accelerates with ever-worsening heat waves, floods, storms and droughts. The U.N. said it is now inevitable that the world will soon blow past the warming threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. And there is also a global energy shock due to the war in Iran. On top of that, a strong El Niño amplifies human-caused warming and causes more weather disasters. "I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. "Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly." Upset youth representative Oumnia Anfer told the negotiators "you have let us down." Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership, which didn't mention fossil fuels. A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision, often reluctantly, saying consensus on something was more important, though it ultimately failed. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document. "It's unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels," Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's climate minister, said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks. Impasses over draft agreements Previously, fossil fuels went unmentioned in COP final decisions for more than 25 years, said Alden Meyer, with the think tank E3G. Then, three years ago in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, a groundbreaking agreement called for "transitioning away from fossil fuels" but since then there's been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai agreement in its entirety, but that wasn't enough for many nations and environmental groups. "Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis," said Guterres. "The continued addiction to coal, oil and gas is fueling climate chaos, exposing economies to price shocks and undermining energy security. We can't put out the fire while pouring fuel on it." Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would undermine efforts to reduce overall emissions. READ MORE: Activists, leaders criticize COP31 climate talks as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft deal "The failure of COP31 is an outrage — it is outrageous that a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels," said former U.S. Vice President Al Gore. As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure. "Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that's disappointing, very disappointing," said Australia's Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations. Bowen said the Dubai agreement's explicit call to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: "Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It's happening. It's happening at speed and it's irreversible." Other issues left unresolved Other climate issues weren't settled, and many were deferred to next year's negotiations in Ethiopia. They include details on transitioning away from fossil fuels, financial help for poorer nations to adapt to the warming world and action on gender and climate. For this year's negotiations, Turkey made global electrification its signature issue. A proposal introduced separately from the main agreement calls for countries to increase the share of electricity in total final energy consumption from about 21% today to 35% by 2035. This would require nations to commit to measures such as switching transportation — including cars, trucks and planes — from fossil fuels to electricity and using electricity instead of coal to make industrial products. Nearly 100 nations signed up for this goal as part of the separate pledge. Meyer, with E3G, also hailed progress on global adaptation goals and on a program that helps countries achieve their emissions-cutting goals fairly. c52a26a8a044.text: By — Christopher Weber, Associated Press Christopher Weber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/immigration-officers-make-arrests-at-seattle-airport-in-distressing-scene-delaying-flight Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight Nation Nov 22, 2026 11:18 AM EST Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight. Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit. WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws." During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed. Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. "We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests." It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect." The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on. ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. WATCH: ICE touts record number of deportations in agency's history Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities." The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred." Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition. "The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform." Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. "Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said. The News
The COP31 climate summit in TÃ¼rkiye collapsed on Sunday without agreement on a final deal, over deep disagreement over the negotiationsâ most basic provision â the first time the talks ended unsuccessfully since calamitous 2009 meetings.
After negotiations stretched to their longest in three decades, Murat Kurum, the summit president, finally acknowledged that a meeting meant to drive forward the âimplementationâ of countriesâ existing carbon-cutting commitments could not even agree on what their overarching goal should be. âThere is no consensus on this document,â he said, marking the first time for COP to conclude without an agreement since the calamitous 2009 summit in Copenhagen. âTherefore, these decisions have not been adopted.â
Timâs view
The breakdown effectively marks the demise of a 2023 consensus, reached in Dubai, on the long-term phaseout of fossil fuels in the global economy. The years since then have been marked by successive global energy crises, including the biggest oil and gas supply disruption in history. While these crises have driven a faster pivot from fossil fuels in some importing countries, they have reinforced othersâ conviction that more, not less, investment is required in the legacy energy system for the sake of security and affordability. COP31 shows that climate action was a casualty of that turmoil.
Overlapping wars and US President Donald Trumpâs rambunctious foreign policy have also undermined multilateralism in general, a critical problem for a negotiating process that requires consensus (a requirement that former Vice President Al Gore criticized this week as âinsaneâ for an issue on which some countriesâ interests are so diametrically, inherently opposed).
In Dubai, it took an oil executive â Sultan Al Jaber, CEO of ADNOC â to bring fellow exporters onboard for the most pointed critique of their own industry in COP history. But that consensus proved fragile. At last yearâs COP in Brazil, the final deal didnât include the words âfossil fuelsâ but did encourage countries to take the Dubai consensus âinto accountâ when developing national policies.
By this year, the most delegates could muster was merely ârecallingâ the consensus, without any indication of what that memory was meant to instigate. Instead, the draft decision included new calls for carbon capture that â while clearly necessary to bend the curve on global emissions â are seen by many negotiating teams as a cover for extending the lifespan of fossil fuels.
Negotiating blocs that supported adopting the draft included the Arab Group, which includes the UAE, as well as China, India, and Japan. But the COP process requires consensus, and the draft was adamantly opposed by the least-developed-countries bloc, as well as the UK and European Union. The US has not been represented at the talks since President Donald Trump returned to office.
While the failure to adopt a conference-wide deal indicates that universal agreement on global energy pathways has become more elusive than ever, smaller groupings did manage to find common ground on the issue. More than two dozen countries (albeit relatively minor carbon emitters) have now adopted some form of policy guidelines for a âtransition away from fossil fuels.â And during COP31, nearly 90 countries signed on to pledge to turbocharge the electrification of their economies.
COP, in other words, has not completely imploded â but it has become deeply fragmented. And meanwhile, the real economy doesnât need a UN-brokered summit to set either the floor or the ceiling for change.
âThe green economy will not win because a text tells it to,â Juan Carlos Monterrey GÃ³mez, Panamaâs former climate envoy, wrote. âIt will win because it is cheaper, smarter and creates more jobs. The future will not be negotiated.â
Notable
- Throughout the summit, Beijing remained focused on lowering trade barriers to its green tech exports. Protectionism is an obstacle to global electrification goals, Chinaâs delegates to COP31 warned.

The News
Semafor is facing scrutiny for hiring high-profile Washington consultants to assist with event bookings, a revelation that underscores the murkiness embedded into a high-level convening business thatâs become a vital and growing revenue source for some global media companies.
As online web traffic and the associated advertising dollars have diminished across the industry, publishers have leaned into sponsored in-person events to support their newsrooms. The growing importance of these events has raised thorny standards and ethics questions regarding sponsors who pay to be onstage at places like Fortune, The Wall Street Journal and The Atlantic â even if their sessions are clearly labeled as sponsored â or regarding media CEOs who strike deals with advertisers while interviewing those same CEOs.
Of the last decadeâs crop of digital media outlets, none have leaned further into the events-driven business than Semafor, which has hosted hundreds of high-profile gatherings since launching in late 2022.
While Semafor primarily relies on an in-house events team to secure bookings of business, political and government leaders, for its flagship April gathering, Semafor World Economy, the Washington Post reported on Thursday that the company enlisted a handful of external consultants to recruit politicians for onstage interviews. Among the consultants were former Trump advisers Jason Miller and Kellyanne Conway, as well as former Kamala Harris and Joe Biden adviser Adrienne Elrod. Miller is no longer on contract, but Conway and Elrod remain consultants at Semafor.
The contracts were intended to help secure the best guests for its flagship Washington event, a multimillion-dollar revenue-driver for the four-year old company. A spokesperson for Semafor said in a statement that âwe donât pay speakers and both our speakers and guests come for tough, fair, and independent interviews,â noting that âmany other media companiesâ employ consultants from across the political spectrum to recruit high-profile guests to attend their events.
But others saw it as a potential conflict of interest.
âBad look all around,â one anonymous media executive told Puckâs media analyst, Dylan Byers.
âWe shouldnât have to learn from court documents in a child support case that Semafor paid Jason Miller $100,000 because Semafor should have disclosed that,â the editor-in-chief of the left-leaning publication MeidasTouch posted.
On Friday, the publication updated 11 stories disclosing the companyâs financial relationship with Miller, Conway, and Elrod.
Maxâs view
The death of the previous generation of digital media startups like BuzzFeed News and Vice, and taught many in the news media a lesson: the free, ad-supported model of digital startup journalism is unsustainable.
In this environment, Semaforâs success has aroused some suspicion. At a moment when many media companies have struggled to stay afloat, Semafor has built a profitable news outlet thatâs still free for online users, prompting some skeptics to wonder what the real reason is for the businessâ growth.
As a four-year veteran of the company, I can say Semaforâs viability is the result of a hardworking and creative commercial team, fairly shrewd financial planning, and talented journalists producing an editorial product readers find to be important. In my time here, Iâve never been asked by any editor â explicitly or implicitly â to lay off a guest or subject for commercial reasons. Iâve watched our editors defend our critical coverage and skeptical questions at events from subjects that arenât always pleased with the content, and, when our offices were much smaller, I occasionally caught a glimpse of our revenue team navigating skittish sponsors who werenât always comfortable with sensitive topics in the news cycle. At Semafor World Economy earlier this year, which occurred weeks after the Iran war began, a number of high-profile guests dropped out after asking us if our journalists could avoid asking about the war. They were told no.
But media organizations are built on trust, and few institutions are less trusted in 2026 than the news media. America is cynical about the real and perceived coziness between politicians, lobbyists and the media companies that cover them. Compensating well-known political hands to ask important players to appear at events deepens that perception, even if they had zero influence on questions that the journalists asked once they got there.
Semafor is not wrong that the use of external firms to help with high-profile events isnât unusual. Many Washington organizations hire strategic public affairs firms for events that require executive wrangling. Two people familiar with the arrangement told me that former Harris adviser Shari Yost Gold had been enlisted for the White House Correspondentsâ Association dinner and Politicoâs major Sunday brunch (though unlike Conway, Yost Gold has not worked in the federal government). Bloomberg has enlisted FGSâ Capricia Marshall, a veteran of the Clinton and Obama White Houses, for its events.
âEvery public affairs firm offers this,â one industry insider told me.
But even if you accept the premise that it is a routine practice, Miller was not just a normal lobbyist; at the time that he was an adviser for Semafor, he was also working for Paramount to help secure its bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, and get the resulting Skydance megamerger approved by federal regulators.
The Semafor reporters and editors covering the deal considered Miller a part of that story, and were completely unaware that he was simultaneously being paid by the commercial side of the business. Miller has also been so close to the White House at times that itâs hard to consider him an outside actor. The directors of You Can See Everything are pushing back against new reporting about the filmâs controversial subject.
At the end of the documentary, which follows disgraced pharmaceutical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmesâ final days before going to prison, it is revealed that her husband, Billy Evans, negotiated â and later relinquished â the rights to payment for the familyâs role in the film.
Last week, The Hollywood Reporter published a story saying the film had omitted key details that made Evans look slightly better â principally, that he âdid retain rights to the payout on You Can See Everything after all.â
âThe payout still went out; it was just redirected to a charity, in a move that puts Evans in a slightly warmer light,â the outlet reported.
But during a Q&A Saturday night at the Darryl F. Zanuck Theater on the Fox studio lot, Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder said that the THR storyâs framing and wording was inaccurate, and that none of the documentaryâs subjects were paid, according to one person in attendance.
An A24 spokesperson declined to comment. But a studio source said that after Evans negotiated a profit participation deal, he ultimately relinquished his right to it. He and A24 mutually agreed to donate the proceeds to charity; as a part of the deal, the source said, Evans gave up his right to participate in the filmâs profits.
Oppenheim told the audience he was surprised by the story because The Hollywood Reporter is a âgreat publication.â
âIt is?â Fielder replied.
In an email, THRâs editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, said that the organization stood by its reporting, and that A24âs view âseems like a pretty semantic argument.â Further, he noted that THRâs Julian Sancton raised the story with Oppenheim during THRâs yet-to-be-released directorâs roundtable yesterday featuring the You Can See Everything director, plus Alex Gibney, Ron Howard, and Ava Duvernay, among others.

d7cbd5a20071.text:
Two years out from the âmanosphere election,â Joe Rogan remains American menâs most trusted voice in media, even as their electoral sympathies have swung back towards the Democratic Party. Thatâs according to a sweeping post-midterms report conducted by Precision Strategies and data firm Tunnl â titled Beyond the Manosphere: The Vote Moved Together. The Culture Didnât â that found an American populace riven by economic anxiety and split across race and gender lines.
Meanwhile, the survey found, thereâs no equivalent consensus voice for female audiences: Forty-nine percent of men (including 41% of Democratic men) said they trust Rogan, a greater share than any other figure polled, while no one person earned more than 22% of womenâs trust. One possible reason why: Sixty-three percent of men said they had no male role models to turn to in their lives, and the potent parasocial relationships Roganâs intimate longform chats can foster have inspired imitators from Theo Von to the US military. (See video podcaster aesthetic, above.)
âThe landscape of influence is changing, and understanding who people trust â and why â is becoming just as important as understanding what they believe,â said Tunnlâs Brent Seaborn.
Another data point from Precisionâs survey may disquiet journalists: Half of Republicans (51% of men, 50% of women) say the US government should be able to restrict media access for outlets that it believes to be biased, while a slight majority of the overall population say press access takes precedence.
On partisan politics, the report broadly tracked with other midterms polling: Americans, particularly Gen Z, shifted towards Democrats without developing an abiding loyalty to the Democratic Party as their fears about job losses and financial difficulties continued to mount. Forty-five percent of men under age 30 reported identifying as independents, despite that groupâs noted Democratic swing.
But some findings underscored a growing weariness with some of MAGAâs cultural agenda: Only 16% of men and 11% of women said the Trump administrationâs crusade against DEI had helped them in some way, while most reported no difference. And just 13% of women and 19% of men want more women to be full-time homemakers, something the Trump administration has sought to incentivize.
Americans also report varying attitudes towards AI usage: A fifth of respondents said theyâd used AI chatbots for companionship, with higher rates among younger Americans. Asian, Black, and Hispanic Americans also said they used AI more often than white Americans.

The highest-grossing film of all time, Avengers: Endgame, grossed $2.9 billion during its theatrical run. Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited next installment of the video game franchise, recorded $3.8 billion in sales on its first day.
In a rave review, The New York Times called it âa game about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful,â while The Washington Post gushed that the game was âan astonishing American epic.â The Miami Heat released special-edition Vice City jerseys.
The record-setting release represents the cultural acceptance of a franchise that was once the center of a backlash to violent video games.
During a press conference in 2005, then-Sen. Hillary Clinton said that the âdisturbing material in Grand Theft Auto and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children,â and The House of Representatives passed a resolution (by a bipartisan 355-21 vote) asking the FTC to investigate Rockstar, the studio that makes Grand Theft Auto. The late Sen. Joe Lieberman (who some GTA fans suspect is parodied by the weedy in-universe character âChaz Liebermanâ) denounced GTA for years.
The franchise outlasted and outgrew the backlash. The game added layers of narrative tenderness in between some of the brutal and comic setpieces, and expanded its range of playable tasks into the comically mundane, like painting your characterâs house and picking up groceries for his girlfriend. Years of research also tamped down some fears about links between video games and real violence.
Beyond some segments in conservative media, the criticism this time around has been fairly muted; in some corners of the incel right, the game has been criticized as, if anything, too respectful to women. The mainstream acceptance of GTA has even reached Fox News, where a former police captain, brought on to warn parents about GTAâs influence on children, admitted: âItâs probably a really fun game.â

873d35bb929d.text: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios has learned. A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity. Why it matters: Clayton, the nation's top intelligence official, will now coordinate cybersecurity policy as outages and reported cyberattacks expose vulnerabilities in America's digital infrastructure. Catch up quick: President Trump announced Thursday he was tapping Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to replace Sean Cairncross as national cyber director. Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser in the Office of the National Cyber Director until she is confirmed. Trump has increasingly turned to Clayton. He became director of national intelligence in August, and then Trump named him AI czar coordinating the government's approach to AI. Now he will temporarily lead the office responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy. What they're saying: "I'm excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director," Clayton said in a statement to Axios. "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate." The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks. The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks. Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's response, telling lawmakers Wednesday that the outages appeared to stem from unrelated technical problems and system upgrades. Driving the news: Clayton spent Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union," ABC's "This Week" and "Fox News Sunday," explaining recent technology disruptions and national security concerns. On CNN, he warned that Americans should expect more "glitches, gaps, interruptions in service" as government agencies and businesses modernize their systems. On ABC, Clayton maintained that recent widespread outages were neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture. On Fox News, he said AI is giving malicious actors more powerful tools and warned that critical infrastructure will need upgrades. Zoom in: Davies oversees the Pentagon's information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernize aging systems and protect military networks. She has nearly two decades of technology experience, including senior roles at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays Africa, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. Behind the scenes: Clayton has already worked closely with the Office of the National Cyber Director, National Security Council, National Security Agency and other agencies through his AI leadership role, according to the White House official.

a9c608bb8196.text: By — Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Kathy McCormack, Associated Press By — Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/lawyer-father-and-daughter-detained-by-ice-at-seattle-airport-were-traveling-to-family-baptism Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lawyer: Father and daughter detained by ICE at Seattle airport were traveling to family baptism Nation Nov 22, 2026 6:46 PM EST A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday. READ MORE: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media. The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed. The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said. "They've done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said of the father and daughter. "She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it's just heartbreaking." Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation's laws." During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said. WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said. She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred. "When somebody's charging at you, you're going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said. "It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they're not wearing a uniform, you don't know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what's going on." Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas. Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities." The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred." Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition. "The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/in-their-own-words-leaders-at-un-climate-talks-discuss-why-negotiations-ended-without-deal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter In their own words: Leaders at UN climate talks discuss why negotiations ended without deal World Nov 22, 2026 6:00 PM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — The words of negotiators and other leaders at the U.N. climate talks illustrate why the meeting failed to reach a final agreement. Each year the annual meeting seeks to hammer out a document known as a cover decision that gives direction on how countries around the world should fight climate change. But at the meetings in Turkey this time, negotiators could not overcome impasses on whether the final document should mention fossil fuels. The burning of fuels such as coal, oil and gas is what causes global warming. READ MORE: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels After reviewing a draft of the agreement released by co-host Turkey, a number of countries spoke up during the final meeting Sunday to say they couldn't accept a deal that failed to include wording on fossil fuels. Others spoke to reporters on the sidelines of the plenary sessions. The co-hosts Turkey and Australia also offered their thoughts. Below are the views of the players at COP31, in their own words. Darragh O'Brien, Irish climate minister speaking on behalf of the European Union's 27 countries: "I want to clearly state that the European Union and its member states object to this cover decision in both its iterations, and that we're saying that on behalf of our citizens, our member states, because these decisions go nowhere near the level of action or ambition that are required for us to tackle climate change, it is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel." Ana Aguilar, Panama's chief climate negotiator and a senior leader in the Climate Change Directorate at Panama's Ministry of Environment: "Our responsibility is not to negotiate the minimum threshold, our responsibility is to do what is right. Our responsibility is to protect the planet. ... This is an issue of justice. President, please allow us to explain briefly why Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed to commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it (relies) too much upon technologies such as, CCS capture storage of carbon, instead of calling for deep changes. And, three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback." The Marshall Islands delegation: "We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people and on providing the finance. To do this, we have been let down on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot. A response that will enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future." Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy and President of COP31 Negotiations Chris Bowen looks on before the plenary session at the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 22, 2026. Photo by Murad Sezer/Reuters The United Kingdom government: "The United Kingdom does not believe the cover decision proposed by the Presidencies meets the moment. We believe it moves us backward on the science when we must accelerate implementation. It has compromised where it should have presented bold collective ambition on climate action." Steven Victor, Palau's minister of agriculture, fisheries and environment: "Palau will support this text, not perfect as it is. We support this because there's clean electrification, there's ocean, there is finance. The only thing that we had issues with, and we were willing to engage in trying to improve it, is carbon capture. But unfortunately, others all forget about all these other good things and focus on one aspect of the negotiation." "Although there's no cover decision, there are these other work programs that got approved today and the last couple of days. So it's not a failure." Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations and minister of climate change and energy for co-host Australia: "Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that's disappointing, very disappointing. Ultimately, looking back, many parties were people of good faith who had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues ... An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels where some parties insisted that it must be mentioned. ... Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable. It's happening, it's happening at speed, and it's irreversible." The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. e604e64dcce1.text: To the surprise of many Democrats and even some of their former aides, Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar now consider themselves friends after their bitter clashes during their campaigns for president in 2020. Their journey from snarky tension to "real respect and friendship," as Klobuchar describes it, is a story of how two ambitious Democrats came to appreciate each other once the heat of a presidential primary had subsided. Why it matters: It's also a reflection of how Buttigieg — who's weighing another run for president — has become a well-regarded Democratic stalwart after many in the party viewed him as a presumptuous lightweight when he ran six years ago as a little-known 37-year-old former mayor of South Bend, Ind. "I'm sincerely grateful for Amy's friendship," Buttigieg, who was President Biden's transportation secretary, told Axios. "My appreciation has continually grown for her substantive leadership and sense of humor alike." "I know there are people that run against each other for president and literally hate each other," Klobuchar, who's in her fourth term in the Senate but will leave in January to become Minnesota's governor, told Axios. "That was far from the case for us." Flashback: A casual observer might see that as a bit of revisionist history. The Buttigieg-Klobuchar spats during the 2020 Democratic primary were some of the most vicious of that campaign. Aides from both sides can still quote the barbs, word for word. "I wish everyone was as perfect as you, Pete," Klobuchar sniped at one debate in Las Vegas before saying "You've memorized a bunch of talking points and a bunch of things." She added after the debate that Buttigieg was "haughty" and that "given the guy [Trump] we have in the White House, maybe you need someone who's a little more humble." Buttigieg repeatedly mocked Klobuchar for not remembering the name of the president of Mexico in an interview. He said Klobuchar was "not able to speak to literally the first thing about the politics of the country to our south." She shot back: "Are you trying to say that I'm dumb?" Asked today about those mutual attacks, Klobuchar says simply: "We both wanted to win." Many Democrats laughed that their feud appeared to continue into 2021, when the two wrote books with opposite titles — "Trust" by Buttigieg, and "Anti-Trust" by Klobuchar. When Buttigieg announced recently that he has a book coming out in January titled "Next," he texted Klobuchar: "Please tell me you're not putting out a book called 'Last.'" Zoom in: Klobuchar said their relationship has become increasingly warm through the years. "We kept consistently in touch, and not just over work. We had lunch when he first got into Washington. I remember I saw their apartment at the time," she said. "I also worked with him extensively on transportation issues." She added that she came to appreciate "how smart and even-keeled he is" at a time when "'hair on fire' is kind of cool to be." Buttigieg, who campaigned with Klobuchar during the 2026 midterms, said he's "looking forward to seeing all that she accomplishes as governor, and also to my next opportunity to join her at the Minnesota State Fair." What they're saying: A former Klobuchar aide told Axios that it's a "very Midwestern friendship story." "You meet someone new with a healthy dose of competition, skepticism, and a little frostiness. And along the way, you find out you genuinely like each other. That's Amy and Pete." What's next: Klobuchar, who has said she's not running for president, didn't want to weigh in on 2028 because she knows many people who are likely to run. As for what she thinks of Buttigieg's potential candidacy: "He has always been impressive."

7af0bf3d71f1.text: By — Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/automation-system-problem-at-delta-causes-flight-delays-as-americans-travel-for-thanksgiving Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving Nation Nov 22, 2026 5:40 PM EST Well over half of Delta Air Lines flights were experiencing delays Sunday afternoon following a problem with an automation system during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The airline said its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they continued to work to restore automation of a system that calculates weight to ensure an aircraft isn't too heavy to fly. Hours later, Delta said that system was once again working, though flights were still not back to normal. About 1,000 of the airline's flights were delayed as of Sunday afternoon. READ MORE: Travelers' concerns spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups grow, but few are dissuaded Earlier Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hourlong ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta's hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. Complying with the weight and balance limits of an aircraft is critical to flight safety, according to an FAA document, and going above the limit can compromise the structural integrity of the aircraft. The agency said on X that the delays weren't related to FAA air traffic systems. Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights. The Delta delays come as Americans have been encountering a growing number of problems with technology that are increasingly disrupting their lives. As of mid-afternoon Sunday, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 67%, or about 1,000, of Delta's flights were delayed. FlightAware said that 54% of flights out of the Atlanta airport were delayed while about 50% of flights destined for the airport were delayed. Delta said about 70% of the delays and cancellations noted by FlightAware were connected to the automation issue and the rest were because of inclement weather. By mid-afternoon Delta was apologizing for the delays, and said it was rebooking customers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed, and offering refunds if a flight was canceled. According to FlightAware, 2% of the airline's flights were canceled. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 7759c31f2325.text: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is quietly working on a book, two sources tell Axios — a project likely to fuel speculation about his making another run for the White House. Why it matters: DeSantis hasn't publicly acknowledged the book project or disclosed what it will be about. But writing a book is often the first step toward a presidential campaign, and it could give the term-limited governor a platform to lay out his vision for the Republican Party's future. DeSantis' state was a rare bright spot for Republicans in this month's midterms, as Democrats made historic gains across the nation. Driving the news: Word of DeSantis' book comes as he's become increasingly outspoken on a range of policy issues, particularly the economic and social impact of artificial intelligence — potentially offering clues about what the book might address. DeSantis has become a vocal critic of the potential dangers of AI, warning that it could eliminate jobs, threaten children's safety and privacy, and drive up electricity bills as data centers expand. DeSantis has pushed for an "AI Bill of Rights" and signed state legislation aimed at preventing tech companies from passing the costs of data centers on to residential consumers. His stance has put him at odds with the Trump administration's efforts to limit states' ability to regulate AI. DeSantis has emphasized affordability, immigration and education — issues likely to remain central to national politics long after he leaves office. Zoom out: DeSantis has made other moves that could keep him in the national spotlight after he leaves office in January. NBC News recently reported that DeSantis is preparing to launch a conservative think tank, which could enable him to retain a political and donor infrastructure. After the midterms, DeSantis embarked on a flurry of media appearances that resembled a victory tour, highlighting how Florida Republicans had largely escaped the Democratic wave. Yes, but: Some DeSantis allies are highly skeptical that he'll mount another presidential campaign after his unsuccessful 2024 bid. DeSantis has sent mixed signals about his political future. He downplayed the prospect of another presidential bid last year and, after the midterms, questioned how much a Republican president could accomplish with Democrats controlling Congress. He also disputed a report that he was building a campaign operation. But he hasn't ruled out a 2028 run, saying he'll assess the political landscape after leaving office. What they're saying: DeSantis' spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment about the book.
