bcdded504cd6.text: By — Samira Mehta, The Conversation Samira Mehta, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/todays-thanksgiving-holiday-was-invented-amid-the-civil-war-to-unite-a-divided-country Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country Nation Nov 22, 2026 5:18 PM EST This article originally appeared on The Conversation. It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence. READ MORE: A historian explains how the Pilgrims took over Thanksgiving – and who has been erased Children learn the story as if it were history — and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn — and, yes, turkeys. The idea of a straight line connecting that "first Thanksgiving" to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it. Creating today's Thanksgiving The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts. On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies — and later, states — declared fall holidays of thanksgiving, but did not coordinate with each other. The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale, who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey's Lady's Book, which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War. Godey's included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family. She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian Elizabeth Pleck, Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving, along with instructions for what the day could look like. READ MORE: The botany behind why cranberries became a Thanksgiving staple Godey's taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of "women's work," at a time when the Industrial Revolution was shifting the economy toward factories and other business, making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious. Hale's idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories — and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving. Hale petitioned five presidents to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country's origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War. Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist Sojourner Truth went door to door, collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops. The holiday caught on gradually. Given the Protestant origins of early Americans' feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day's emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated. Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey's Lady's Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine's op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims' courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier. Assimilating immigrants Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants. This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist Thomas Nast. "Uncle Sam's Thanksgiving Dinner," which appeared in Harper's Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey. The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the 13th Amendment formally ended slavery. Nast's image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called "Uncle Sam's Thanksgiving Dinner," that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller's disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American. But many Americans believed they could — although they demanded most immigrants give up their "Old World ways" and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation. WATCH: How teachers are debunking s

US immigration authorities faced criticism after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers as they were boarding a flight in Seattle.
The incident happened on Saturday morning local time at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), when ICE said a man and a woman, both Mexican nationals, were arrested for allegedly overstaying their visas.
It said that, during its arrest of the man - named as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza - "other travellers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers", which it described as a "federal crime and a felony".
The Port said in a statement that it was "outraged" about the incident.
Alaska Airlines said the incident happened during the boarding of one of its flights to Los Angeles and that it was not given "appropriate notice of the enforcement action".
It also said it was "concerned" about the arrests and recognised "how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests".
Both the airline and the Port of Seattle, which owns and runs the airport, said they were looking into whether the proper protocols were followed.
The Port said: "Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge."
According to ICE, the woman they arrested - named as Sofia Hernandez Mejia - "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Olia Catala, a lawyer for both Mendoza and Mejia - who are father and daughter - told local NBC affiliate King 5 News that they have "absolutely no criminal history".
"They're not fugitives. They're going through a legal process," Catala added.
The family has reportedly said that the ICE officers were in plain clothes and approached Mendoza and Mejia without identification.
"You can imagine if somebody's running at you who is not dressed as an officer, you don't know who they are," said Catala.
"So, there was a lot of panic, a lot of chaos, officers grabbing her, coffee spilling."
Video of the arrests taken by eyewitnesses appears to show two agents wearing masks, plain jackets and khaki trousers.
One eyewitness, John Gaedeke, who was also boarding the plane, told the Reuters news agency he thought the agents were passengers and that they "didn't have any identification".
Gaedeke said the agents "pointed and then they said now, and then they just lunged forward, didn't identify themselves" before "tackling" a man.
"Coffee definitely went flying, but to me, it looked like the passenger was holding it in their hand, and when they were tackled, it went everywhere. I didn't see anyone throw coffee," he added.
The Port of Seattle said it had "continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] on whether any of these protocols were breached".
According to the port's website, federal agents have access to airport property and port officials cannot interfere with operations. It says that the port has not historically been given advanced information about immigration enforcement, even when this takes place on its property.
Alaska Airlines said it is "required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials".
"We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible," it added.
Washington's Democratic Governor Bob Ferguson told a press conference on Saturday that "ICE is completely out of control".
"We need a system of immigration enforcement, border security that is effective, ethical, and humane and ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."
Katie Garrow, the executive secretary of MLK Labor - which represents flight attendants, pilots and airport employees - said the incident had been "so upsetting and disturbing to workers" that four of the six crew on the flight chose not to fly.
Deportations of people found to be in the US illegally have ramped up significantly under Donald Trump's presidency but the tactics used by ICE have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly.
Immigration raids have caused controversy in a number of US cities, including Minneapolis, Minnesota, where ICE agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti earlier this year.

The News
African governments have spent decades promising to turn their countries from exporters of raw materials into manufacturing economies. But concrete progress has been limited. Now, after years in which Chinese companies appeared mostly focused on extracting African resources, a new report shows they are pivoting to building a manufacturing presence across the continent.
At least $19 billion in Chinese manufacturing investment was made across 113 projects in 19 African countries between Sep. 2024 and June 2026, according to Development Reimagined, a consultancy. Thatâs nearly double the $10 billion pledged by Chinese companies at a 2024 China-Africa summit in Beijing, and is separate from $41.2 billion in mining and mineral processing investments identified in a companion study.
âWe last saw a big government push on Chinese FDI into Africa around 2015/2016, it seems now, post-COVID, that push is back, and it seems with more gusto than ever,â said Hannah Ryder, chief executive of Development Reimagined.
The renewed interest comes as Chinese manufacturers deal with excess capacity and intense price competition at home, while trade barriers in the US and Europe make these export markets harder to access. But itâs also clear Africa offers growing consumer markets, lower-cost production opportunities and, since May, duty-free access to China for 53 of 54 countries.
A bigger Chinese manufacturing footprint does not mean Africa is about to become the worldâs next industrial hub. The continentâs share of global manufacturing output has actually fallen to less than 2% today from about 3% in the 1970s, according to the UN Industrial Development Organization. Familiar obstacles still give investors pause including unreliable electricity, poor transport links, and limited access to finance.
But the opportunity remains significant: Global supply chains are shifting just as demand grows for locally made construction materials and clean-energy equipment. Chinese companies that already operate on the continent are expanding, Ryder said, suggesting the trend has commercial momentum.
The question to consider is whether African governments can turn that interest into something more durable with local suppliers, skilled jobs, and technology transfer. Attracting manufacturers is a start but ensuring more of the value stays in Africa is the harder test.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [thereâs punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,â he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.
In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,â he said.
Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (Â£1.5bn) investment in a new EastâWest Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the countryâs former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.
Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.
It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

Investec, a South African banking heavyweight, will expand its business by extending its corporate and investment expertise via local partners in at least three African countries, a top official told Semafor, betting it can tap fast-growing banking markets without joining the acquisition race among some of the continentâs biggest lenders.
The strategy, outlined by head of Investecâs South African unit Cumesh Moodliar in an interview, is a sharp contrast to the wave of dealmaking by African lenders seeking growth beyond their home markets. Rivals have pursued acquisitions, especially in East Africa, where Kenya has emerged as a battleground thanks to its role as the regionâs largest economy.
âWe have chosen not to go, at this point, bricks and mortar. We have chosen partnerships,â said Moodliar, adding â without naming them â the agreements were signed with banks in Kenya, Tanzania, and Ghana. Investec believes it doesnât need to own a bank to find out whether its expertise can travel.
Itâs a strategy Investec is also beginning to deploy in a different form at home after announcing an alliance with Shoprite, under which Africaâs largest grocer will use the bankâs license to support its expanding financial services.
The fifth largest South African lender, best known for servicing wealthy South Africans and businesses, expects to conclude a further partnership with a bank in Namibia. A series of large oil discoveries off Namibiaâs coast have attracted oil companies such as Dangote Refinery and promise to transform the country into sub-Saharan Africaâs hottest oil play.
Moodliar, who declined to disclose the identity of the partners, said the idea is that Investec would work with established local lenders, giving them the specialist capabilities the local partners may lack. These include global markets and corporate and investment banking expertise drawn from Investecâs South African and UK operations. Investecâs southern Africa business increased its operating profit 14% in the six months to the end of September, helping offset weaknesses in its UK operations.
The bankâs strategy lands amid a wider expansion by African lenders across borders as Western banks pull back from parts of the continent. European groups including BNP Paribas, Credit Agricole, SociÃ©tÃ© GÃ©nÃ©rale, and Standard Chartered, have sold or are selling their operations, citing tighter capital requirements, compliance costs, and sometimes weaker adjusted returns.
The beneficiaries include South African and Nigerian banks, with Nedbank buying a controlling stake in Kenyaâs NCBA, while Absa is looking for additional scale in Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia. Nigeriaâs Access Bank has also built its international footprint through acquisitions.

The News
Since the moment ChatGPT burst onto the scene in 2022, money has flowed freely into all corners of AI. Now investors are getting choosier.
âGetting air out of the tires is not a bad thing,â Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said in a Nov. 16 interview at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. âIâm not worried about it. I think selectivity is a good thing, and weâll see some discipline in how capital is allocated.â
Hyperscalers are working hard to keep their borrowing off their balance sheets, while the bonds of weaker players like neoclouds have plummeted. The Nasdaq is in correction territory after a tech selloff fueled by AI fears, a hot inflation print, and midterm results that returned Democrats to power.
Citi is near the center of every pressure point in global finance right now â an AI credit cycle that is starting to turn, a US-China trade truce set to expire in January, newly empowered Democrats who want to see Wall Street reined in, and a new class of AI-powered cyber threats that the biggest banks have spent the past six months trying to get ahead of.
Q&A
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Liz Hoffman: We have seen some real jitters in the AI debt world. Youâve been on Wall Street a long time. Does this feel like music slowing down to you?
Jane Fraser: When I look at and take a step back on AI, the genie is out of the bottle. This technology is transformative and that genie is not coming back in the bottle. What we are seeing in the capital markets side is selectivity. Capital has become a tad more scarce than it was before. Iâm not worried about it. I think selectivity is a good thing and weâll see some discipline in how capital is allocated.
But when you talk to the big hyperscalers, they are, many of them, working very hard to keep this debt off their balance sheets. Thereâs a lot of complicated structuring going on. When you talk to investors and lenders, they say [the companies] are money-good. Is there a mismatch between those expectations?
Weâre seeing companies, particularly the largest companies, being very thoughtful about their capital stack. They have plenty of options. Theyâre looking at bonds, theyâre looking at equity, theyâve got their own cash flow as well. What weâve seen this year has been a responsible building-out of that capital stack and making sure itâs well diversified.
In some different areas, thereâs a few more challenges. Obviously thereâs a large number of neoclouds; we could expect to see consolidation there. And companies that donât have strong cash flows, big bodies of data, diversified earnings, donât have strong assets behind them â thatâs a harder story for investors and banks to get behind.
The one bit Iâd add to the picture as well, there is a big refi wall coming up and that will happen in an environment where rates are higher, where liquidity is a bit tighter. The industry needs to be ready for that, not surprised by it.
One more on the markets: Youâve said the tech selloff was largely hedge funds getting spooked and de-risking some kind of technical things. The Nasdaqâs in correction territory. At what point does it start to feel a little more fundamental?
Certainly weâre not there at the moment. I think weâve had quite a week â you had the inflation print come in a bit higher. We had the [tech] outage[s] and we also had the market absorbing a pretty dramatic shift in the results from the US election. So there was a lot going on and it takes a bit of time to absorb that. What weâre seeing is the market doing that, in a market that was priced to perfection. We all felt that that was a challenge, so getting air out of the tires is not a bad thing.
A lot of people are expecting a major AI cyberattack sooner rather than later. The US banking system feels like a soft target. Citi was part of Anthropicâs Glasswing drill. What specifically did you see in those run-throughs that scared you?
Thereâs been a huge amount of work that has benefited many, because when we identify a vulnerability in a third-party application or indeed in open source, we catalyze getting the patches put in place, tested, and then made available for everyone. Weâve been in a six-month window where thereâs been an ability to do a lot of hardening and use the frontier models to our benefit to do that. I do think things are now changing and we are getting into much more of a disruptive phase, where similar capabilities â not quite at the cutting edge that you see with Anthropic and OpenAI models â are now getting into many more peopleâs hands. And not all of those have good intentions towards America, towards the world, towards different companies. So I believe that weâre in for a bumpier, more disruptive road.
Citi just got its securities license in China. Would you underwrite a Chinese AI deal right now?
This is a relationship where there is much to be gained from some collaboration and stability. Thereâs far too much for both sides to lose. To the extent that the national security interests and other things are addressed, we happily support companies that it is appropriate to have in our client base as a global and American firm. But where thereâs areas of competition, I donât think theyâll be coming to the US firms the same way.

It seems like whatever comes out of this Nvidia news cycle, thereâs going to be more scrutiny around where stuff is being shipped and how itâs being financed on its way there. We have a lot of diligence around our [anti]-money-laundering capabilities and put a lot of money behind making sure that weâre in compliance and helping our clients be in compliance as well. Trade isnât in retreat. It is, as you say, rerouting. Weâre seeing new corridors opening up. The most important thing in the world at the moment is to make sure that weâre building wha

078cab4f34b3.text: AI could put doctors who disagree with it in greater jeopardy of losing a malpractice suit, according to researchers who have tested some legal scenarios with mock juries. Why it matters: The public may still be wary about how AI is used in a hospital or doctor's office, but there's also a baked-in assumption that it's never wrong. That can put physicians in a bind when they disagree with an algorithm that flags an abnormality. Some may opt to order costly, possibly unneeded tests if they think it reduces their legal liability. Driving the news: Researchers are using simulated malpractice cases to examine how much AI influences the perception of whether a doctor exercised "duty of care" in treating a patient. The implications are significant: AI systems are used extensively to analyze medical images and improve the accuracy of diagnoses, and demand for tests is rising. But the systems invariably make mistakes. Experts say there are few established legal precedents for how AI might change the nature of malpractice liability in a field like radiology. Physicians are demanding more protections. The American Medical Association this month called for new federal and state legislation that shields clinicians from liability when AI products harm patients. What they found: In a series of simulated court cases, researchers discovered that mock juries were more likely to side with the plaintiff in a malpractice suit when AI disagrees with a radiologist than when AI agrees with them. One scenario involved a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage. When AI disagreed with the radiologist by flagging the condition when the radiologist didn't think there was one, the jurors sided with the plaintiff more often (72.9% of the time). A second case was built around a missed lung cancer on a CT scan that resulted in the patient's death. When AI was at odds with the physician by saying the patient had lung cancer when the doctor didn't think so, participants also sided with the plaintiff more often (78.7% of the time), the researchers wrote in NEJM AI . Yes, but: A smaller percentage of jurors ruled against the physician when they were given data on the AI system's error rate. Experts say that's significant because false positive readings are almost inevitable and can temper the belief that the technology is always right. What they're saying: "We're uncovering an unintended consequence of AI adoption," said lead author Michael Bernstein, an associate professor at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University. "AI can do a lot in radiology, but it's not all uniformly positive." Bernstein said one concern is the prospect of more "defensive medicine," in which clinicians overcorrect and order follow-up scans and exams, which can drive up costs and patient anxiety. Radiology is a closely watched specialty because AI is used extensively — and because missing an abnormality can be fatal. It's also among the fields with a high risk of being sued . But research on perceptions of blame is cutting across many medical disciplines and underscores how physicians who are expected to rely on AI to cut down on medical errors still have to know when to override the systems. "Because human operators are perceived as having control over the technology's use, responsibility unduly shifts to the human operator," Johns Hopkins researchers wrote in JAMA Health Forum last year. They noted that physicians were consistently viewed as more liable than AI vendors, health systems that adopted the technology or regulators. What we're watching: Bernstein and his colleagues found that double-checking AI results could reduce doctors' malpractice risks and prospective jurors' perceptions of whether a doctor met the "duty of care" standard. The question is whether they can find the time. The AMA is trying to shift the burden on AI developers and vendors — and pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data.

4a35ae62a525.text: The collapse of UN climate talks without an overarching deal is deepening doubts about the effectiveness of these summits — and bringing fresh calls for a shakeup. Why it matters: Warming is on pace to far exceed the Paris Agreement target of holding long-term temperature rise under 2°C above preindustrial levels — and the more ambitious 1.5°C goal has slipped away . 🏃 Catch up quick: The COP31 talks in Turkey ended Sunday without a high-level "cover decision" of wide-angle agreements and goals. Vulnerable island nations and the EU, among others, objected to a draft deal after some oil-producing countries blocked explicit endorsement of moving away from fossil fuels. ⚔️ Friction point: There was also pushback against proposed text that endorsed carbon capture as a major climate solution. Finance discussions also disappointed advocates, with climate think tank E3G noting that "little or no new and additional money reached the table." 🏀 State of play: Sunday's events reinforce criticisms that the decades-old summit process — which birthed the 2015 Paris deal — is not suitable for spurring policies that meet the scope of the problem. It could add urgency to years-long efforts to revamp how they work. "I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here," Simon Stiell, the top UN climate official, said as the talks closed, per Reuters. 🥊 Reality check: Ending the practice that decisions require consensus — which effectively gives veto power to individual countries and blocs — would be a steep uphill climb. Yes, but: There was some progress at COP31, per groups that track the granular talks. For example, the climate group E3G cites procedural advances on the "Just Transition Work Programme," an initiative created in 2022 to support workers and communities in the energy transition. And dozens of countries endorsed a pledge to bring electricity's share of global energy use up to 35% by 2035, compared to 23% today. 💭 My thought bubble: The failure in Turkey came just days after the Senate easily passed a permitting bill that would make it easier to build out renewables and fossil fuel projects. Competing views on the COP process and the permitting bill among advocates shows a wider tactical rift in climate and clean energy circles. For many activists, COP31's meltdown shows a dangerous failure to confront planet-heating fuels, and that thwarting them must be a central, science-guided policy aim. "In the same year that science warned we are on track to exceed the 1.5°C threshold, COP31 failed to face that reality head-on and name fossil fuels as the root cause of climate change," Bryan Bixcul of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change said in a statement. But for other advocates, the real action is with duller, nitty-gritty steps (like permitting reform!) that help competitive clean energy grow faster, and anti-fossil fuel red lines are a distraction or even politically counterproductive. What they're saying: "I may be too cynical but if this mess is what finally convinces people that it's not worth all this effort to get unanimous agreement on symbolic statements, maybe that's a blessing in disguise?," Columbia University climate economist Noah Kaufman posted on X . What we're watching: Keep an eye out for any signs that the fracas in Turkey will bring changes to how these COP summits unfold.

670c3d494be5.text: Democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin is moving to restrict candidates' ties to super PACs and dark-money groups in the party's 2028 presidential primary, a shift that could shake up the race for the White House. Why it matters: Most likely Democratic candidates for president were expected to rely on super PACs to boost their messaging — and go after other contenders. The DNC's new rules could complicate their plans and set up a clash between the party chair and soon-to-launch campaigns. Martin's plan will be a real-time test of whether party-driven campaign finance restrictions can function in a presidential primary that will follow a midterm election driven by billions in spending by PACs and dark-money groups. Zoom in: Under the rules that the DNC is announcing Monday, Democratic presidential candidates must disavow any super PACs or dark-money groups that either back them or attack their opponents in ads. If presidential hopefuls don't follow the guidelines, the DNC warns, they won't be allowed on the stage at primary debates. A DNC official said the change is backed by progressives such as Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), as well as more moderate Democrats such as Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison. For years, the party's left wing has pushed for party primaries to ban super PACs and dark-money organizations, a term for 501(c)(4) groups that aren't required to disclose their donors. Yes, but: It's not clear whether the DNC's shift will be substantive — or merely symbolic. Super PACs, which can raise unlimited amounts of money, already are barred by law from directly coordinating with candidates. Even so, such groups often work alongside candidates while remaining technically separate. The DNC rules stipulate that candidates must sign a pledge to disavow such funders. Super PACs could, however, continue to spend on behalf of candidates that distance themselves from them. In practice, though, Democratic presidential candidates often have blessed the super PACs set up to help them. In the 2020 primary, for example, Joe Biden's campaign effectively cleared the way for super PACs to have an active role by publicly ending its opposition to them. A pro-Biden super PAC launched soon afterward. In the 2012 campaign, then-President Obama's team also openly promoted a super PAC that championed him. The intrigue: The DNC is planning to put a tracker on its website keeping tabs on candidates' disavowals of any super PACs and dark-money groups that aid them, as well any complaints alleging that candidates aren't following the rules. The rules won't apply in the 2028 general election, the DNC says, or to political organizations that attack Republicans without backing a particular Democrat. Zoom out: A person close to Martin said "the party is looking to double down on successful messaging from the midterms opposing dark-money and the corruption of [Elon] Musk and other ultra-wealthy special interests, which resonated across the ideological spectrum." Martin signaled previously that he wanted to move in this direction. In August 2025 he introduced a plan to DNC members to explore limiting corporate and dark-money spending in the presidential primary. The DNC also is announcing Monday that it plans to hold a dozen debates during the presidential cycle: five in 2027 and seven in 2028. The first two debates will be in June and July of next year. Candidates will need to meet polling and fundraising requirements to qualify for the debates. Specific details for the early debates will be announced in January. The DNC also revealed the leadership of the party's debate planning committee: Longtime Democratic strategist Minyon Moore and DNC executive director Roger Lau will lead it, and the panel includes alumni from the presidential campaigns of Sanders, Obama and others. What they're saying: "Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle," Martin said in a statement. "The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we're announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House."

‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them
Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said.
Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’”
It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer.
Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit, Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t.
Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues.
Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment.
The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court.
Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.”
Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future.
“The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.”
The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “the world’s first and only” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices — from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors — that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance.
However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes.
There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data — is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect.
Monitoring Every Step
Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries received that service, known as “remote patient monitoring,” according to the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General. Medicare, the federal program covering older Americans and some with disabilities, paid medical providers $536 million for remote monitoring, more than double what it paid three years earlier. A review by the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker found about 300,000 adults with employer-sponsored insurance received at least one remote monitoring claim in 2023.
Medicare has proposed pulling back on some reimbursements after the department’s inspector general warned remote monitoring poses fraud risks: About 43% of patients in 2024 didn’t receive the full suite of services defined by the program — which includes educating the patient about the device and monitoring data for changes in health. The watchdog also cautioned that companies sometimes cold-call patients to offer and sign them up for devices they may not need.
The internet-connected devices may also pose risks to privacy or expose patients to unexpected consequences. In 2018, ProPublica reported that insurers watched the performance of CPAP machines and, determining some patients weren’t using them, denied coverage for replacement supplies such as masks.
In the case of Zimmer, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services spokesperson Christopher Krepich emailed KFF Health News that “CMS payment does not mean the agency endorses a manufacturer’s marketing claims or guarantees that a technology improves outcomes for every patient.” He said the agency regularly evaluates its reimbursement policies.

The predicted blue wave in the 2026 midterms not only appeared — it overperformed, with Democrats sweeping into majorities in the House and Senate. That sets up a new focus on health policy, with Democrats seeking to undo cuts imposed by President Donald Trump and the GOP-led Congress and advance their own agenda to increase coverage and lower costs. In this special episode, host Julie Rovner is joined by Mollyann Brodie, executive vice president and chief operating officer at KFF; Larry Levitt, KFF’s executive vice president for health policy; and Amanda Seitz, Washington health policy reporter for KFF Health News.
History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That’s certainly true of the coming fight over “Medicare for All.”
The midterm elections saw victories by several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there have cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act — which, despite incendiary politics, made incremental reforms — barely squeaked into law after similar disputes in 2009.
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
‘It’s Cosplay’
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase “Medicare for All” actually means. “It’s cosplay,” said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. “When you say ‘Medicare for All,’ people think ‘Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.’”
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF’s public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
“I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs,” she said of survey respondents’ support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. “I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program.”
Medicare Faces Headwinds
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump’s second term began. “Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs,” Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as “a socialist takeover of our healthcare system” — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It’s the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
A Deeper Dissatisfaction?
There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. ANDERSON, Ind.—Inside a cavernous former General Motors plant, furnaces melt scrap metal into high-purity metal ingots at one of the world’s largest magnesium recyclers.
Until recently, Advanced Magnesium Alloys Corp. was also the country’s largest emitter of sulfur hexafluoride, the most potent greenhouse gas on the planet.
In 2023, the company used 10 metric tons of the climate pollutant as a “cover gas” to prevent molten magnesium from burning. Once used, the gas was released directly into the atmosphere. The emissions from a plant with just 40 employees were equivalent to the annual greenhouse gas pollution of nearly 60,000 automobiles.
Then, in 2024, the company switched to a climate-friendly alternative. Its SF6 emissions fell to zero.
SF6 “served this industry for many years, but it’s also proven to be not very good for civilization,” said Arie Shaked, chief operations officer for Advanced Magnesium Alloys.
During a recent tour of the facility, Shaked walked past rows of freshly cooled, carefully stacked bricks of lightweight magnesium alloy that others will cast into automobile parts, such as steering wheels or car seat frames, or blend into aluminum alloys. A cloud of magnesium oxide dust rose from the open hatch of a nearby furnace as workers scrubbed the unit between production cycles.
SF6 is invisible, non-toxic and effective at preventing fires. The gas is also 24,300 times more effective at warming the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, pound for pound.
The U.S. has no federal regulations prohibiting its use in magnesium production and casting—the process of pouring or injecting molten metal into molds to form parts—and Indiana hasn’t enacted any rules of its own. But California and the European Union banned its use for those purposes roughly a decade ago.
The U.S. instead took a voluntary approach to reducing emissions. From 1999 to 2010, the Environmental Protection Agency and the International Magnesium Association worked with manufacturers to develop best practices with the goal of eliminating SF6 use by 2010. The effort included a 2008 study at Advanced Magnesium Alloys, where researchers tested alternative cover gases.
SF6 emissions from U.S. magnesium production and casting fell 74 percent between 1999 and 2010 but have since plateaued. In 2023, the most recent year for which data is available, emissions totaled 1.1 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, EPA records show. That’s equal to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of more than a quarter-million automobiles.
Before joining Advanced Magnesium Alloys, Shaked managed a magnesium planet in Israel, where he oversaw the company’s transition from SF6 to sulfur dioxide in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Although sulfur dioxide is widely used as an alternative cover gas, it is also corrosive and toxic. Drawing on that experience, Shaked was reluctant to make the same switch at the Indiana plant. The company twice tested an alternative, fluorine-based cover gas, but neither trial succeeded.
Shaked said low winter temperatures, incorrect gas mixtures or insufficient amounts of the gas may have contributed to the failures.
A few years ago the company began testing the fluorine-based gas again, initially hoping it might work for part of their process. But after experimenting with different volumes and concentrations, they found the gas, known as BestSolv Zulu, could replace SF6 throughout the plant. The company is now seeking carbon credits for its emissions reductions. It remains unclear how potential revenue from the credits will compare to the cost of the transition, Shaked said.
While Advanced Magnesium Alloys transitioned off SF6, other Midwest manufacturers, many of whom supply the automotive industry here in one of the nation’s major industrial regions, continue to rely on it.
Magnesium Products of America, a die caster in Eaton Rapids, Michigan, released 6 metric tons of SF6 in 2024, according to data the company reported to the EPA, making it the largest emitter among magnesium producers in the country that year. However, the company also used about 7 metric tons of an alternative, climate-friendly cover gas, allowing it to reduce the amount of SF6 it would otherwise have needed.
Jonathan Weiler, chief engineer for Meridian Lightweight Technologies, its parent company, confirmed the figures and said the company aims to eliminate routine use of the climate pollutant at its Michigan facility within three to five years. The company also operates plants in Canada, where it reduced SF6 use by more than 90 percent since 2023, said Weiler, who is also the president of the International Magnesium Association.
Terves, a magnesium and aluminum alloys producer in Euclid, Ohio, emitted 3.7 metric tons of SF6 in 2024, according to EPA data based on information submitted by the company. But Andrew Sherman, Terves’ founder and chief technical officer, disputed the figure, saying the company only emitted a fraction of that amount. Sherman did not respond to questions about whether the company plans to reduce its reliance on SF6.
Spartan Light Metal Products in Sparta, Illinois—one of the first magnesium casting companies to join the EPA’s SF6 emissions reduction partnership in the late 1990s—released 5.3 metric tons of SF6 in 2024. The company did not respond to requests for comment.
Auto manufacturers, the largest consumer of cast magnesium in the U.S., also had little to say.

The House Democratic campaign arm is trumpeting its role in the partyâs big wins this cycle by encouraging top recruits to run, as House Democrats prepare to take their biggest majority in decades.
âI think you know the reality is that the committee is often the first call or typically the most convincing to get most of these folks to run. And I was happy to be a lot of their first conversations about â¦ running and what that looked like,â said DCCC National Political Director Brooke Butler.
She pointed to recruitment successes, like incoming Reps. Christina Hines of Michigan and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania, both of whom ran in districts that were top DCCC targets this cycle. Butler said before Hines launched, she listened to the Michigan Democratâs âquestions, hesitancies, and things like that, and encouraged her to go for it.â
Party leaders also encouraged the campaigns of some repeat candidates who came up narrowly short in previous cycles, like incoming Reps. Christina Bohannan of Iowa and Janelle Stelson of Pennsylvania, Butler said. Despite some intraparty drama over the DCCCâs backing of certain candidates in contested primaries this cycle, Butler said, the committee felt that all of the candidates they backed could win.
It was ânot the case that the DCCC was ever going to give up on or not get behind anybody,â she said.
She also pointed to Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, as an example of a successful party-backed first-time candidate. The DCCC and party leaders intervened in that primary to ward off a candidate accused of making antisemitic statements.
Democrats face an expansive map to defend next cycle, including some incoming lawmakers who werenât even on party leadersâ radar. But the broader House battleground has shifted, with Maineâs 2nd Congressional District, set to be the bluest state held by Republicans when Rep.-elect Paul LePage takes office.
The future House battleground was âa lot of getting a sense of the opportunities come 2028, and then obviously we have a lot of defense we have to do as well. So [weâre] making sure we can reelect a lot of the people that we were able to get here,â Butler said. And with runoff elections still to come in Louisiana, âI never could write anything off, given what we saw, come Tuesday,â she said.

Oregon Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley isnât making it easy on himself as he pitches Democratic colleagues on his proposal to alter the Senate rules.
Thatâs because many of them are perturbed by his decision to block a vote on a managerâs amendment to the bipartisan permitting reform bill that just passed the Senate.
âThe irony was not missed,â said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., one of the billâs Democratic authors.
Without commenting on the specifics of Merkleyâs rules reform proposal, Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, said he âdid not like itâ when Merkley objected to the bipartisan amendment, after other senators prevented a vote on banning data centers from public land.
âI couldnât understand what the rationale was. The bill was going to pass. So why not make it better? It didnât compute for me,â King said.
Merkleyâs rules reform proposal, with Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., would fast-track popular bills out of committee to the floor; his proposed fix wouldnât have applied to the permitting bill because it didnât go through the regular committee process, according to a Merkley spokesperson.Â
âThe proposal is premised on the idea that bills receive special fast-track status only if there is robust, bipartisan support from members of the committee,â the spokesperson said.
âDirtyâ or fair play?
The Democratic anger at Merkley is real. Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., called it âdirtyâ and said that Merkley blocked âa largely Dem amendment that would have improved the bill significantly in the hopes that [the] bill is so unpopular that it will die in the House.â
One Democratic senator who opposed the permitting bill told Semafor that the failure to attach the managerâs amendment would ultimately tamp down support for the bill among progressives, making it trickier in the House. But not all Democrats feel that way.
âPeople fight by the rules that we have. I donât think thereâs ever an element where people are unilaterally disarming,â said Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., who has expressed interest in Merkleyâs rules reform.
So has Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the job of Democratic leader and has endorsed Merkleyâs package. Of course, Schumer is highly likely to win the leader race â and Merkley has endorsed Van Hollen, which wonât build goodwill with next yearâs probable majority leader.
GOP support
Current Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he âreallyâ likes the idea of getting rid of time-wasting procedures and making it easier for bipartisan bills to reach the floor. But heâs bearish on getting a deal with Schumer to vote on that before the next Congress, citing the dwindling calendar.
âItâs getting impossible to do anything around here,â Thune said in an interview. âI agree with Daines that if you donât do something to modify the rules around here, one side or the other at some point is going to blow up the filibuster.â
Asked if Merkley endorsing Van Hollen hurts the effort, Thune demurred: âYou observed that.â

AI is already reshaping the US economy, staunching job growth in white-collar industries and making it harder for young Americans to find entry-level jobs, according to a new report shared first with Semafor.
The report â prepared by the group RAISE US, led by former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo, and the Burning Glass Institute, a labor research think tank â found that, overall, white-collar industries have 1.5 million fewer jobs than they would have had under pre-pandemic trajectories.
In industries that use AI widely, the number of early-career opportunities shrank 3-8% on average between 2021 and 2026.
Middle-skilled jobs that involve office and administrative work fell by 780,000 between 2023 and 2025, according to the report.
âThis analysis should be a wakeup call to leaders from Washington to Silicon Valley that we need to act now to prepare our workers for the transition to an AI economy,â Raimondo said.
She launched her group with former GOP Indiana Gov. Eric Holcomb to help the US workforce adapt to the AI economy.

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., plans to introduce a resolution when Congress returns making clear that Congress must not âbail out corporations and wealthy investors taking speculative bets on the AI boom at the expense of working families, should the AI industry falter,â a source familiar with the matter first told Semafor.
Schiff would be the first senator to do so, and his plans are a signal that Democrats think harping on AI companiesâ precarious financing is a message that will resonate with voters wary of AI and corporate power.
Others on Capitol Hill have already been pushing a âno bailouts for AIâ message: In the House, Reps. Greg Casar, D-Texas, and Maxine Waters, D-Calif., introduced a similar resolution last month. And Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said last year that âshould this bubble pop, we should not be entertaining a bailout.â
Schiff wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed last week that billionaires should not expect Congress to help them like during the 2008 housing crisis: âCongressional majorities should be clear: We wonât bail them out.â

The Democratic National Committee will require candidates to denounce âdark moneyâ if they want to be part of presidential debates next year, according to updated party rules released on Monday.
Most of the DNCâs debate guidelines will carry over from 2020, the last wide-open primary. The first debate will take place in June, a mix of poll and donor numbers will be required to get onstage, and debates will be broken up over two nights if the number of qualified candidates becomes unwieldy.
Thereâs one new rule for this year: a Fair Campaign Practices Pledge involving commitments not to accept backing from super PACs and not to form a joint fundraising committee with the party.
Both changes stem from 2016, when supporters of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., accused the DNC of favoring Hillary Clinton; Sanders has since called on the party to restrict âdark money.â

The State Department plans to bypass objections from leading Democrats to move forward with distributing more than $170 million in health assistance to three countries in Africa, Semafor has learned.
The decision comes after the State Department sent a notification to Congress about the planned funding, which is being sent to Kenya, Malawi, and Uganda, at the end of August. Days later, Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Foreign Affairs Committee placed holds on distributing the funds. The State Department says that the Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy provided briefings for relevant congressional staffers on the topic, and it ultimately requested the committees lift their holds by October 31.
Now, the department says it will push past the holds and begin obligating the funds anyway.
âThe Trump administration is determined to follow through on its commitment to these bilateral health agreements,â State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement to Semafor, criticizing what he described as an attempt by Democrats to âblockâ the funds and arguing that it will go to âcritical health effortsâ like HIV treatment and malaria prevention.
Health aid shifts
The State Department has been negotiating bilateral agreements with African countries to provide health aid after drastically cutting back foreign assistance with the closure of the US Agency for International Development. Democrats have criticized the Trump administration for cutting back traditional health assistance and not releasing details about its bilateral deals with other countries.
The hold on the funding stems from concerns from Democratic lawmakers about the way the State Department was handling government-to-government financing and was meant to ensure the department is meeting requirements laid out in appropriations legislation, said a Democratic aide.
âInstead of funding the corrupt NGO industrial complex that wasted taxpayer money with no end in sight, we have reformed foreign assistance to focus on partnerships,â Pigott said. âWe are encouraging burden sharing and capacity building so that countries can take control of their own health infrastructure.â
In September, Emily Bass, a writer focused on global health policy, argued on Substack that the departmentâs congressional notification was overly âbrief,â adding that it âeffectively asks appropriating lawmakers to take it on faith that USD$176 million will be well spent in Malawi, Kenya and Uganda, which failed a 2026 US government assessment of âcontrol of corruption and accountability.ââ
The State Departmentâs move overrides the committeesâ normal oversight process, though itâs not a first for the Trump administration. In September, the State Department redirected $52 million in military aid to Latin American countries despite objections from top Democrats on both foreign affairs committees.
Nicholas Wu contributed to this report.

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna GnassingbÃ© as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).
DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.
The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.
On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.
