The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
- Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external
- The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
- Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths â that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible â it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.
Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts â countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (Â£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
COP31 had some good news
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits â money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases â will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.
Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.
Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.
In a Telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.
Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.
Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".
Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".
Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".
The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.
In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.
Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.
All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.
He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.
These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.
How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.
Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.
Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.
That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.
As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.
Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.
The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”
A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic â which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries â are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (Â£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco â no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles â be preparing for a possible crash?
One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come downâ¦ and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.
One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism â which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness â are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

New questions are being raised about ICE's training and enforcement tactics after officers arrested a father and daughter as they were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The incident comes as The New York Times reports new findings from the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general. Geoff Bennett discussed more with Hamed Aleaziz of The New York Times.
Seattle airport arrests renew protests over ICE enforcement tactics
Read the Full Transcript
Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.
Geoff Bennett:
New questions are being raised tonight about ICE's training and enforcement tactics after officers arrested a father and daughter as they were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport this weekend. The confrontation was captured on video by several passengers.
The daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and the father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, say they were traveling to California for a family baptism when officers forcibly removed them from the jet bridge. Their attorney says the two have been seeking asylum since 2015. ICE says both had overstayed their visas and alleges that Sofia threw hot coffee at officers. That's not captured on video, and her lawyers say the coffee spilled.
Woman:
(SPEAKING IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE) We have a work permit.
Geoff Bennett:
The incident comes as The New York Times reports new findings from an upcoming investigation by the Homeland Security Department's inspector general. The report details sweeping changes to ICE's training program under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, including allowing thousands of new recruits to complete basic training online and sharply reducing the number of hours of instruction they receive.
Joining us now is Hamed Aleaziz, who covers immigration and the Department of Homeland Security for The New York Times.
Thanks for being with us.
Hamed Aleaziz:
Thanks for having me.
Geoff Bennett:
What does this investigation reveal about how ICE is preparing agents to carry out immigration enforcement?
Hamed Aleaziz:
Yes, what this investigation reveals is that, as the Trump administration undertook a massive hiring blitz in the last year, hiring thousands of new officers, they cut down on training substantially, not only for those new recruits who did not have past law enforcement experience.
They cut training for those folks by nearly 50 percent. But also for those individuals who had past law enforcement experiences, that training changed substantially. They went from a in-person one-month training program to allowing these individuals to do their training virtually.
And what that led to was a lot of officers actually zooming through their training, some of them within a day.
Geoff Bennett:
And as we have seen in this incident and others, these agents are given enormous authority, including the authority to detain people and use force. What did investigators find about whether these recruits were actually prepared to exercise that force?
Hamed Aleaziz:
Yes, I actually ended up speaking with some of the instructors, some of the ICE instructors who were teaching these new recruits, to get their sense of how they felt this new training regimen was going.
And many of them were very concerned. One of them called it a catastrophic failure. Another said that this could be a potential liability for the agency down the line.
Geoff Bennett:
Were there any internal warning signs, based on your reporting? Did anyone inside ICE raise concerns about the training changes?
Hamed Aleaziz:
Well, earlier this year, there was a ICE whistle-blower who actually had left the agency and came out and said that the recruits were getting substantially less training than necessary.
And he basically protested this idea that what ICE had done here was appropriate. That is probably the most significant ICE official to actually come out and say this. Otherwise, what was happening was really unclear inside of the agency. There wasn't any type of explanation that these investigators found as to why these changes were being made the way they were.
In fact, the head of training, when they went to go interview him, he said that his decision was -- he was basically he insinuated that he was told by the deputy director of ICE to make these changes and that those changes were supported by Kristi Noem her adviser, Corey Lewandowski.
Geoff Bennett:
Meantime, the current DHS secretary acknowledges that some of these decisions need to be reversed. Can additional training realistically close the gaps?
Hamed Aleaziz:
Yes, that's what these -- that's what the DHS I.G. wants. The I.G. wants ICE to go back and to essentially retrain these officers, to put them through extensive training to allow them to do their job competently.
But the main issue with that is that ICE right now is under pressure, as they have been the entire Trump administration, to arrest thousands of people. They want major -- this White House wants major arrest numbers, deportation figures. And so if you take these officers off of the streets and into training programs that will last weeks, months on end, that could really put a dent in those numbers that this administration wants.
Geoff Bennett:
Major numbers. And do they also want major spectacles like what we saw at this airport, the Seattle-Tacoma Airport? I mean, why else would someone be detained while they were boarding a plane like that?
Hamed Aleaziz:
Well, for the past year, ICE has undertaken this really unprecedented enforcement spree at American airports.

Severe drought pushes millions in Afghanistan deeper into crisis

Afghanistan is in the throes of a severe economic crisis. By the end of last year, nearly three-quarters of the population were living in poverty, according to the United Nations. Now millions of Afghans are also facing drought and have no access to clean drinking water.
Special correspondent Leila Molana-Allen and videographer Eric O'Connor traveled to the northern Bamyan province, one of the country's poorest regions, and have this report.
Leila Molana-Allen:
The rolling green hills of Bamyan. Each morning, farmers cut through the fields in the shadow of the now-destroyed great Bamyan Buddhas, blown up as false idols by the Taliban in 2001.
This was once Afghanistan's agricultural heartland, but now swathes of it are bone-dry. Yasin and his family have farmed these lands for generations. But each of the past five years, another one of their fields has shriveled, dry and brittle, its soil unplantable. Now they have just one field left.
Yasin, Afghan Farmer (through interpreter):
We work very hard, but we get no yield. This year we had no harvest at all. Everything we have depends on agriculture. If our crops don't do well, we have nothing. It didn't rain this year either. And the people here have suffered very heavy losses.
Leila Molana-Allen:
He doesn't know how much longer they can survive here. Several of his neighbors have already left, fleeing to the city.
Yasin (through interpreter):
There's a person down there who unfortunately had land, but couldn't cultivate it or farm it. So he left.
Leila Molana-Allen:
The farming methods here are so basic that each field depends on its closest water source. All they need is a rudimentary piped irrigation system to help distribute the water more evenly. But with no support from the government or aid agencies, these communities can't begin to afford to build one.
Yasin (through interpreter):
We worked very hard and dug canals so that water could reach our land, but it didn't work. If we can't get water through another route, we will be forced to move away.
Leila Molana-Allen:
U.N. documentation of the water shortage says half the residents of Yasin's district, Yakawlang, have left this year, while tens of thousands are leaving central Bamyan altogether.
Further up the hill, Mah Gol and her children are still getting water to their fields. But as the drought creeps closer, she fears what will happen when it catches up to them.
Mah Gol, Afghan Farmer (through interpreter):
Our area is still better because we have some water, but many other people didn't get enough. Their fields are drying up, and their crops are being damaged.
Leila Molana-Allen:
Women have traditionally farmed alongside men in this region. As work for women becomes increasingly scarce under Taliban rule, holding on to this way of life to support her children is more crucial than ever.
Mah Gol (through interpreter):
Things have only recently become like this. Under the previous government, there were job opportunities for men and women. There were schools, and girls could go to school and work. People are afraid, and their economic situation is very bad. There's no money. That puts a lot of pressure on families and causes problems and violence within families.
Leila Molana-Allen:
More than half of Afghanistan's provinces have faced severe drought in the past year, and with aquifer stores dropping by more than a quarter, NGOs warned the country may run out of groundwater altogether by 2030.
This park was once a place to gather for Bamyan's women. Now it and the women's market it once hosted are dying. The woman who founded it, Benazir Ebrahimi, says her countrywomen now have graver concerns.
Benazir Ebrahimi (through interpreter):
They're not thinking about where they can go for recreation. They're simply thinking about what they can do to make sure they and their children don't go hungry.
Leila Molana-Allen:
The U.N. says 22 million people in Afghanistan currently need humanitarian assistance. But as of mid-2026, only 14 percent of the $1.7 billion needed to support them this year had been funded; 3.7 million children across the country are now facing acute malnutrition due to poverty and water scarcity.
The water shortage is now so dire. People are spending a significant portion, in some cases up to 30 percent, of their income just to buy clean drinking water. The average Afghan salary is now around $200 a month.
Benazir Ebrahimi (through interpreter):
One bottle of drinking water costs around $2. Some people can't afford to buy bottled water, so they're forced to use water from the streams, which may be full of germs, dust, and waste.
Leila Molana-Allen:
Benazir has a newborn. Clean water is absolutely essential, or her breast milk will make her baby sick. She says she's been sick for the past two months because of the water quality. And now she tries to only use bottled water, but they're struggling to afford it.
Benazir Ebrahimi (through interpreter):

Leila Molana-Allen:
For others here, affording bottled water is a distant dream.

One thing Haley Harman learned quickly as a military spouse stationed overseas is that the commissary "is not the place to go for produce."
She and her husband have been stationed in both South Korea and Japan in their four years of marriage. In both places, "a lot of the items that are sent to the base arrive expired since it's being shipped from the states."
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
She learned many seek produce from local farmers off base. But transportation options can be limited; the base where Harman is stationed only authorizes one vehicle per family. And many families, including Harman's, also rely on U.S. food assistance, which isn't redeemable at off-base markets or grocery stores.
"We are on WIC (the USDA's Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children). My husband is 10 years into his career and an E6" — a midlevel enlisted position — "and we still qualify," Harman said. "I can't think of any other career where you work for 10 years and you still qualify for food assistance."
Harman is among the more than 1.4 million spouses and dependents of active duty U.S. military service members around the world. Issues with housing, employment, childcare and healthcare can greatly affect quality of life.
These challenges have long been well known within the military community, and while legislative efforts have addressed some of them, spouses interviewed by PBS News say there is more to do to improve quality of life for military families.
In nearly a dozen interviews and more than 230 responses to a callout from PBS News, military spouses highlighted maintaining employment as one of the biggest challenges they've faced, with more than half of all responses referencing the issue. Also cited: challenges navigating the Exceptional Family Members Program, meant to support family members with special medical or educational needs, and the financial burdens of permanent change of station (PCS) moves.
Committees and initiatives focusing on this goal have existed under previous administrations, and President Donald Trump has ordered his own. The President's Military Spouse Commission, created via executive order in August, has started to meet monthly to identify quality of life challenges in key areas, such as employment, education and deployment-related support. A "state of the spouses" report is expected sometime this month.
While this commission is tasked with identifying issues and solutions, new policies would have to be implemented by Trump or Congress. There is skepticism around how much a commission like this can accomplish with only about two years left in Trump's presidency.
"Most commissions produce wonderful summaries of the challenges; few are effective at implementing the results impactfully," said Retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, now senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
As the commission kicked off its work, and as a new Congress prepares to take office, PBS News asked military spouses about what issues matter most to them, and what they'd like to see. Here's a closer look at what they said, and what's ahead.
What is the President's Military Spouse Commission?
The President's Military Spouse Commission is a two-year advisory commission chaired by Jennifer Hegseth, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's wife. All of its members are spouses of senior leadership from each military branch and the Department of Homeland Security.
Past commissions and advisory boards have fallen under the Pentagon and advised the acting secretary, so "being really proximal to the president and advising directly to the president gives them a visibility and insight that they haven't had before," said Retired Air Force Lt. Col Doug Lindsay, now a deputy editor at Military.com.
The commission "explicitly places military spouse and family quality-of-life issues within the broader context of military readiness and retention," he added.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act designated roughly $9 billion to military quality-of-life issues. However, this commission won't be in control of where that money goes.
"Some of these are policy issues which can be done directly, either through the president or through the other judicial bodies. But some will require resources, which means that these recommendations will then have to flow through Congress for the appropriate funding," Lindsay said.
According to the executive order establishing the commission, each member will serve unpaid, but may receive travel reimbursement.
In a statement to PBS News, a White House spokeswoman reiterated that military spouses "are essential to the strength, readiness, and retention of our military."
"President Trump has rebuilt America's military and is ensuring that the amazing families who support our service members receive the support they deserve," she added.
Montgomery, who ran a federal commission on cybersecurity, is more skeptical about what results the commission can produce.
"The challenge is that changing laws requires congressional buy-in on the front end," he said. "Ours was considered successful and drove a lot of legislation because we actually had four serving congressmen on it."
Montgomery said if recommendations from the commission are implemented, "it might not even have an impact before the current administration is out of office." Increasingly, he added, "administrations seem to ignore what their predecessors had 'in process.'"
Members of the military community have noted that all the spouses on the commission are married to senior-level service members, raising questions about how well they will reflect the experience and needs of the average service member and their family.
"I think there just needs to be due diligence" that recognizes experiences can differ greatly between ranks, Lindsay said.

The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

On Saturday night, the midnight skies over west Alabama lit up as a massive fireball leaped hundreds of feet in the air, visible from more than 50 miles away.
The source of the explosion, officials later confirmed, was a segment of Southern Natural Gas Company pipeline running through rural Sumter County, about eight miles east of the Mississippi state line in Alabama’s Black Belt.
The explosion occurred at approximately 11:27 p.m. in an empty field near the unincorporated community of Ward. The blast was significant enough to be visible on weather radar, according to local meteorologists.
No injuries were reported, according to the company and local officials.
Shortly after the explosion, Mayor Renee Ward Pringle of nearby York, population 2,400, said she’d heard from many residents asking about the seemingly apocalyptic views of a massive blaze on the horizon.
“We understand the concerns of our citizens, especially with the light from the flames being visible from York,” Pringle wrote on social media. “While the preliminary information is encouraging, we do not want to make any premature assurances regarding public safety.”
Southern Natural Gas Company is jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Southern Company and operated by Kinder Morgan. The company operates about 7,000 miles of pipelines distributing fossil gas throughout the Southeast, including to major gas-fired power plants operated by Southern Company and its subsidiaries, Alabama Power, Georgia Power and Mississippi Power.
Kinder Morgan described the explosion as a force majeure incident, meaning the company claims the incident was caused by circumstances beyond human control, which it characterized as “a natural gas release and fire on a pipeline segment.” No further information on the cause of the explosion has been released as of Monday afternoon.
In response to questions about the explosion, the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration confirmed to Inside Climate News that its staff has been deployed to the site of the pipeline failure and that the agency’s investigation is ongoing.
Portia Shepherd, executive director of the environmental justice nonprofit Blackbelt Women Rising, said she sees the explosion as a warning shot.
“This could have happened in any community along this pipeline,” Shepherd said. “These explosions are happening again and again, and they want to expand.”
Federal regulators issued orders forcing SNG to take corrective actions following explosions along other sections of the pipeline in 2022 and 2026, records show.
Still, SNG plans to expand the pipeline at issue as part of a multi-billion project called South System Expansion 4 that would increase the company’s pipeline capacity by about 1.3 billion cubic feet per day—enough methane to fill nearly 15,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Shepherd and other community leaders across Alabama’s Black Belt are opposed to the expansion, which they have said will lead to increased risks for communities that are already suffering.
In October, attorneys for the Southern Environmental Law Center filed a lawsuit on behalf of impacted landowners and nine nonprofits across the South, including Shepherd’s, asking a federal court to review and set aside a ruling by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission that authorized the major methane pipeline expansion across Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia.
Megan Gibson, an attorney for SELC, said that Saturday’s explosion is a “stark reminder that the risks of building another pipeline alongside aging, existing pipelines are very real for the families and communities living along these routes.”
Gibson called on FERC to act immediately to address safety concerns raised by the incident.
“In our ongoing challenge to FERC’s approval of the massive SSE4 expansion of this aging infrastructure, we raised serious concerns about the dangers of constructing new high-pressure pipelines alongside existing lines with a history of failures—and FERC should immediately order a stop to any and all construction activities and fully examine and address these risks, including in partnership with the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration,” Gibson said.
The explosion has also raised concerns about the passage of federal permitting legislation that would cut red tape for major energy infrastructure projects like SSE4.
“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, will fast track pipelines like this one, hindering our ability to have a voice in the process and putting more Alabama communities in immediate danger,” the Alabama Rivers Alliance, an environmental nonprofit, wrote in a statement in the wake of Saturday’s explosion.
Shepherd said she’s grateful that no one was injured in the incident, but residents in Sumter County and across the Black Belt that she’s spoken with are concerned that no comprehensive safety plans exist for when incidents like this happen. Even when limited planning is in place, she said, companies and public officials don’t do a good job of informing the public about what they should do in case of an emergency.
“Where is the plan that these communities can actually see?” Shepherd asked. “Where are the safety measures?”
In the end, Shepherd said she doesn’t believe that companies like Kinder Morgan have communities’ best interests at heart.
“These companies’ executives need to look at these communities as places where they would actually live, because I think they’d be doing a better job if these risks were in their community,” Shepherd said.
“But the reality is these discussions don’t come up in their community, because they don’t let companies do stuff like this in their communities. It’s always us. We’re the ones who get dumped on.”

Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
The company had come under pressure from Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to reverse course and bring Huang back.
But Democrats have accused the Trump administration of selling out national security for financial gain. Huang is due to testify before Congress in early December.
His comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory.
Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.
But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.
Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.
In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
"Probably so," Trump said.
Congress vows investigations into Huang and Nvidia
The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.
Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".
"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.
Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
Sen Tom Cotton, fellow Republican who represents Arkansas, vowed that Congress would investigate.
"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," he said.
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already promised to launch Nvidia investigations.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".
Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a member of the House foreign affairs committee, also condemned the move in a statement to the BBC as "premature" before multiple investigations are concluded. Fellow Democratic Representative Andre Carson, a member of the House intelligence committee, told the BBC that "Congress needs a full accounting of whether any controlled technology was diverted" to China.
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.
Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.
Trump's personal Nvidia investments
Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.
A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (Â£18m and Â£66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
The BBC has contacted the White House.
Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

US Representative Jimmy Gomez has said he will resign from Congress after an ethics committee said it found credible evidence that he engaged in sexual misconduct, according to CBS News.
A report released on Monday by the House Ethics Committee stated that Gomez, a California Democrat, made "unwelcome sexual advances" towards a House staff member, "disregarding the power imbalance" between them.
Gomez, 51, said he disagreed with the report's findings but would resign on 1 December. The five-term congressman lost his seat representing part of Los Angeles in the midterm elections this month and was set to leave the House at the end of the year.
The BBC has contacted Gomez's office for comment.
Gomez said in a statement on Monday that he had "strong disagreements" with the committee's findings, but that he saw "no other alternative than to resign", according to CBS, the BBC's US media partner.
He added: "I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage."
The panel originally investigated a report that Gomez had been seen kissing a younger staffer at a party hosted by then-Congressman Eric Swalwell. That report came shortly after Swalwell, also a California Democrat, resigned over sexual misconduct allegations of his own.
The bipartisan committee announced its investigation into Gomez, who is married, in August, after lawyers for the House staffer accused him of inappropriate sexual contact. He had maintained at the time that while he had made mistakes, his actions were consensual.
The ethics committee interviewed a woman, referred to only as "Witness 1" in the report, who said the congressman made unwanted sexual advances toward her on two occasions, once in public and once in his congressional office, while she was a House staffer.
She alleged Gomez "put his hand down my skirt" while they were at a bar in Washington DC in February 2024, describing the incident as "nonconsensual whatsoever".
Gomez's conduct caused the House staffer "significant and ongoing distress", contributing to her decision to leave her job, according to the report.
The woman's attorneys, Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, said in a statement on Monday that Gomez "abused the power given to him by the voters" and that in his actions "he was effectively destroying her dreams of a career in public service".
While they applauded the report, the attorneys said Gomez's conduct "did not occur in a vacuum", calling for immediate steps by Congress to "rein in what the report describes as a 'toxic and predatory culture'".
The committee said in its report on Monday that it did not have enough time "to pursue an adequate House sanction" against Gomez as he is set to leave Congress next month.
The House Ethics Committee last week approved changes to how the bipartisan panel handles sexual misconduct investigations, including ways to speed up its inquiries.
Gomez lost to Angela Gonzales-Torres, also a Democrat, in this month's election by some 25 percentage points after a campaign in which the sexual misconduct investigation became a focal point.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The House Ethics Committee said in a report released Monday that there is "substantial evidence" that Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California engaged in sexual misconduct by making unwelcome sexual advances and sexual contact toward a House staffer.
The report said Gomez's conduct caused the House aide significant and ongoing distress and contributed to her decision to leave House employment altogether.
"Representative Gomez's conduct also reflects a broader environment of sexual misconduct and toxic working conditions in some Capitol Hill offices which the Committee is determined to address," the report stated.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
In response, Gomez announced that he would be resigning from the House on Dec. 1, even though he has "strong disagreements with the Committee's report and its conclusions." Gomez was already set to depart Congress at the end of the year, having been defeated in his bid for reelection this month by a fellow Democrat, Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres.
Gomez said he recognizes the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and takes full responsibility for the "personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage." He also said he cooperated with the investigation and responded voluntarily to requests for information.
The finding is just the latest involving allegations of sexual misconduct by a House lawmaker. Two lawmakers resigned earlier this year rather than face the prospect of an expulsion vote. Another member was censured for his interactions with two female aides on his staff.
The committee did not recommend any particular sanction for Gomez, who is serving his fifth term in the House. The panel said the Constitution charges the House with policing the behavior of its own members.
"The House should take whatever action it deems appropriate in light of the Committee's findings," the Ethics panel said.
Gomez had previously said he would cooperate with the investigation but also stressed that his actions were consensual in nature and did not violate the law or House Ethics rules. He also apologized to his family and constituents.

The Trump administration on Monday added the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors.
The Singapore-based company was added to the Commerce Departmentâs entity list on Monday afternoon, plans that were first reported by Semafor.
The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
According to a filing from Commerceâs Bureau of Industry and Security posted to the Federal Register Monday afternoon, seven total entities were added to the list from Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including various affiliates of Megaspeed, MSFusion, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, and Swiftdata.
âThese additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,â the filing reads. âThese entities will be added with a license requirement for all items subject to the [Export Administration Regulations] and licenses will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.â
Technology exports already en route to the targeted companies will be allowed to go through, the filing suggests.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the departmentâs entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list âfor monthsâ but that âCommerce holds the pen.â Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.

112d4168f4f3.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Members of Congress responded with swift, bipartisan fury Monday over the Nvidia board's surprise decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang at the behest of President Donald Trump, opening a new phase of questions about the chipmaking giant and potential national security lapses.
Sen. Tim Scott, the outgoing Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang will testify publicly before the panel on Dec. 3. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair, said the Trump administration needs to explain what role U.S. officials played in what she called a "reckless" decision.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's direct involvement with Nvidia's decision-making "raises serious national security and corruption questions."
"We must investigate these actions," said Garcia of California.
Nvidia was already facing sharp scrutiny from Congress after Huang acknowledged a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy. Putting Huang back in charge, after Trump said the board did "what we wanted them to do," raised stark concerns over the administration's role in the company that is central to the AI economy.
As Democrats prepare to take charge of Congress in January, they are mounting investigations into the Trump administration, particularly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has close ties with the company. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month said he was frustrated by the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed, the company whose CEO, Alice Huang, was involved with Jensen Huang.
Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, who is expected to become the chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said Huang's reinstatement does not change the fact that he will be expected to testify on Capitol Hill.
"Though the NVIDIA Board of Directors may be convinced that reinstating Mr. Huang 'poses no national security risk,' the Congress still has questions that require answers," Himes said in a statement.
Huang is expected to sit for an interview with three House committees next week, along with his public hearing at the Senate panel.
At issue is the sale of chips to China
Of concern to Congress is whether Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, has been selling its chips to China, in violation of export controls as the U.S. tries to protect certain technology that is at the core of the AI race.
Earlier this year, members of Congress urged the U.S. Commerce Department to "suspend or reconsider" Nvidia's export licenses to China and to conduct a full national security review, according to a release earlier this month from Warren and a key Republican on the Senate banking committee, Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana.
"Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China's military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.," they wrote in a statement in November.
"NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer," the two senators said.
Republicans and Democrats are demanding answers
While senior Republican lawmakers were mostly quiet on Huang's return to Nvidia, several Republicans — particularly those who are leaving Congress — spoke more forcefully Monday.
Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his seat after Trump endorsed his GOP primary opponent, questioned the company's comment that the U.S. said there was no security risk.
"No national security risk? Based on what?" Cornyn posted.
Cornyn asked whether the FBI did a defensive briefing of Huang to conclude there was no risk. "If not, why not?" Cornyn asked on X.
Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon wrote on social media that the U.S. cannot say it wants to win the AI competition and then give China its best technology. "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China," wrote Bacon, who is retiring from Congress.
Ahead of the announcement but after Trump's call for Huang to be reinstated, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who lost reelection to a Democrat, posted: "Ummm… she was, and is, a spy. How about we get serious about making sure China doesn't steal US company technology?"
Utah Sen. John Curtis asked similar questions.
"Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?" Curtis asked. "And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
Democrats add to their anti-corruption agenda
Democrats are preparing to dive more deeply into questions of national security and political corruption in Washington as they take over the committee gavels in January.
"The guy who was having an affair with a Chinese spy while working relentlessly to help China get access to as many AI chips as possible? Really?" posted Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, who is poised to become the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when Democrats take the majority.
Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, said that Congress should investigate "what stock positions took place before the announcement."
Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who will chair the Senate finance committee and serves on the Senate intelligence committee, said Huang's restatement shows that under Trump and his administration, "our national security is for sale."
"In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable," Wyden said.
Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani, Joey Cappelletti and Chris Rugaber contributed to this report.

ebd04280b997.text:
The U.S. Army's controlled detonation of 68 barrels of unstable lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday is expected to produce a plume of dust containing lead particles that could extend as far as 100 miles away, a plan that residents, lawmakers and environmental groups say was not communicated appropriately.
The date of the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, has changed several times as a result of court challenges, which in part contend that the government failed to adequately warn local communities about environmental and health risks.
Lead is a toxic metal that can cause severe health problems, particularly for children and people who are pregnant. No amount of lead exposure is safe, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Originally scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, the detonation was initially moved to Monday, the latest the Army said the event could happen before dropping temperatures threatened to further destabilize the degrading lead azide.
A federal appeals court on Friday temporarily suspended the Army's permit for the detonation as a federal judge considers a lawsuit brought by environmental groups seeking to block the blast.
The Justice Department said the Army is invoking its emergency powers that allow it to move forward with the explosion without the Environmental Protection Agency's permit.
On Sunday night, the Army announced its decision to proceed with the detonation, rescheduled again for Wednesday.
But President Donald Trump on Monday said he ordered the Army not to go through with the detonation without court approval. Trump said the decision would be subject to the courts and Iowa's incoming Democratic Gov., Rob Sand, though he doesn't take office until Jan. 12, 2027.
"If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," Trump said in a Truth Social post.
To prepare for the detonation, Iowa's Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds activated a State Emergency Operations Center on Nov. 20 and created a website with information. The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted flights in the area between Monday and Wednesday.
Here's what to know about lead azide, the planned explosion and safety measures.
What is lead azide and why does the Army say it needs to detonate Iowa's stockpile?
Lead azide is an explosive agent that is highly volatile. It's used to initiate munitions.
The Army said it found the stockpile of degraded and crystalized lead azide during a March safety review at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. When lead azide crystalizes, it becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock and friction, making it unsafe to move, as it can explode.
It's unclear why the Army did not dispose of the lead azide barrels before they deteriorated.
In his Truth Social post, Trump blamed the Obama administration, saying it "improperly stored a vast number of explosives" in 2009. However, Iowa Public Radio reported that the Army launched an explosives project in 2004 because of concerns about a then-40-year-old stockpile of deteriorating lead azide in the Iowa plant. George W. Bush was president at the time.
The Army filed an environmental assessment this September seeking an emergency permit from the EPA that would allow it to detonate 9,500 pounds of lead azide in the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
In October, the Iowa plant hosted an open house about its detonation plan for residents of Middletown. The EPA granted the permit on Nov. 13, and it's set to expire on Feb. 11, 2027. On Nov. 15, the Army announced it had scheduled two controlled detonations for Nov. 20.
According to the Army's assessment, controlled detonation at the Iowa plant is the only way to dispose of the lead azide.
The lead azide can't be packaged or transported to a different facility, as it could accidentally detonate and harm the people handling the material as well as the greater public, according to the Army's Q&A on the blast.
Chemical neutralization would avoid the plume of dust, but it would increase the probability of fatal detonation during handling, according to the Army, as it would require more physical manipulation of the drums.
The New York Times reported that the Army in March awarded MuniRem Environmental, a company that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions, a contract to dispose of the lead azide. Two months later it terminated the contract without giving the firm a reason for the cancellation.
Environmental groups suing the Army's emergency permit argue that it did not thoroughly consider other alternatives.
What are the health and environmental risks of detonating lead azide?
The Army is planning two detonations to dispose of the lead azide.
Before the blasts were postponed, Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park neighborhood residents were asked to vacate from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Friday. The explosion was scheduled for noon.
The explosions are expected to potentially break windows and cause noise and ground vibrations, as well as produce a dust plume containing lead, according to the Army's public advisory. Residents in the area were advised to evacuate temporarily due to potential window damage.
When the lead azide is detonated there will be larger lead particles that will fall to the ground first; smaller particles will travel further from the detonation site, according to Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters.
How far the lead travels is dependent on environmental conditions, he said.
David Cwiertny, director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination at the University of Iowa, said the direction the wind blows will determine where
