NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court on Monday gave President Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush money criminal conviction, moving the case to a federal court where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds.
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court decision that had kept the case in state court in New York, where Trump was tried and convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
The panel ordered a lower court to promptly issue a decision on whether the case should remain in federal court. If that happens, Trump could then argue that verdict should be discarded because of presidential immunity.
The decision also set in motion a halt to proceedings in Trump's simultaneous state court appeal. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment in the case, which made him the first U.S. president convicted of a crime.
In a two-page order, the 2nd Circuit panel said it disagreed with the late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein's earlier denial of Trump's request to move the historic case from state court to federal court, a process known as removal.
The appellate judges ruled that Hellerstein "erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case" after a conviction and erred in denying that Trump had good cause to make two attempts at moving the case — once after his indictment and again after his trial.
The ruling came a week after 2nd Circuit Judges Raymond J. Lohier Jr., John M. Walker Jr. and José A. Cabranes spent more than an hour questioning Trump's lawyer and a state prosecutor on the matter.
Lohier and Cabranes were appointed by Democrats. Walker was appointed by a Republican.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Trump's legal team said the president "appreciates the 2nd Circuit's prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System."
The Manhattan District Attorney's Office, which prosecuted the case, declined comment.
Trump's lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., had urged the judges to rule swiftly, arguing that without federal court intervention, the president "will likely have to wait years" for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Steven Wu, chief of the appeals division at the Manhattan DA's office, urged the 2nd Circuit panel to uphold Hellerstein's ruling and leave the case in state court.
Trump had been waging a traditional appeal through New York's state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule and could be prevented from doing so indefinitely under Monday's ruling.
Trump asked the 2nd Circuit to step in after a federal judge in August ruled against the president for a third time. Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, wrote in his decision that "paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity."
Trump first sought to move the case to federal court weeks after he was indicted in March 2023. He tried again after his conviction and the Supreme Court's July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can't be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can't use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal.
After Trump appealed Hellerstein's second denial, the 2nd Circuit ordered the judge to reconsider, finding that he had failed to weigh "important issues relevant" to the president's request to move the case.
That panel, which also included Lohier, said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties.
Giuffra told the 2nd Circuit panel last week that prosecutors at Trump's trial had used the type of official acts evidence that was later barred by the Supreme Court's immunity ruling, including testimony about his Oval Office conversations, workflow and social media posts.
Giuffra also took issue with the prosecution's description of the hush money payment as an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act, arguing that such allegations belong in federal court, not state court.

1b7f2ed36014.text:
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month, after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy - he was also accused of an affair with an Nvidia executive.
US President Donald Trump says he "made the deal" to encourage Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and president.
The BBC's business correspondent Michelle Fleury explains the role Trumpâs support may have played in Huangâs return to the companyâs top job.

512453057e1c.text:
- Published
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.
His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.
Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.
On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.
Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.
"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.
"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.
"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."
Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."
She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

646ccdb8bd5c.text:
A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.
Now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.
By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.
A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.
“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.
Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.
Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.
The result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”
The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.
Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.
Alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”
AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.
And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”
Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”

018c83201c90.text:
The U.S. Army intends to detonate nearly five tons of lead-based explosives in southeast Iowa on Wednesday.
The Army had planned to use an emergency provision to proceed despite a now-lifted court-ordered pause on the federal permit authorizing the operation.
Dozens of barrels of volatile lead azide, a material used to make bombs, are stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. After decades in storage, their explosive contents have reformed into irregularly shaped crystals that are highly sensitive to friction and shock. The Army argues that freezing temperatures will make the crystals even more unstable and the barrels must be disposed of before winter sets in.
“A permit is not even necessary for the Army to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material,” reads the Department of Justice brief filed with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit on Sunday.
Late Monday, the court lifted its administrative stay on the permit for the detonation and rejected a request from petitioners to block the detonation for a longer period. The petitioners are suing the Environmental Protection Agency over its approval of the permit.
Maps released by the Army for last Friday’s planned detonation, which was called off, show a lead dust cloud spreading across potentially hundreds of miles of Eastern Iowa, with projected concentrations of the neurotoxin exceeding federal benchmarks for levels in homes and childcare facilities. Lead exposure isn’t safe for anyone, but it’s particularly dangerous for children.
In a post on Truth Social Monday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he ordered the military not to proceed with the detonation until both the appeals court and Gov.-elect Rob Sand agree to it.
In his post, Trump also blamed the Obama administration for improper storage of the explosives and said that Sand, a Democrat who does not take office until Jan. 12, would be held responsible for any catastrophic explosion caused by further delays.
Current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, a Republican, has activated the State Emergency Operations Center in preparation for the detonation. “While the detonation is a federal operation, it’s important for the state to be engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans,” Reynolds said in a statement published Sunday.
The Army initially intended to detonate the barrels last Friday. Residents of Middletown learned of the plans at a town hall a month earlier. But most Iowa residents, including state agencies and officials such as Reynolds, received just five days’ notice. Army maps detailing the extent of the lead dust cloud were also released just a few days beforehand.
The maps, along with the short notice and limited information about cleanup efforts following the release of the plume, have sparked widespread concern in Iowa and neighboring states.
Last Thursday, the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter sued the EPA over the emergency permit it granted the Army for the detonation. That same day, the Army announced it would postpone the operation and the court granted the petitioners’ motion for an administrative stay. Responding to the court’s stay, the Army and the Justice Department insisted that the detonation could and must take place, regardless of the permit’s status.
In court filings this weekend, the Justice Department cited a provision in the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 that allows for emergency treatment or containment of military munitions and other explosive materials without a permit, if the materials present an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Since submitting its emergency permit request to the EPA in September, the Army has repeatedly asserted that controlled detonation is the safest option for the barrels’ disposal, though doing so would release a neurotoxin-containing dust cloud over surrounding communities. Lead particles in the air can settle into soil, exposing people—particularly children—long after its arrival.
All alternatives to detonation would require opening or moving the barrels, the Army wrote in correspondence with the EPA submitted as evidence to the court this weekend. The sensitivity of lead azide crystals to friction and shock meant that any manipulation presented “an acute risk of unintentional detonation.”
The choice is “between a planned detonation … and an unplanned explosion that could come at any moment, with no warning and safeguards,” the Justice Department legal brief reads. “The United States recognizes that the controlled detonation will release lead dust. But a controlled detonation is the only way to minimize the release.”
A scheduled detonation would at least allow the Army to plan for weather conditions, notify the public and track the spread of lead dust, the Justice Department writes.
In a video released this weekend, Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson advised against further delays. “Each day that the disposal is delayed is another day that could increase the risk of major catastrophe. It is also another day that the lives of our residents are put on hold,” he said.
There is no safe level of the lead exposure for children, the EPA advises. It is especially harmful to infants and children with rapidly growing brains and nervous systems.
The Army has not disclosed when on Wednesday the detonation will occur, nor released updated plume maps outlining the regions most likely to be affected by lead deposition.

Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks â what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" â have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
Impact elsewhere in Europe
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much â but not all â of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states â Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania â all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid attacks
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

8e7d30f2ee9b.text: Mississippi is facing two fights over its election rules after Democrat Scott Colom 's historic Senate victory: one over voters marked inactive and another over deadlines for receiving mail-in ballots . Why it matters: The disputes could affect how easily eligible voters cast ballots and which mail ballots count when Mississippi elects a new governor and other statewide leaders next year. Driving the news: The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus demanded an investigation Thursday into whether the state's use of credit-reporting data to verify voters' addresses led election officials to incorrectly mark voters as inactive. Lawmakers want to examine the credit-reporting data contracts, instructions sent to county officials and how many eligible voters were incorrectly marked inactive. In one case, a Hinds County voter learned she'd been marked inactive when she arrived at her usual polling place, according to Angela Grayson, director of civic engagement and voting rights at the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable. Her vote ultimately counted, Grayson said. The caucus acknowledged it doesn't know how many voters were flagged in error. Advocacy groups are seeking records to find out. What they're saying: "Nothing has changed fundamentally here in Mississippi," Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, tells Axios. "The laws are still the laws. The governor is still the governor. The state legislature is still overwhelmingly Republican," he said. "It's also plainly obvious that the playbook of reducing turnout, culling the active voter rolls, that's not going to stop." By the numbers: More than 230,000 voters were listed as inactive before the 2026 midterms, up from roughly 171,000 in 2024, according to the Associated Press . Mississippi recorded 21,484 affidavit ballots, the state's version of provisional ballots, this year. That's nearly identical to the 21,321 cast in 2024's presidential election, when overall turnout was higher, per a statement from Secretary of State Michael Watson. About 75% of affidavit ballots were accepted statewide. But in majority-Black Hinds County, which includes Jackson, just 34% of 2,426 were accepted, down from 60% in 2024. It's unclear whether credit-reporting data contributed to the decline. "Those are huge alarms and red flags for us," Grayson told Axios, calling for more information about why ballots were rejected. Yes, but: Watson defended the state's voter-roll practices as legal and effective. He said election officials review flagged voter registrations and that voters still had an opportunity to cast affidavit ballots. "Our team welcomes an investigation because we have continuously followed the law," his office told Axios, adding that local election officials maintain voter rolls. Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves and Secretary of State Michael Watson support eliminating the state's five-business-day grace period for receiving mail-in ballots, with Reeves pitching that ballots should instead arrive by 5 p.m. on Election Day. Watson successfully defended Mississippi's authority to maintain the grace period before the Supreme Court months earlier, despite personally opposing the practice. Reeves had called for its repeal months before Colom's victory. "We see that as just a further suppression of voter rights here in the state," Grayson said of Reeves' proposal. Zoom out: Reeves said last week he intends to call a special legislative session to redistrict before Mississippi's 2027 elections, amid President Trump's push to redraw political maps to benefit Republicans. King imagined Republicans responding to Colom's win: "Holy crap, we've got to figure out how to build a moat around our majority in the state legislature." What we're watching: It's unclear whether lawmakers will launch an investigation, proposed voter-roll reforms will attract GOP support or Reeves' mail-ballot proposal will become a bill. King is skeptical: "The Mississippi legislature is not known for oversight." Go deeper: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test

Trump has said that Attorney General Todd Blanche had affirmed no national security risk from Huangâs rehiring, but the Justice Department is currently conducting ongoing investigations that could affect that question.
Huangâs closed-door appearance before the House panels is currently expected to move forward as planned, people familiar with the plans said, but spokespeople for the panels did not respond to requests for comment.

3d02e8891425.text: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore criticized President Trump's involvement in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang , calling it "troubling and problematic" in an interview for "The Axios Show." Why it matters: Moore, chair of the National Governors Association and often seen as a 2028 presidential contender, is one of the most outspoken state leaders pushing for stronger federal oversight of AI companies — but not like this. Driving the news: Trump told CNBC Monday that he spoke directly to Nvidia's board about Huang's return. Trump had previously pushed for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to become Nvidia's leader, but changed tune over the last few days to favor Huang. What they're saying: "The president is not a board member of Nvidia. So, why he is involved in board dealings, I have no idea. ... It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee," Moore told Axios' Mike Allen in an interview just minutes after the news broke. "You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate, where, frankly, if that was any of us, we would be held to a different type of standard." Zoom in: Moore said the "market is being inflated essentially by seven companies," including Nvidia. Huang's return — which led to a stock surge — "highlights how problematic this entire thing is," Moore said. "We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires, who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves, making this decision because they know this company is that important." Subscribe to "The Axios Show" on YouTube to watch the full interview with Moore when it's available.

4ab2d002625b.text: Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is drawing criticism and scrutiny — including about national security risks — from members of Congress in both parties. Why it matters: President Trump's push to reinstate Huang creates a headache for Republicans and new fodder for Democrats eager to deploy their investigative powers when they take control in January. "No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked in a social media post following the news. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in a statement to Axios. "The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) posted on X . Driving the news: The House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees have announced that Huang would testify next week. His reinstatement "changes nothing," an Intelligence Committee spokesperson told Axios on Monday. "When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts." The spokesperson added: "There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee's commitment to oversight." Huang is scheduled to appear before the Senate banking panel on Dec. 3. What we're watching: Top Democrats say they will open their own investigations into Huang's reinstatement when they take power next year. "Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said. "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,"Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a post on X . Said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Finance Committee: "In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable." Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told Axios: "We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC's access to our most sensitive technology." What Democrats are saying: "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security," Schumer said. Jeffries called for the annual defense authorization bill to include "ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries." "The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom," Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said . "Jensen Huang's reinstatement shows that under Trump, Vance, and Rubio, our national security is for sale," Wyden said . Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the top Banking committee Democrat, called the decision "reckless" and said the board still owes Congress "answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," adding that the Trump administration "needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement." "Yet another example where, in Trump's America, the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard," Meeks told Axios. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), the top Democrat on the China Select Committee, called the decision "outrageous." Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), a member of House Democratic leadership, blasted it as "irresponsible." What Republicans are saying: " Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions," Curtis said in his statement to Axios. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?" "Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking 'candor.' ... His behavior does not support reinstatement," said Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), adding that he looked forward to Huang's testimony next week. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Monday morning that it would reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, president a board member after ousting him earlier this month. The board voted unanimously for Huang's return. The reinstatement comes after Trump repeatedly urged the board to bring Huang back. Stocks saw an early, massive rally following the news. Huang's departure had sent the stock market into correction territory. The bottom line: Both sides have a lot of questions. Democrats will soon have the power to get answers. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Sen. Kevin Cramer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

President Donald Trump said he has ordered the US army not to move ahead with plans to detonate five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa on Wednesday until a court rules on the issue.
The administration previously had planned to go forward with the plans despite legal challenges and public outcry over the potential health risks to nearby communities.
A court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation.
"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward," Trump said, referencing the court that halted the detonation.
He added in his post on Truth Social that the US had "an opportunity to do a highly controlled detonation of these dangerous and rapidly corroding materials" because of optimal weather.
Even after the court pause ordered on Thursday, the justice department told the court that the army intends to move forward with its plan, because of an "immediate risk" that those materials could "spontaneously explode".
Environmental groups have accused the government of skirting the judicial process.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says no level of lead exposure is considered safe. Lead exposure through inhalation or ingestion can pose serious health risks to humans and animals, particularly children.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. In its court filing on Saturday, the justice department said the army would carry out the detonation on Tuesday.
Later, in a social media post on Sunday evening, the army announced that the detonation had been rescheduled for Wednesday to allow for "optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced".
"The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority," it said.
Middletown's Mayor Rodney Johnson weighed in on Monday saying the detonation "must take place".
"It doesn't matter who dropped the ball on the removal of these expired munitions, the ball is now in November 2026 Court," Johnson said in a statement. "The buzzer is ticking and if we don't take this opportunity to Safely dispose of the problem, then actual lives may be at stake !!!"
He added that "every possible precaution" had been put into place to ensure people's safety.
The government has argued that, because this is an event that requires immediate action, the army can move forward without a permit for detonation.
The justice department's court filing describes this as an "emergency situation" in part because of the incoming cold weather.
"As the outside temperatures drop the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures," the filing said.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing stated.
It said that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed the legal case on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause. The advocacy groups accuse the government of bypassing the judicial process.
"Despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.
Iowa's newly elected Democratic Senator Josh Turek has called for a full probe into how the lead azide "was allowed to degrade into this critical state and why safer methods of disposal were not pursued".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.
Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible. They also said they had been preparing for the event since March.
"Agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the agencies said in a joint statement released on Friday.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

3f18993f1432.text: President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after allies argued he was " too big to fail " for the U.S. economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios. Why it matters: Trump put the weight of the presidency behind a private company's decision about who should run it, an intervention that strengthened Huang's allies inside the administration and put officials critical of the company in an increasingly uncomfortable position. Driving the news: "Jensen is too big to fail," one source familiar with the discussions told Axios. Huang resigned amid allegations he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and subordinates. The stock market's slump prompted President Trump and allies within the administration to push for his reinstatement. "The President was pushing harder than Jensen," one source said. Trump called into Nvidia's board meeting Sunday night to argue for Huang's reinstatement, he told CNBC. Behind the scenes: Huang's allies appealed to Trump's longstanding distrust of the intelligence community, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders. A Trump adviser said allies sought to convince Trump that "deep staters" were working against Huang. The intelligence included findings about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated to senior officials in a memo earlier this year. A Rubio ally said the secretary of state was "mortified" when the memo leaked with his name attached. Zoom in: The memo came as Nvidia lobbied the Trump administration to open up China's access to its chips. Despite the intelligence, Huang remained close to the president while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's inaction fueled tensions between him, Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and others. A senior administration official argued the intelligence never established Huang was compromised, knowingly violated U.S. law or had sex with a spy. "People are weaponizing some true information and spinning it to reflect as negatively as possible against Huang. That's the president's concern," the official said. Vance's role Trump and Vice President JD Vance viewed Huang as an important champion of open models offering Americans more control and lower costs than closed models like OpenAI's and Anthropic's. The two were briefed on the national security concerns involving Huang and concluded they had not seen evidence of personal wrongdoing, the source said. Anthropic has been warning the Trump administration that Nvidia's advanced chips power Chinese open source models closing in on the AI race. Yes, but: These conclusions come as more and more connections between Alice Huang — the alleged Chinese spy Huang had an affair with — and the Chinese government and military come to light. "He let the U.S. stock market and economy demand his return — along with the pressure from the president — and the outcry was deafening," the source said. Huang's reinstatement is a "big win" for Vance, a source close to Rubio said. Vance's Silicon Valley relationships helped the administration navigate the board's concerns, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Keeping Huang as CEO was seen as the best option for national security, a source close to Vance said. What we're watching: Huang's opponents in the administration now risk backlash from the president. Bessent has been the loudest, criticizing Lutnick's inaction on TV and calling for the Nvidia board to find a new outside CEO and a "dramatic shakeup," but on Sunday softened his stance. What's next: Trump's intervention settled the immediate fight over Nvidia's leadership but raised questions about the U.S. government's role in the board's decision. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wants to know which officials provided the national security input that Nvidia cited in reinstating Huang. Three Republican-led House committees have scheduled interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. Nvidia says its independent investigations and cooperation with government inquiries will continue.

71dfa39f2e5b.text:
Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past weeks, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.
No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
On top of all that, there's concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
Flight delays and cancellations
The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.
First there was the Federal Aviation Administration's network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
"You do your best to be patient, but it's also helpful to have some context of what's going on, because our lives are literally in your hands," said Chianti Blackmon, a college administrator who was at the Atlanta airport on Monday.
Delta said that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.
"Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers," the airline said.
Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper.
Wicked weather on both coasts
Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation's mid-section, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service's Weather Prediction Center.
Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day and reach Maine by Friday, he said.
The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the big balloons will be able to fly during the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy's from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).
The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.
READ MORE: FAA grounds all flights at U.S. airports due to air traffic control communications problems
"This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day," Wegman said. "Perhaps better timing that it's happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after."
Rainy and windy weather also was expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.
Thanksgiving snow for some in the US
Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday, and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.
Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state and northwestern Pennsylvania.
"Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays," Wegman said. "I think weather won't be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day."
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press reporters Emilie Megnien in Atlanta; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

07536a5aae32.text:
President Donald Trump on Monday said he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.
The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for Friday, but the Army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. They had planned for a detonation on Wednesday, saying the weather was most favorable that day.
The Army had no immediate comment when asked about the president's social media post. Environmentalists sued last week in an effort to stop the detonation, winning a stay from the appeals court pending a decision on the validity of an emergency permit approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that cleared the way for the operation. Trump said he prefers to take care of the volatile material as soon as possible and that a controlled detonation would be much safer. "At the same time, have ordered the military not to do so until such time as the 8th Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation," Trump said in a statement. If Sand and the court don't agree, Trump said the administration will have no choice but to not proceed with the planned detonation, adding that he would hold the incoming governor responsible for "any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."
Sand said in a social media post on Sunday that because of previous decisions that have already been made, "No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been."
He questioned why a contract to remove the explosive risk was canceled, why nothing was done and "why we are rushing to demolition now in late November."
"The safety of Iowans should be the top priority of everyone involved," he said. "All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted."
Some residents near Middletown, where the ammunition plant is located, have been sealing their windows and doors as a precaution to keep out any lead dust that might result from the detonation. Others who live farther away were raising concern on social media about the possible paths that the plume could take depending on shifts in the wind.
READ MORE: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
Officials acknowledge that lead is toxic and have recommended that people stay indoors whenever the detonation happens and to clean off outdoor surfaces with water afterwards to limit exposure to any lead particles.
In court filings over the weekend, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, explained that less liquid inside the barrels means the solution inside is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the sensitivity of the crystals that have formed around the inside of the rim and underside of the lids.
"Even a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction," he said in his declaration to the court.
In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums' contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their court filings that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
Officials contend that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius) in the coming days.

a2822e4d8e59.text: President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate unstable explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant, saying the blast cannot proceed without approval from an appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand . The big picture: State officials said last week they only recently learned of the plan to detonate tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, sparking frustration about a perceived lack of transparency from federal officials. The Army, which had delayed the detonation until Wednesday, advised people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors and clean surfaces once the branch declares the airborne exposure risk over. But the threat also sparked warnings in neighboring Illinois, with the American Lung Association saying that residents of eastern Iowa and western Illinois could be exposed to lead. Driving the news: Trump warned Monday that he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation. " If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," he wrote in a pointed Monday Truth Social post . State of play: The Middletown, Iowa, blast was initially set for Friday, then delayed to Monday and then to Wednesday. In a Friday letter to Gov. Kim Reynolds, regional EPA administrator Jim Macy said the Army had documented recrystallization of the lead azide, raising the risk of an accidental explosion. The lead azide "is now so sensitive to temperature, friction and shock that it cannot be safely moved, opened, or treated without a significant risk of explosion," per an administration court filing . Friction point: Earthjustice sued last week to halt the detonation on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter. A federal appeals court subsequently paused an EPA emergency permit allowing the blast. But even with the permit stayed, the administration argued in a Sunday filing to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that the Army could still move forward with a controlled detonation. Catch up quick: The Army announced Sunday night that the controlled detonation plan would be pushed to Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced." "The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority," the Army added. But on Monday, Trump halted those plans. What they're saying: Incoming Hawkeye State leaders Josh Turek, who will join the Senate in January, and Sand , the incoming Democratic governor, have condemned the Army's communications. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning," Turek said in a Sunday statement . Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) slammed the saga as "an extreme failure of communication, planning and leadership," adding the Army "must be held accountable for the harm done." Go deeper: Iowa leaders ask Army to delay planned lead detonation

Hours before Nvidia reinstated ousted CEO Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump dialed into Nvidiaâs Sunday board meeting to argue for his return.
The remarkable direct engagement by Trump, first reported by Semafor and confirmed by multiple sources, underscores how fully he has redefined the role of the US government in private enterprise.
Trump wasnât alone. Vice President JD Vance and other members of the administration have also gotten actively involved in the inner workings of one of the USâ most valuable companies, even as members of Trumpâs own party raise questions about his statement that reinstating Huang poses no national security risk.
By Monday morning, the company had announced Huangâs return and made no secret the decision was made based on âinputâ from the White House, which told the company the administration felt comfortable despite Huangâs extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The pitch that resonated with Vance and Trump, who had been close to Huang, centered around the Nvidia CEOâs role as a protector of open-source models, and a check on the increasing power of closed frontier model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor.
The pressure was also heightened by the tech rout in the markets, which sent the S&P 500 into correction territory over worries of AI risks. On Monday, Nvidiaâs stock jumped 30%, the biggest increase in more than two decades, lifting the entire market with it.
Despite multiple active legal and regulatory probes that touch on the company â and potentially Huang personally â the president and vice president pushed back privately and publicly on allegations that he posed a threat to national security. Both were personally engaged over the weekend to bring Huang back, the person added.
âPresident Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,â White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.
Unanimous vote
Two weeks after the board voted unanimously to accept Huangâs resignation, which came after allegations of affairs with two subordinates, Nvidiaâs board met late Sunday night and voted unanimously to bring him back, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Huang, who co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and built it into an AI giant, benefited from a mounting defense campaign by some Silicon Valley figures who called for his return. Semafor had previously reported that despite a unanimous vote to oust him a couple weeks ago, a faction of directors had continued to push for him to come back.
The anti-Huang camp was dealt a blow when they learned a leading replacement candidate, Arm CEO Rene Haas, wouldnât be available since he had signed a new contract with Arm extending his employment until 2033, according to another person familiar with directorsâ thinking.
âThe Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,â Harvey Jones, who was elevated to board chairman at the time of Huangâs Nov. 12 ouster, said in its statement.
Nvidiaâs senior leadership was not aware of the decision to restore Huang until shortly before the general public knew, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Washington probes
Huangâs return is guaranteed to amplify the already vocal bipartisan calls for Congress to investigate his behavior and the companyâs lobbying against export controls that would curtail Nvidiaâs overseas chips business.
He is already slated to appear in private before House members and in public before senators next week. Several Republicans greeted his reinstatement with open skepticism of the Justice Departmentâs claim that there was no evidence Huangâs affair presented a national security risk.
Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, questioned the âbasisâ for that judgment. Huang âwas right to step down when the affair came to light,â he posted on social media.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the ranking member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, called the decision to reinstate Huang âreckless.â
Huangâs return âonly increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk,â she wrote.
DOJ continues to probe two key Nvidia customers, Alice Huangâs Megaspeed and Supermicro, over export control violations, and Nvidia itself over antitrust concerns, Semafor previously reported and confirmed with a Justice Department official.
â Ashley Gold and J.D. Capelouto contributed reporting.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Democratic Party's incoming senators haven't even been sworn into office yet, but the decision over who will lead their new majority is already testing the promise of change they made as candidates.
The 13 new Democrats are part of the largest incoming Senate class in decades, with several winning in Republican strongholds by promising to shake up Washington and be independent voices. Now they are caught up in a classic insider fight, forced to decide whether to stick with longtime Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York or back challenger Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.
Newly elected progressives, including Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, have backed Van Hollen, who is taking on Schumer with promises of a more aggressive legislative approach. Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who is returning to Washington after losing his seat in 2024, supports Schumer.
But the incoming senators from traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, whose victories helped deliver Democrats the majority, have so far largely avoided taking sides publicly. Annie Andrews of South Carolina has said she is talking with both candidates. Scott Colom of Mississippi says he wants to get to know them better before deciding and describes himself as being in "listening mode."
Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said Thursday he would not back Schumer, but declined to endorse anyone.
"I'm looking for someone who is going to bring people together," Hamilton told MSNow. "Right now, in places like Kansas, there's a lot of people who don't feel that in Chuck Schumer."
Schumer's long-standing relationships and knowledge of Senate machinery are a big advantage heading into the Dec. 1 vote, which will be held by secret ballot. He also oversees Senate Democrats' campaign spending group, funneling millions into many of the races and, in some cases, recruiting the candidates to run in the first place.
But the reluctance of many incoming senators to commit has put an unusual spotlight on first-term lawmakers who could help shape the party's direction in the new Congress.
"We should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here," said Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono, who is supporting Schumer. "We have to make sure that all these voices are heard, and they've got a lot of talent to bring to the table."
The senators who campaigned for change
Many of the incoming senators campaigned as political outsiders, promising to bring fresh perspectives to a Washington establishment they argued had failed ordinary Americans.
Andrews, a 46-year-old pediatrician, became the first Democrat in nearly three decades to win a Senate race in South Carolina. She called for "generational change" and said that she would not support Schumer.
But she has also rejected policies that Van Hollen supports, such as "Medicare for All." On a press call Tuesday, Andrews said she has made "no decision" on the majority leader's race.
"The way I assess the situation as it is right now is that the generational change is represented by this incredibly dynamic incoming freshman class of senators," Andrews said.
Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico called for "new blood" in the Democratic Party, arguing that fresh perspectives were needed to change a political system that had failed. But Talarico has stopped short of rejecting Schumer, saying in a CBS interview two days after the Nov. 3 election that he would meet with the leadership candidates and ask "tough questions."
Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek has taken a similar approach, saying his decision will depend on which candidate best reflects the priorities he campaigned on. During a news conference Monday, he said that he had met with Schumer and Van Hollen and was waiting for "further updates" on questions he had.
"Whoever provides those answers to me that most closely align with my common sense, prairie populist agenda that I've been running on for the last year and a half, that's who I'll support," Turek said.
Alaska Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, whose race was officially called on Wednesday, told The Associated Press soon after that she had not yet thought about the leadership race.
El-Sayed and Flanagan have been among the staunch supporters of Van Hollen. Another progressive, Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, has said he wouldn't support Schumer but hasn't yet said he would vote for Van Hollen.
Schumer backed alternative candidates during the primaries in all three races. He supported all three once they were nominated.
A private decision has become a public fight
Senate leadership elections have traditionally been private affairs, decided by lawmakers in closed-door, secret-ballot votes that are shaped by the complicated inner workings of the Senate. The job requires holding together a caucus with competing political interests, a responsibility that doesn't always align with the demands of the party's most vocal activists.
Schumer's allies point to his success in doing that job, most recently in the midterms. He helped recruit candidates such as Brown, Peltola and North Carolina Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, while his allied super PAC was the largest Democratic spender in tightly contested races such as in Michigan and Maine.
"When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract," Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego said.
But Democrats are also facing pressure from some in their base to confront Republican President Donald Trump more aggressively while delivering on ambitious policy promises. Large progressive organizations, including MoveOn and Indivisible, have endorsed Van Hollen, while many senators' offices have been flooded with calls urging them to reject Schumer.
"Our members are tired of politicians content with incrementalism — they want bold, creative leadership that will help Democrats usher in affordability and accountability without delay or compromise in the next Congress," MoveOn's executive director

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is set to condemn California Gov. Gavin Newsom's clemency to the state's death row inmates in a speech at the Justice Department on Monday, his second address in less than two years at an agency that has moved aggressively to fulfill his White House's agenda and pursue criminal cases against his adversaries.
Watch in our video player above.
The White House said the speech, in the building's ceremonial Great Hall, would be about protecting American families and Newsom's decision to commute the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to punishments of life without parole.
But it was unclear to what extent the address would also function as a forum for the Republican president to again encourage the prosecution of his political opponents and revisit years-old grievances about a Justice Department that has repeatedly investigated him over the past decade.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Newsom earlier this month said he will change more than 500 death sentences in his state to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The Democratic governor, who frequently trades barbs with Trump and is considering a run for president, said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims' families.
Trump's speech is unfolding against the backdrop of sweeping Republican losses in midterm elections this month that gave Democrats control of Congress and that tee up possible House and Senate investigations over everything from the mass firings of agents and prosecutors who investigated Trump to a series of politically charged investigations by the Trump administration Justice Department that have been rejected by grand juries and judges alike.
Trump's sway over the department is embodied by a banner of his face that hangs outside the building's exterior, an indication of what critics say is the erosion of the institution's historic independence.
Trump will be joined by Attorney General Todd Blanche, his former personal defense lawyer, who has been unapologetic in his view that the president is entitled to exert his will on the Justice Department. Blanche was elevated from deputy attorney general to the top job in April after Trump ousted Pam Bondi, who struggled to satisfy the president's demands for retribution and endured bipartisan criticism over the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Presidential addresses at the Justice Department are rare but not unheard of.
Trump last visited in March 2025 for a speech meant to rally support for his administration's policies on violent crime, drugs and illegal immigration. But he used the occasion to air a litany of complaints about the criminal cases he faced during Democratic President Joe Biden's administration — when prosecutors charged him with hoarding classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, and with conspiring to overturn his 2020 election loss to Biden — and to vow retribution for what he described as the "lies and abuses that have occurred within these walls."
He pledged at the time to expose the "egregious crimes and severe misconduct" of his foes. The Justice Department since then has accelerated efforts to investigate his enemies but has encountered multiple setbacks, with cases either thrown out by judges or spurned by grand juries that have refused to issue indictments.

NEW YORK (AP) — Ta-Nehisi Coates, M. Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson are among more than 100 writers, editors, agents and others in the literary community seeking to establish a chapter of PEN that is independent from PEN America, the longtime free expression organization that has endured tensions with various members in recent years over the war in Gaza and other issues.
The new group, called PEN Writes US, would be "guided by the PEN Charter's vision of 'one humanity, living in peace and equality in one world,'" Monday's announcement by the proposed organization reads.
Novelist Maaza Mengiste told The Associated Press during a recent telephone interview that PEN Writes does not seek to be a rival of PEN America and will likely share common ground about fighting censorship and oppression and encouraging discussions among writers. But she did say that PEN Writes will differ in its structure and in some of its priorities, ideally becoming "a center where sustained and equal advocacy for all writers guides principles, rather than institutional caution."
Differences over Gaza and boycotts
Numerous writers and activists have been unhappy with PEN America's response to the war in Gaza, contending that PEN America has been reluctant to criticize Israel or to defend the rights of Palestinian writers with the same force it has advocated for writers elsewhere.
"I think there's been a feeling for quite a while that PEN's response to the war in Gaza has been inadequate," says PEN Writes member Francine Prose, a former president of PEN America.
Fallout from the war in Gaza led PEN America to call off its annual awards show and "World Voices" festival in 2024 because so many participants dropped out. (Those events resumed in 2025 and 2026). Last summer, PEN America President Dinaw Mengestu resigned after PEN published a report about obstacles and harassment faced by Israeli and Jewish writers since the war began in 2023.
Mengestu, a prize-winning novelist who is now a member of PEN Writes, at the time cited the report's criticism of cultural boycotts and expressed support for the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, or BDS. Organizers advocate economic and cultural pressure on Israel to end the country's occupation of territories captured in the 1967 Mideast war, grant full equality to Arab citizens of Israel and promote the rights of Palestinian refugees to return.
READ MORE: PEN America, facing criticism over its response to the war in Gaza, gathers for annual gala
According to its website, PEN America "emphatically opposes any efforts to inhibit the free international exchange of literature, art, information, or knowledge, including academic and cultural boycotts," while also defending the rights of individuals to "be protected from retaliatory efforts" for participating in boycotts. Mengiste told the AP that PEN Writes takes a broader view, supporting boycotts themselves.
In a statement shared with the AP, PEN America said that it "remains focused on the work we have done for more than a century: defending free expression as a universal right that must be protected regardless of viewpoint. We are committed to building a literary community that makes room for a diversity of voices to defend the very things that unite us — our freedom to write, read and speak our minds."
In July, in the aftermath of Mengestu's departure, PEN America issued a statement citing such initiatives as its direction of $500,000 in emergency aid to Palestinians in Gaza, its legal support for a pro-Palestinian activist threatened with deportation by the Donald Trump administration and a 2025 PEN report entitled "All That Is Lost: The Cultural Destruction of Gaza."
Writers at the center
PEN Writes is aiming for recognition next September at the PEN International Congress in Montenegro. The process includes forming a steering committee, establishing communication with the PEN International Secretariat and "seeking interest from the full diversity of writers" in a given country, according to PEN International's guidelines.
PEN was founded in London in 1921 and has centers in more than 100 countries. PEN Writes would not be the first PEN chapter in the U.S. besides PEN America, which began in 1922 and now has more than 2,300 members. A Los Angeles-based branch operated for decades under various names, including PEN Center USA, before merging with PEN America in 2018.
Coates and Gessen are prize-winning authors and journalists, while Woodson is an acclaimed novelist for young people who has served as an ambassador for the Library of Congress. Other prominent members of PEN Writes include Pulitzer Prize winner Percival Everett, literary agent Nicole Aragi and novelist Hannah Lillith Assadi, who last week won the National Book Award for fiction.
The new PEN chapter is unlikely to approach the size and scope of PEN America, which has more than $20 million in annual revenue, according to its most recent financial statement. But Mengiste says PEN Writes aims to be effective as a more stripped-down, egalitarian organization run entirely by writers on behalf of writers.
"I think writers know firsthand what self-censorship or lost contracts or de-platforming looks like," she says. "We know that what comes for one writer will very likely come for others. We are guardians of each other as much as we are stewards of literature. We do not work with a writers organization, we ARE writers, organized and mobilized to defend all writers."

DR Congoâs government will implement a decree forcing foreign mining companies to open their local units to Congolese shareholders by the end of January, the mines minister said, despite failing to agree key terms with the companies.
The worldâs largest cobalt producer and second-largest copper producer hosts operations run by Glencore, Chinaâs CMOC and Zijin Mining, Canadaâs Ivanhoe Mines and Barrick, and Kazakhstan-backed Eurasian Resources Group.
The decree would apply a 2018 rule reserving 10% of mining companiesâ shares for Congolese citizens, half for employees and half for other individuals. This is on top of the stateâs own mandatory 10% stake. Several foreign mining companies lobbied in June for more time to comply with the new rules.
âI have a draft decree on my desk,â Louis Watum told mining executives at the Makutano Mining business forum in Kinshasa on Monday. âGive it two months, it will pass. And those who donât agree, too bad. See you in court.â
Miners have reportedly questioned how the shares would be priced and whether the rule applies to mines that predate it.
âThis is no longer up for discussion,â Watum said. âWe are moving to action.â
âNo more time for legalismâ
The minister accused the industry of a double standard, arguing that miners sell stakes to other companies but resist Congolese buyers. âThe law must be applied, thatâs all,â he said.
Glencore is negotiating to sell 40% of its interests in its two Congolese mines, Kamoto and Mutanda, to a consortium backed by the US government and Abu Dhabi, in a deal that would value them at about $9 billion. The non-binding agreement, signed in February, would let the buyers direct where their share of the copper and cobalt is sold, as Washington and its allies try to loosen Chinaâs grip on DR Congoâs minerals.
Watum compared the proposed ownership rule to the stock options multinationals grant senior executives, a practice DR Congo was now âdemocratizing,â and said shares reserved for other Congolese investors would be sold at market value. He did not say whether employees would have to pay for their stake, though a draft reported in October proposed giving it to them for free.
Analysts and mining executives have warned that uncertainty over the reforms could undermine investor confidence, just as Kinshasa courts Western capital. Watum, however, said he was prepared for a repeat of the 2018 confrontation, when Ivanhoe Mines, whose DR Congo operations he then ran, was among the major miners that quit the Chamber of Mines industry body over a new mining code. âI donât want it to come to that, but if you want it to come to that, thatâs where weâll end up.â
