King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".
Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.
"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."
Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.
Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.
After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.
There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confrontÂ widespreadÂ violence against women
In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."
He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.
The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."
Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.
Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.
Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

GisÃ¨le Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.
Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms GisÃ¨le Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.
After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.
If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority â marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.
The UK is joined by several other countries, external in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."
The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.
Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."
Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attachÃ© after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention, external.
In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021.
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US, AP reports.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms ensure it had a competitive edge.
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

The Trump administration will soon unveil a fresh batch of tariffs, a person familiar with the plans told Semafor â despite midterm exit polling that found most voters viewed them negatively.
After eight in 10 voters told NBC News that they think President Donald Trumpâs tariffs have hurt the economy, Senate Majority Leader John Thune signaled to Semafor that more Republicans may join Democrats in pushing back on the presidentâs trade agenda.
But Trump isnât deviating, with Trade Representative Jamieson Greer expected to roll out the results of an investigation into market-distorting production levels in dozens of countries, including China, as soon as Tuesday.
The probe of so-called excess capacity, an issue Democrats have also raised concerns about, began prior to the election.
The resulting Section 301 tariffs will vary by country and not surpass levels set by trade deals, the person said.

TORONTO (AP) — The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday said Ottawa had failed to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
"Canada's defense shortfalls speak for themselves," it said. "Canada must get serious and focused."
Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada's defense minister, said Canada had committed 81.8 billion Canadian dollars ($56.9 billion) over five years to rebuild its armed forces and reached NATO's 2% defense spending benchmark five years ahead of schedule.
"Canada is also on track to meet NATO's new commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually in defense by 2035 and is taking concrete steps to build the capabilities needed to meet that goal," he said in a statement.
The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was "laser focused" on modernizing Canada's military after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its defense.
Canada reached NATO's previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but only 2.6% of GDP would go toward core defense.
The Pentagon accused Ottawa of having no credible, fully costed plan to meet NATO's 5% target and postponing the largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. Canada's parliamentary budget watchdog has also questioned how the government will meet the target.
The criticism follows a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts U.S. military officials' participation in Canadian think tank and social events. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.
Wesley Wark, a Canadian national security expert and former government adviser, titled his Monday newsletter "Pentagon Pete strikes again," calling the criticism "insulting and infuriating." He suggested Washington was discounting Canada's NATO deployment in Latvia and its support for Ukraine.
In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby paused a U.S.-Canada defense advisory board established in 1940, accusing Ottawa of failing to make credible progress on its military commitments.
The Pentagon said only 41.9% of Canada's air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%.
It also criticized Ottawa's review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.
Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada's four submarines was seaworthy. His government plans to buy up to 12 replacements.
"We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America," Carney said in June.
Other NATO allies also remain short of the new 5% target. Yet Colby praised Germany's military buildup Sunday as a "tectonic shift" and called Poland a "true model ally."
The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025. The forum's president, Peter Van Praagh, previously served as a senior adviser to a Conservative government in Canada.
Before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Van Praagh warned that Trump might undermine the results if Republicans suffered major losses. If those efforts succeeded, he said, it would mean "the end of the United States as we know it."
Speaking at the Halifax forum Saturday, Rounds said Hegseth's directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

44219b0dcf35.text:
MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.
The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.
Proposed law mirrors European online rules
The legislation is similar to the European Union's Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later.
The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.
"We can't cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks," Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra.
Wells announced on Tuesday her center-left Labor Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.
Greens say bill 'takes power back' from US corporations
Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill.
"Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely U.S. corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits," Shoebridge said in a statement.
The Senate will likely pass the bill on Wednesday and the House of Representatives, where the government holds a majority, would pass it into law before Parliament rises for the year on Thursday.
The Greens' amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million) to 5% of a tech company's global revenue.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration expressed "serious concerns" in a submission in September to a parliamentary committee examining the draft law. U.S. concerns included how Australia would designate what constitutes "foreseeable harm."
US warns bill would lead to censorship of lawful speech
U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said he had conveyed his government's objections to the amended legislation to Wells on Tuesday.
"Vaguely defined 'harms,' backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech," Brat posted on social media.
"As Australia's largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors," he added.
Wells said of their conversation: "There are points of difference and we're ironing them out."
The conservative opposition Liberal Party shares U.S. concerns that the bill empowers government ministers and the nation's online safety watchdog to judge what was harmful. Opposition lawmakers oppose the legislation.
"This bill undermines both the online safety of Australians and our freedom of expression," senior opposition senator Sarah Henderson told reporters.
The Greens' amendments would also give people a legal right to sue social media companies in Australian courts for harms suffered online.
It follows Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest having to go to U.S. courts to sue Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission. The case is not yet resolved.
In October, a U.S. judge ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Bill would let social media users opt out of algorithms
Australia's bill would also let social media users opt out of algorithms that send them content and empower Australia's online safety watchdog to remove apps and websites that fabricate naked images from genuine images of people.
It would also require protections for children against content that promotes eating disorders, hostile ideas about women, pornography, crime or dangerous stunts, or causes serious mental health distress.
Lisa Given, an information sciences expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, described the draft legislation as "very good" and largely in line with European laws.
"It'll be very interesting to see what happens now globally," Given said. "I've always been of the view that if countries can band together and put through similar legislation, collectively we have a better chance of actually pushing Big Tech to make real changes in terms of the design of their systems."

5e855f7da76d.text: President Trump honored a time-worn Washington tradition Tuesday: pardoning poultry — after using the pulpit to praise his White House ballroom and deliver a rally-reminiscent speech. The big picture: Freedom and Feathers, this year's honored birds, continue a bizarre American tradition officially dating back to 1989 — but building on far older presidential lore. Driving the news: "Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests," Trump said at the event, held on the White House's South Lawn. He continued, "I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built." Trump's hotly contested project will be a 90,000-square-foot addition, far larger than the main White House. "I've heard better," he said about the birds' names, though they still earned presidential pardons. Both birds will dodge the oven and retire at Texas A&M University. State of play: The collective 82 pounds of white-feathered flamboyance traveled from West Virginia's Deans Gap Farm for the event. Pointing to his large 2024 election win in West Virginia, Trump said Tuesday, "I won it by a lot. I don't know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me." The pair are just four months old. Per a White House fact sheet , Freedom's favorite treat is Dr. Pepper. Feathers prefers to snack on Golden Delicious apples, which — like the turkeys — hail from West Virginia. Between the lines: Trump has never shied away from using the event to ruffle feathers. Last year, he jabbed at former President Biden and attacked Chicago leadership, derailing the focus on his feathered guests by calling Gov. JB Pritzker (D) a "fat slob." During his first term, he joked that the turkeys trotting before him had were slated to "appear in Adam Schiff's basement," a nod to the Democrat who led the 2019 impeachment inquiry into Trump. While Trump has taken presidential rhetoric to a new level, he's not the first to have stuffed political zingers into the bizarre tradition. In 2022, Biden seemingly poked fun at Trump's false claim he'd won the 2020 election, saying : "The votes are in. They've been counted and verified. There's no ballot stuffing. There's no fowl play." Worth noting: PETA called on the White House to end the event, saying presidents are "conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers." President Tracy Reiman called the idea of retirement for the birds "all squawk, no substance, " noting fattened-up turkeys often die prematurely. Flashback: While George H.W. Bush formalized the pardon in 1989, the White House's quirky turkey ties stretch back well over a century. Abraham Lincoln is frequently credited with sparing the first turkey on record at the urging of his son in the 1860s, according to the White House Historical Association. Harry Truman welcomed a live turkey from the National Turkey Federation in 1947, and the photo-op was hatched. But that bird wasn't such a lucky duck — perhaps becoming part of the Thanksgiving feast. Since then, the NTF has presented the presidential bird. And President John F. Kennedy was gifted a turkey in 1963, but decided instead to "let this one grow." The bottom line: Through decades of conflict, campaigns and chaos, presidents have come face-to-beak with the ubiquitous Thanksgiving birds. Go deeper: The turkey pardon: A quirky White House custom

edd2bb6573a2.text:
Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.
That's because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws — those that ban abortion at six weeks or all stages of pregnancy.
And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.
Officials in 2 states are calling for constitutional protections for abortion
Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy — with some exceptions — and four more do so after about the first six weeks.
In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states — Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — already allow abortion through until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.
Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.
Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states' constitutions to create a right to abortion.
Voters in a dozen states already have passed similar amendments, including two — Nevada and Virginia — this year. Voters in November also kept such protections in Missouri but defeated an initiative to add them to state law in Idaho.
Georgia Democrats could attempt to repeal a ban
In Georgia, where Democrats gained the House and the governor's office, abortion is banned in most cases after fetal cardiac activity can be detected — around six weeks into pregnancy and before many women realize they're pregnant.
Josh McLaurin, the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor, is optimistic that one Republican state senator would be willing to join Democrats to repeal that law.
READ MORE: Abortion rights amendment passes in Virginia
The measure could get at least a vote in the Senate, he said, because Republicans will have a 29-27 majority and may not take a "hyper-partisan approach" to block it.
McLaurin said that voters see the ban as a healthcare issue, especially after a state review board in 2024 found that two women died in Georgia after doctors were hesitant to perform abortions that could have saved their lives.
Still, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms acknowledged that a GOP-held state Senate could be an obstacle.
"If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we're going to take that opportunity," Bottoms said at a news conference. "And it may not be this session."
A new Texas attorney general will end some legal challenges
After winning the attorney general election in Texas, Democrat Nathan Johnson said he would not sue out-of-state medical providers who prescribe abortion pills via telehealth and ship them to patients in the state as the outgoing attorney general, Republican Ken Paxton, has done. Paxton dropped his suits in November.
Those pills often come from states that seek to protect medical professionals who prescribe them through telehealth and ship them to patients in places with bans. That practice is why the number of abortions has been higher since the fall of Roe. It's also the heart of the current abortion legal battles.
Johnson could also withdraw Texas from a lawsuit challenging federal policy on the abortion pill mifepristone and decide not to defend the state's abortion restrictions against lawsuits.
"It is deeply gutting that now we don't have Texas to be fighting with the pro-life side on this," said Kelsey Pritchard, spokesperson for SBA Pro-Life America.
Abortion opponents are focused on access to pills
Pritchard and other anti-abortion activists are pushing the Trump administration to make mifepristone harder to get by persuading the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is studying the drug, to bar filling prescriptions through the mail or at pharmacies. The FDA has said it'll have more information by March.
They're also counting on remaining Republican state attorneys general to keep up the fight.
Ohio lawmakers this month passed legislation to bar telehealth prescriptions for mifepristone sent into the state and to reimpose a 24-hour waiting period before obtaining an abortion. It's not clear whether outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine will sign them into law — or how courts would rule on legal challenges. Voters passed a constitutional amendment protecting abortion access in 2023.
Ingrid Duran, state legislative director at the National Right to Life Committee, said her group will keep pushing measures that Democrats sometimes support — such as supporting ways for women to anonymously and safely give up newborns for adoption. And, she said, it will encourage anti-abortion bills that may not have much of a chance of passing now as a way to build for the future.
"We're not going to give up just because it's going to be more challenging," she said.
Republicans still control the White House
Some congressional Democrats are planning to push forward a measure that would bar states from banning abortion before viability and rescind restrictions that some states have — such as requiring multiple doctor's visits or ultrasounds.
With a Trump veto expected if it reaches him, the effort would be aimed largely at forcing him to reject a policy that

cd514e041eeb.text: Prosecutors in Mecklenburg County, N.C., announced Tuesday they are dropping a criminal charge against Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) related to an un-returned rental car in 2019. Why it matters: The charge had been a bothersome footnote for Womack since her sudden rise from obscurity on Election Day, when she unexpectedly won a heavily Republican district. Womack, a 49-year-old minister and consultant, is one of several "wave babies" who were largely unknown to national Democrats before their upset midterm victories. Driving the news: Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather said in a statement released Tuesday afternoon that his office has submitted a voluntary dismissal and that the matter is "closed." Womack was charged with "Felony Failure to Return Hired Property" after failing to return a rental car in 2019 following two renewals, Merriweather said. The car was recovered by law enforcement. A criminal summons was issued against Womack in 2020 but only served on Oct. 11 of this year, just days before the start of early voting. Merriweather said that the unidentified rental dealer has reached an agreement with Womack, in which she paid them the "assessed rental cost" of the car from its overdue date to its return, and does "not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved." What they're saying: " For almost seven years Ms. Womack was unaware a criminal summons had been issued," Womack's lawyer Harold Cogdell said in a statement shared with Axios. "Upon learning of this unresolved matter, Ms. Womack promptly and fully resolved this matter with the rental car company." Cogdell said there are "questions remaining" about the timing of the summons being served, but that "Ms. Womack's [sic] is laser focused on preparing to serve the residents of the North Carolina's 14th Congressional District." Womack, who has said she was experiencing housing insecurity in 2019, referred Axios to Cogdell's statement when sought for comment.

One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.
The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.
The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.
Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.
He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.
Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.
Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.
On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.
She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.
After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.
According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.
The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.
It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.
However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.
The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

- Published
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down more than 7% in early afternoon trading, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's return was announced.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

WASHINGTON (AP) — A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington, marking another instance of federal enforcement at airports.
Eva Yi Xie, a third-year doctoral student at Princeton, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she tried to fly back to New Jersey from a conference in the nation's capital, her university adviser Carlos Brody said in a social media post.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, says Xie overstayed her visa and did not have authorization to study in the United States.
"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Rodney Priestley, dean of the university's graduate school, said in a statement. "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."
Two days after Xie was taken into custody in Washington, masked immigration officers detained a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge in Seattle. ICE has ramped up detentions at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed their visas.
Kerry Doyle, Xie's lawyer, said she came to the U.S. at age 14 with her family from China and has had an asylum application pending for years. Doyle insisted that Xie has permission to live, work and study in the U.S. while her case is pending.
Doyle said Xie is being held in ICE's Caroline Detention Center in Virginia.
DHS said in a statement that Xie came to the United States on a temporary visa on March 16, 2016, but "chose to violate our nation's laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016."
The agency said she did not have valid permission to study in the U.S. and "a pending application does not confer legal status."
"Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," the DHS statement said.
Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey said in a statement that his office contacted ICE and didn't get a "satisfactory response" about why she was detained. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, also a Democrat, directed her administration to coordinate with federal lawmakers and the state of Virginia to get more information.
"While ICE claims to go after the worst of the worst, time and again the record shows they do not — and their tactics are making New Jerseyans less safe," Sherrill's spokesperson, Steve Sigmund, said in an email.
On her professional website, Xie said her research at Princeton Neuroscience Institute "seeks to understand the neural basis of decision-making." She said she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024.
Gisela Perez Kusakawa, executive director of the Asian American Scholar Forum, demanded that Xie's rights be protected.
"Due process and the rule of law build the trust that lets scientists, researchers, and students feel safe pursuing their studies and work here," Kusakawa said in a statement. "That trust is what attracts the world's best scientific talents to the United States, and it is the foundation for our country's next generation of scientific leaders."
Associated Press writer Heather Hollingsworth in Mission, Kansas, contributed to this report.

2018c49adb0d.text:
This year's U.N. climate talks in Turkey failed to deliver consensus on how the world should confront climate change, even as it triggers more natural disasters that hit hardest in vulnerable countries that didn't cause the problem.
Dozens of nations on Sunday objected to the final text — meant to guide climate actions — presented at the summit, called COP31, because it didn't mention fossil fuels, primarily the use of coal, oil and gas that drives climate change. It also didn't include increased financial commitments to help hard-hit nations adapt to a warmer world.
That leaves a lot of questions about what happens next — and what it means for ordinary, everyday people — as scientists warn that the world is on track to exceed goals to limit warming, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement.
Here's what to know:
Some progress can still be made without an agreement
Even though there wasn't a final agreement at COP31, climate action is still moving forward, as nations, states, provinces, Indigenous groups and even local officials take action on their own.
That includes a new voluntary initiative on transitioning away from fossil fuels that falls outside of the United Nations' purview. Almost 60 countries participated in the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Colombia this year, and the second is scheduled for next year in the island nation of Tuvalu.
Rather than being held back, countries "are building new networks to work together," said climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe from The Nature Conservancy.
She said most climate action takes place below the national level — including in the United States, which did not participate directly in the U.N. climate talks for the second year in a row. Although President Donald Trump pulled the U.S. out of the Paris Agreement, a delegation from the U.S. that included California Gov. Gavin Newsom attended the summit to pledge climate action.
Experts warn that the world must urgently and drastically reduce emissions to avert the worst effects of climate change.
A new urgency to confront climate change
This year's climate summit came after a year of devastating natural disasters made worse — and far more likely — because of climate change.
A summer heat wave in Europe killed more than 50,000 people, with nearly two-thirds of the deaths blamed on human-caused climate change. In Nepal, a partially collapsed Himalayan glacier triggered flooding that washed away entire villages and left thousands dead or missing — with more melting glaciers at risk of doing the same.
READ MORE: The collapse of UN climate talks over fossil fuels was years in the making
Wildfires raged across the globe, including in Canada — with the smoke making air quality in several U.S. cities among the worst in the world and prompting warnings that everyone's health was at risk.
Still, those and many other climate-related disasters failed to move developed countries to more forcefully confront the underlying problem of fossil fuels at COP31. Nor did stark warnings about where the Earth is headed, as heat records fall daily, monthly and annually.
A report released during the summit by the independent nonprofit Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years — meaning the world is almost certain to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
Countries have established plans to reduce fossil fuel emissions. But even if they fulfill all their promises — increasingly unlikely — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said.
Experts say without action on climate, inequality will continue to grow
Transitioning away from fossil fuels takes money, and vulnerable nations went to the U.N. summit demanding that wealthier nations most responsible for the climate crisis do more to help them.
At past summits, rich nations promised to help poorer countries finance the transition and harden their infrastructure against natural disasters. The summit failed to produce an agreement on increasing support — experts say the amount currently pledged falls vastly short of future needs — or on determining who pays what and getting rich countries to pay what they already promised.
That means things like early warning systems in Nepal, devastated by this year's flooding, will be more difficult to build, said Hayhoe. Island nations that are being battered by rising seas also might not be able to afford projects without easier access to money.
Yet, as such disasters intensify, international climate adaptation and disaster preparedness aid programs have been slashed. That includes the Trump administration's abrupt cuts to U.S. foreign aid in 2025 that eliminated or sharply curtailed programs serving millions of people worldwide, including for disaster preparedness.
Climate change also is affecting rich countries, including the U.S. and countries in Europe, which are experiencing larger, more intense heat waves, droughts and wildfires, record flooding and other costly disasters.
That just underscores the scale of the crisis in poorer, even more vulnerable countries, experts say.
"If we fail on climate, the inequities we see today will grow almost beyond imagining: widespread crop failures, people losing access to water, rising conflict over basic resources, mass migration and growing tensions between countries," Hayhoe said.
Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, said developed countries were to blame for the failed U.N. talks.
"We are witnessing human suffering on an unimaginable scale, and we had hoped this COP would take steps to protect people from the worsening climate crisis," Essop said. "Instead, rich nations gutted the very measures that could have made a difference."

2a4a16b8eb30.text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — High tides along the Pacific Coast could break 40-year-old records and flood low-lying coastal communities, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach 2.6 feet above normal Tuesday before peaking Wednesday at 2.8 feet above normal, said Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.
The Bay Area's highest recorded tide reached 2.9 feet above normal in San Francisco on Jan. 27, 1983, he said. San Francisco's famed Embarcadero waterfront, which flooded during heavy rain last week, is again at risk of flooding.
King tides, the highest tides of the year, occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.
The weather service issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area on Wednesday, when breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.
"Remain out of the water and stay off of jetties, piers, and rocks. Never turn your back to the ocean!" the agency said in a social media post.
Heavy rain forecast for Tuesday evening into Wednesday could worsen street flooding.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, who urged people over the weekend to consider avoiding holiday travel because of an "extremely serious" situation, later said the forecast had improved somewhat.
"As you make plans for Thanksgiving, keep the weather in mind. Check conditions before traveling, and avoid unnecessary trips when roads are flooded or winds are strong," he wrote on social media on Monday.
Farther north, in Humboldt County near the Oregon border, the sheriff's office ordered evacuations in a small coastal community where some buildings flooded on Monday, saying people needed to leave by Tuesday morning.
"The tides are expected to be higher by Tuesday, and the southerly winds will have been blowing for 24 hours by then, and so that will push the storm surge even higher," said Matthew Kidwell, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Humboldt County.
Coastal flooding also possible in the Pacific Northwest
National Weather Service offices in Portland and Seattle warned of coastal flooding through Friday. The most significant flooding could occur Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day as several weather systems bring strong winds and rising surf coinciding with high tides.
Waves can sweep people off rocks or knock them off their feet and pull them into the ocean, the agency warned.
Washington State Ferries has canceled several sailings because of high tides. About 300,000 people are expected to use the ferry system over the holiday weekend, and extreme tides could disrupt their trips.
Heavy snow in the mountains could slow holiday travel over passes, especially along Interstate 90 east of Seattle.
More flooding forecast for Florida
In South Florida, king tides are expected to cause coastal flooding from Palm Beach to Miami. Water levels could remain elevated for several hours before and after high tide Wednesday and Thursday mornings.
A storm arriving Tuesday night could increase the risk of flooding if it moves over land, the National Weather Service said.
Many South Florida communities were just beginning to dry out after slow-moving storms dumped more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) of rain less than a week earlier.
The St. Johns River has been above flood stage near Cocoa since Nov. 2. Last week, it broke a record set in 1953. The river is forecast to remain at least 2 feet (0.6 meters) above flood stage, according to the weather service.
Associated Press writers Martha Bellisle in Seattle and John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia, contributed.

f696ef9bf1a2.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City is once again facing what's become its eternal foe: wind.
An incoming storm is expected to bring heavy winds and rain to the region, and the parade's iconic character balloons — which have graced the canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers for decades — could be grounded if it gets too windy.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower balloons or cancel their flights entirely, with local officials wary of strong winds knocking them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
What could ground the balloons?
City rules have long stated that large balloons can't fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 kph).
These measures were implemented after an accident in 1997 where a balloon careened into a lamppost near Central Park and critically injured a woman.
What weather is expected for this year's parade?
Brian Hurley, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service, said the parade crowd should be ready for a wet and windy day. But for the balloons, he said, the big headache could be the wind gusts.
Sustained winds will range from 15 to 25 mph (24 to 40 kph), with gusts of 30 to 40 mph (48 to 64 kph) in the morning that could grow stronger in the late afternoon, Hurley said. The parade kicks off at 8:30 a.m.
READ MORE: High-flying balloon characters star in Thanksgiving parade
Hurley also noted that gusts could feel more concentrated because Manhattan's tall buildings often create a wind tunnel effect.
When will a decision be made?
Whether the balloons take to the sky this year will be a decision made on the morning of the parade, Macy's said in a statement, as officials keep tabs on wind gauges along the route.
The New York Police Department has previously described it as a game-day decision, with officials adding that the balloons can be steered off the route and deflated on a side street if weather conditions get bad enough that handlers can't control them.
In past years, balloons have flown a bit lower than usual because of weather, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight, and an optimal altitude for wind speeds.
Have the balloons been grounded before?
Balloons were grounded due to weather in 1971.
"Our team is closely monitoring the weather forecast with our City and agency partners, and as always, the safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority," Macy's said in a statement.

e236fe549aab.text:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday will award the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani.
Giuliani was hailed for leading New York after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Trump has called Giuliani, a fellow New Yorker, the "greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."
Giuliani's public life has undergone a rise and fall in recent years. After leading the nation's biggest city through Sept. 11, he mounted a brief campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008, becoming one of the most recognizable U.S. political figures.
As Trump's personal lawyer, he was a central figure in efforts to overturn Trump's 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Courts rejected the fraud claims he advanced, and two former Georgia election workers won a $148 million defamation judgment against him.
He was later sanctioned by courts and disbarred in New York and Washington for repeatedly making false statements about the election.
Trump said last year he would award the medal to Giuliani, shortly after he was seriously injured in a car crash.
Giuliani, 82, said in a statement he was honored by the award.
"I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together," he said.
In his second term, Trump has awarded the medal posthumously to Welles Crowther, an equities trader who became known as the "man in the red bandanna" after rescuing several people in the Sept. 11 attacks. Trump also posthumously honored Charlie Kirk, the assassinated activist who had inspired a generation of young conservatives and pushed the nation's politics to the right.
Trump has awarded a string of presidential medals going back to his first term, including to golf legend Tiger Woods, ex-football coach Lou Holtz and conservative economist Arthur Laffer as well as to New York Yankees Hall of Fame closer Mariano Rivera and conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh, who got the award during the 2020 State of the Union.
He also awarded posthumous medals to Babe Ruth and Elvis Presley.

f47ff55bcca2.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr.'s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.
The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years' worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether U.S. President Donald Trump's eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Both Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital, which is based in Palm Beach, Florida, deny any wrongdoing.
The investigation was opened over the summer
The letters ramp up an investigation that Raskin opened in August into Trump Jr.'s firm, which he said "suddenly struck investment gold" after naming the president's son as a partner in 2024. As one of the lawmakers who will be spearheading Democrats' oversight of the Trump administration when they take control of Congress in January, Raskin has said that uncovering information about bribery and financial corruption will be among his top priorities.
Trump Jr. has repeatedly rejected accusations that he has exploited government access for profit. At an Axios event last week, he acknowledged that he understood people's corruption concerns, but said that they weren't accurate, noting he has been an investor for decades.
"I can see what they are saying. It doesn't make it so," he said. "The notion that I should somehow sit in a corner, suck my thumb and wait, you know, eight years — in this case 12 years — till we're out of the political game, it's not real."
1789 Capital also has forcefully denied claims of wrongdoing. In a letter to Raskin in September, the company's lawyers defended the firm's investment thesis as predating Trump's administration and said that while it "welcomes legitimate congressional oversight," it "has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship."
On Monday, the company's attorney, Bill Burck, said the September letter explained flaws in Raskin's understanding, but Raskin "never bothered to reply."
"Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here, but persists in his tall tales against 1789," Burck said. "These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."
The firm was founded in 2022 and Trump Jr. was announced as a partner in November 2024.
'Serendipitous timing' of investments, Raskin says in letters
In his letters to the four companies obtained by The Associated Press, Raskin outlined how federal policies or contracts had benefited their businesses and claimed that 1789 Capital had suspiciously "serendipitous timing" when it invested in them.
Hadrian Automation, he wrote, received nearly $1 billion in U.S. Navy and Army contracts in March — its first-ever federal contracts — after bringing 1789 Capital on as an investor in 2025.
Juul, Raskin wrote, received Food and Drug Administration clearance to keep its electronic cigarette products on the market in July 2025, four months after 1789 Capital had taken a stake in the company.
The congressman wrote that GrabAGun got help from 1789 to go public and put Trump Jr. on its board before the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives issued a proposed rule to ease the process of shipping guns to people's homes.
Raskin also raised questions about the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission closing investigations into Polymarket in July 2025, after 1789 Capital already had invested in the prediction market platform.
GrabAGun said in a statement that Raskin's letter "is a political document, and its allegations are baseless."
"ATF's review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment. GrabAGun's only input came through public comments on several of those proposals," the statement read.
Juul Labs said that it was reviewing its letter closely.
"As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking," it said in an emailed response.
The other recipients of the letters didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump administration has begun to push back on Democrats' investigations
The Trump administration has taken steps to push back on the Democrats' oversight efforts, including an executive order on Friday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged.
That could complicate compliance with Raskin's investigation for at least one of the companies, Hadrian Automation, which is a federal contractor.
Raskin has called Trump's order "blatantly unlawful" and said that public contractors have a "duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls."

295ca193a63e.text:
- Published
A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.
The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.
Twenty-four-year-old Wesley Sothole, who pleaded guilty, was handed a five-year suspended prison sentence and was ordered to be deported from South Africa.
He is one of five Zimbabweans who were arrested at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg on 8 November. South African prosecutors have not confirmed which side the Zimbabweans allegedly intended to fight for.
Sothole's four co-accused have yet to enter pleas and are due to return to the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court on 1 December for further plea and sentencing proceedings.
Another four Zimbabweans were arrested at a hotel in Johannesburg at the same time in a joint operation and are facing a different court process.
The investigation has involved South African police, Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies.
South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.
There has been growing concern across Africa over the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war in Ukraine, with some reportedly being lured to Russia by promises of lucrative civilian employment.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Some have been captured and are being held as prisoners of war.
In March, Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia.
Kenyan Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue. He said an agreement had been reached for Russia to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In the same month, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.
The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 of its nationals who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
South Africa's government said it condemned "the exploitation of young vulnerable people by individuals working with foreign military entities".
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.
Additional reporting by Khanyisile Ngcobo in Johannesburg.

0539d824b827.text:
Along England’s southern coast lies a fishing community whose existence can be traced back almost a millennium. From its shingled shore, Hastings once housed the largest beach-launched fleet in Europe. But when retired fisherman Jerry Percy visited a few weeks ago, he could count the operational boats on his fingers.
“If you take the argument to the end game, then you’ll have nothing but a picture-postcard fleet bobbing about in little pretty harbors and bugger-all else,” said Percy, describing a “spiral of decline” across the U.K.’s small-boat fleet.
This hollowing out of coastal livelihoods is part of a “rigged system,” according to a new report by Oceana UK. Unequal government subsidies, outdated quota systems and catch limits that routinely ignore science have concentrated wealth in large corporate fleets at the expense of coastal communities and the marine ecosystems they rely on.
“The non-compliance, the discards, the very poor transparency and the quota inequality is all really adding up,” said Izzy Ross, Oceana UK’s habitats and fisheries campaign manager. “It’s not a fair playing field for those who want to do things right and want to do things more sustainably.”
Fishing vessels over 39 feet were found to have falsified logbooks, deployed illegal gear or dumped fish during 66 percent of at-sea inspections in English waters between April 2025 and March 2026, according to Freedom of Information data obtained from the Marine Management Organisation.
For vessels under 33 feet, these activities were documented just 10 percent of the time.
Operating “out of sight and out of mind” in rough seas where boarding is often impossible, larger vessels easily evade scrutiny, said Percy, who spent decades fishing the entire circumference of the U.K., and jokes he’s been both “poacher and gamekeeper.” Even when violations were documented, authorities merely issued “verbal advice” in almost 70 percent of cases.
Only 1 percent of infringements resulted in any financial penalty—totalling less than $37,000 across the entire fleet between April 2024 and March 2025.
“When you compare it to the amount of millions of pounds going out in fuel subsidies and some of the profits that these large [boats] are pulling in, that’s a very, very small amount,” said Ross. “It’s not even something they probably notice.”
Crews scrapped more than 100,000 metric tons of dead or dying fish, across 57 U.K. quota stocks, last year—equal to the weight of around 8,300 of London’s red double-decker buses. From spotted dogfish and silver smelt to haddock and whiting, crews often chuck lower-value catches to keep space for potentially more profitable products, or dump “choke species” with low quotas that would otherwise force boats back to port.
Ross warns the “disgusting level of discards” is pushing some populations toward total collapse. For Irish Sea plaice, a popular flatfish, over 80 percent caught between 2023 and 2025 was thrown back overboard, despite unsustainable fishing pressure for the species and a recommendation of no catches for 2027.
Because accurate discard data relies on occasional observers and voluntary disclosures, the 100,000-ton figure is likely an underestimate. When remote monitoring cameras were deployed on fishing boats in New Zealand in 2024, the true discard rate jumped 46 percent above original estimates.
Though the U.K. government recently announced the requirement of cameras and GPS monitoring for large pelagic boats—those that catch fish in the water column rather than from the seabed—from November 2028, the rules exclude bottom trawlers, which have the highest discard rates.
“It’s a step in the right direction, but it’s not far enough,” said Ross. “It’ll be 2028 before that’s implemented, and we’d like to see the government going further because it’s a really pressing issue. If we’re discarding another 100,000 tons next year and the year after, we need it to come sooner.”
A Marine Management Organisation spokesperson told Inside Climate News the agency “takes non-compliance with fisheries rules seriously and uses a risk-based, intelligence-led approach to target inspection and enforcement activity where the risk is greatest,” highlighting discards are not always illegal, and said it’s working with regulators to keep monitoring “operationally effective.”
While boats under 33 feet make up three-quarters of the fleet, they’re allocated just a few percent of the quota—part of what Oceana UK describes as the “systemic injustices” of British fisheries.
Nearly 90 percent of U.K. quota is still allocated based on what vessels caught between 1994 and 1996, turning a brief historical snapshot into a tradeable commodity controlled by a small handful of large companies.
“Our ocean is for everyone, and our fish stocks are a public resource. Yet successive governments have created a system that favours a handful of large companies, allowing them to profit at the expense of the ocean and local communities,” said Hugo Tagholm, executive director of Oceana UK in a press release.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Last year, the five largest quota-holding companies pocketed over $160 million in combined profits while drawing disproportionately from taxpayer-funded fuel subsidies. Traveling farthest offshore with the heaviest gear, vessels over 130 feet benefited from an estimated $300 million in British fuel subsidies between 2012 and 2022.
Across European waters, these “mega-industrial” trawlers burn the most fuel, scrape the seafloor with vast trawl nets and swipe the most marine life.
Percy, now senior advisor to the Low Impact Fishers of Europe organization, believes the small-boat fleet he’s spent decades advocating for is “finished” if current trends continue.

Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.
The pair deny any wrongdoing.
Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence â of which six months were suspended â over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.
In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail â two of them suspended â and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.
The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the â¬50m (Â£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.
At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file â the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.
So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" and benefiting from witness tampering. They deny any wrongdoing.
