Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).
It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.
While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.
The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".
Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.
But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.
There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.
Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.
But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers, external warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.
The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.
On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".
However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.
This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".
Localised trapping and culling was trialled in Wales on nine farms between 2017 and 2024, but the cost involved drew criticism after hundreds of thousands of pounds was spent on killing a small number of badgers.
Officials told a briefing for journalists that "selective removal" of badgers was a possibility in future, but "[we] cannot give you a timeline".
Changes to cattle testing were also being proposed by the government, to help spot infection earlier.
They will work with the farming industry to explore "safe ways" of moving cattle out of TB restricted herds, to help businesses continue to operate.
Farms experiencing persistent issues and under so-called enhanced management will be offered more choice in how their situation is handled.
There is talk of a new advisory service for farmers and vets - and moves to provide better, more up-to-date data on the latest disease risk.
Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".
"We will not stand by while farmers face uncertainty and anxiety, nor will we pursue a mass non-selective cull," he added.
"Instead, we will be taking evidence-based and science-led action, incorporating the three pillars of cattle, people and wildlife.
"Farmers and the public will rightly judge us on whether we prevent disease and reduce its impact, even when the decisions are difficult."
NFU Cymru president Abi Reader said farmers needed to see action quickly on measures promised in the government's announcement.
"Going for a mass badger cull was never going to be on the cards - that's quite a seismic change," she said.
"There's certainly this leaning towards what we call a trap, test and remove (programme) - that's really good, but we need to see that starting and actually being acted on."
"That's what farmers will have wanted to see today from this statement," she said.
"For those farmers who are right in the eye of the storm - and have been dealing with TB for a very long time - I think they were hoping they would have seen something that would have given them more hope for the future."
Ian Rickman, president of the Farmers' Union of Wales, said it was "positive to note that targeted and proportionate action will now be taken on TB in wildlife where evidence supports this approach".
He said the loss of 92,000 cattle under bovine TB meant it was now time to intensify cooperation between groups including the industry, the veterinary profession and government.
RSPCA Cymru said it "cautiously welcomed the majority of today's statement".
"However, the fight has not been won yet. The killing of wildlife is not off the table, which is a concern," said Billie-Jade Thomas, the charity's senior public affairs manager.
"The Welsh government must prioritise a science-led, cattle-focussed approach towards combating this awful disease," she added.
Nigel Palmer, chief executive of The Badger Trust said he was "disappointed".
"It's good that the mass cull has been ruled out [but] we still don't see any need on a targeted or any other basis to bring badgers back into the equation."
"Wales has led for so long on bovine TB and actually has really good performance figures," he said.

The EU and the UK agreed to link their carbon markets in a deal that will reduce trade friction while helping to lower the costs of decarbonization. Since Brexit, Brussels and London have operated similar, but separate, emissions-trading systems that cap industrial emissions and require power plants and factories producing steel, chemicals, and cements to acquire allowances for every ton of carbon they emit. From 2028, allowances will be used interchangeably, creating a larger and more stable market that reduces the risks of investing in clean technology.
The agreement also paves the way for mutual exemption of emission-intensive goods from carbon border levies, with the UKâs own carbon tariff coming into force in the new year. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said work would also continue on the UKâs participation in the blocâs electricity market, which industry groups say would make cross-border trading more efficient and strengthen the case for investments in interconnectors.

LONDON (AP) — Two men were arrested on the British royal family's Sandringham estate, police said Tuesday, after a reported break-in at the country home of Prince William and Princess Catherine.
Norfolk Police said that officers were called Monday evening to reported "suspicious activity" at an address on the rural estate in eastern England. After a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing.
The suspects were being held in custody Tuesday and hadn't been charged.
Police said that "the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident."
The Sun newspaper reported that masked men made their way into Anmer Hall on Monday night, when William, Kate and the rest of their family weren't present.
William was in London on Tuesday and met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham for talks at 10 Downing St.
William and Kate's Kensington Palace office said that it wouldn't comment on security matters.
Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II. William and Kate use the secluded red brick Georgian mansion about 110 miles north of London as a country residence on weekends. The couple and their three children spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, west of London, which they have described as their "forever home."
Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.
In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. Charles and Queen Camilla weren't at Windsor Castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Kate were in their nearby house.
Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Elizabeth.
In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the queen's private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.
Fagan was sent to a psychiatric hospital, then released and was later jailed for unrelated criminal offenses.
Jill Lawless contributed to this report.

Timâs view
The breakdown of COP31 reveals a process in need of an overhaul, but the solution shouldnât be hard to find.
Depending on your perspective, the failure of negotiators in TÃ¼rkiye to reach a consensus deal on transitioning away from fossil fuels may not actually be a failure. The UN process worked as designed: The minority of countries that wanted to avoid naming the root causes of climate change were blocked by the majority from pushing through a weak agreement. The compromises needed to achieve consensus in past COPs, the former UK climate advisor Michael Jacobs wrote this week, mainly served to dilute any sense of urgency; failure to reach an agreement is, in this telling, actually a stronger political signal about how deeply committed most countries are to decarbonization.
The most obvious solution is to scrap the consensus-driven elements of the COP agenda altogether. In past summits, the topline âcover decisionâ agreement of the sort that crumbled in Antalya was primarily a kind of thesis statement, framing negotiations on a host of niche tracks, from carbon markets to adaptation finance. But in the decade since the Paris Agreement, thereâs very little left to be negotiated. Instead, the cover decision wastes time and political capital trying to bring along a tiny minority of countries â primarily Saudi Arabia and Russia â that are unlikely to ever share the same views on climate change as, say, Tuvalu.
Itâs probably time to give up on this element of COP so that countries have more bandwidth to hash out action plans in smaller groupings, such as the electrification target that dozens agreed in TÃ¼rkiye. The EU, which led opposition to the COP31 cover decision, and a number of African nations â next yearâs COP32 will be in Ethiopia â have already said this week that the consensus approach is no longer fit for purpose.
âThe absence of agreement on the wording of the âcover decisionâ does not mean an absence of action,â Angela Wilkinson, secretary-general of the World Energy Council, told me. âThe test is whether we can change how we produce, deliver, and use energy: replacing fossil fuel use with cleaner electricity where it makes sense, and cutting emissions from the fuels we still need.â
Notable
- Private sector investment in carbon-cutting and adaptation projects in Africa tripled in four years, reaching $26.5 billion in 2023-24, pointing to a shift in the continentâs climate finance landscape.

- Published
A federal court has unsealed heavily redacted documents related to the search of US lawmaker Ilhan Omar's home last month, despite an attempt from prosecutors to block the release.
Some 169 pages of court documents show investigators were looking for potential criminal violations involving Omar going all the way back to 1980.
The Minnesota Democrat, who has not been charged with a crime and has denied any wrongdoing, moved to the US from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalised citizen in 2000.
Omar, who has been an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search on social media as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement".
After the search of her home in October, immigration agents offered limited details saying it was related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation.
The exchanges in the released court documents show a back-and-forth between a judge and federal prosecutors over executing a warrant and releasing the documents to the public.
Although heavily redacted, the documents offer a glimpse into what the investigation may involve.
The records show the government applied for a warrant to search her Washington DC home for evidence of crimes "involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present". The specific offences are redacted in the unsealed documents.
Prosecutors said they were pursuing evidence of crimes that allegedly happened decades ago and do not have anything to do with Omar's work in Congress.
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and earlier this year, a fellow congresswoman, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.
In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", and made allegations of marital fraud against Omar.
Separately, the White House's border tsar, Tom Homan, told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar denied the allegations.
"I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said.
Last month, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.
The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it is being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.

- Published
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.
The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.
Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.
The UKHSA said summer 2026 was "exceptional", and that it recorded the highest annual number of heat episodes, which it defines as days when the average Central England Temperature (CET) is at least 20C.
There were seven heat episodes between May and August, adding up to a total of 41 days.
A summer of persistent heat
The UK experienced widespread heatwaves as 2026 became the hottest summer on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.
A heatwave in May smashed the temperature record for that month by more than 2C, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.
A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.
Both were caused by heat domes - stalled areas of high pressure that trap hot air over the region.
Another heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.
The UK's hottest day on record was 19 July 2022, when temperatures hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.
A lack of rainfall this year also saw droughts declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires caused devastation in some parts of the country.
UKHSA said the findings "underline the need for longer-term adaptation" to a warming climate, and that adapting homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings would be "increasingly important".
Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at UKHSA, said this summer's hot weather had a substantial impact on public health, "particularly during the early heat episodes in May and June".
He added that periods of extreme heat are expected to become "longer, more frequent and more intense" as the climate continues to warm.
Speaking in the Commons, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she wanted "to offer the deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer".
"The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, and that is why I have asked the NHS to now prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter," she said.
During a speech at the COP31 summit earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke about the extreme weather experienced in the UK this summer, describing it as "not normal".

e9ae2fb1ebf6.text:
For Democrats eyeing the White House, President Donald Trump's coziness with tech executives was already a potent target even before he successfully pressured Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive.
Now his extraordinary intervention has crystallized their concerns about the growing power of artificial intelligence companies and his blending of government and business interests.
Huang had lost his job because of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing. Eleven days later, Nvidia's board put him back in charge.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Although Democrats lack a unified vision for how to handle the proliferation of artificial intelligence, the episode was an opportunity for them to speak largely in unison as they called Huang's return a threat to national security and described Trump's role as corrupt.
Nvidia's decision sends a message "that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with President Trump," said Sen. Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, in an interview with The Associated Press.
"We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn't take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it's OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more," Gallego said.
Nvidia is under scrutiny over whether it's complying with U.S. restrictions on the export of its most advanced semiconductors to China and their use by Chinese tech firms.
The company's share price dropped sharply during Huang's brief absence, dragging down the broader stock market to one of its worst weeks since the 2008 financial crisis, before recovering with Monday's announcement of his reinstatement.
Trump argues that Huang's leadership at Nvidia is necessary
Still euphoric over their sweeping midterm victories, many ambitious Democrats are still feeling around for the right message on artificial intelligence, which carries both promise and peril as it becomes increasingly intertwined with the economy, infrastructure and daily life.
Trump's intervention put a spotlight on his own financial stake in the company, which his latest financial disclosure report says was worth at least $12.5 million at the end of 2025, and on the millions of dollars Huang contributed to Trump's ballroom project.
Writing on social media that "rules should apply to everyone," California Rep. Ro Khanna noted that "the rich & powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price."
Trump worried that Huang's ouster was not only tanking the stock market but also risked putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for tech dominance.
"I'm doing it for the country," Trump said on CNBC.
Huang's reinstatement reinforced the message, which many Democrats delivered in the midterms, that the system is rigged against average Americans, said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project and a former aide to Democrats. Big tech leaders can be a powerful foil.
"They are the most unlikeable men in America, and yet it seems like the system is working very well for them," Haworth said. "The news this week just reinforced that idea. So the mission that Democrats have now is to continue to prove to voters that they are fighting against this corrupt system, against the influence of tech CEOs and on behalf of Americans."
Nvidia's board and Trump himself left no ambiguity over who drove the decision.
It was based on input from "senior levels of the United States government," Nvidia said in a press release announcing Huang's return.
Trump said in an interview with CNBC that "I spoke to them, let me just put it that way. And I convinced them."
Democratic candidates see corruption, security risks
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro tied Huang's reinstatement to "the sheer corruption and weakness" of the president, calling it "another example of the dangerous combination governing this country: a rigged system that protects those at the very top no matter what, and a corrupt White House that cannot be trusted to put the economic well-being and safety of American families first."
Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said that Trump's pressure campaign made clear that, to the president, "making money is more important than America's national security or the rule of law."
Slotkin, a former CIA analyst, added, "If ever there was an issue that deserved national security oversight, it's this one."
And Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker drew a comparison between Huang's reinstatement and Democrats' broad wins in this month's midterm elections, calling the CEO's return an example of "the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected."
Pritzker urged Democrats "to speak with one voice and not be afraid to fight the Trump administration," saying Trump and Vice President JD Vance "will move mountains for tech billionaires."

f10fb9241afd.text:
After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was currently looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.
“Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” says the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy. “That was one of the first things that I noticed,” he says. “And the cat even took on resemblances of people.”
It was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”
Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December issue of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a new context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.
The researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” says clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of big data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”
Karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” says Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”
Duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.
Karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine says. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.
“What is new about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” says Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”
During a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine says. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case shows some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.
“It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl says, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”
Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in new spots.
Using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom says. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”

22611af2cbec.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday.
The unsealed filings reveal how Justice Department attorneys and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress' private residence for a criminal investigation.
The heavily redacted documents — released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations — do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself or disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation that Omar claims is politically motivated.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, The Associated Press reported last month, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.
The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the "Speech or Debate Clause" implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures.
Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government's argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices.
"That logic does not hold," the magistrate wrote.
Sharbaugh concluded that the government's law-enforcement interests needed to be balanced against Omar's constitutional rights as a member of Congress. He said the government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke a privilege over any Speech or Debate Clause material before agents carried out the search.
Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. She hasn't been charged with any crimes and has denied any wrongdoing.
Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing of court filings related to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. He ruled after over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, argued that the public has a First Amendment right to access the records.
Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.
An attorney for Omar didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment Monday on the unsealed documents.
Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.
Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children's book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift.
Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.

ab180ce3b4c9.text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Francis saw the "gates of hell" when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published Tuesday by the Vatican.
"The Private Diary of Pope Francis" also reveals the Argentine pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-22, connected to his own temptations to exercise power omnipotently. He overcame the crisis by entrusting himself entirely to God's mercy.
The book, released globally in several languages, offers a deeply personal view of Francis' mind and heart, revealing his innermost fears, insecurities, dreams and temptations. It shows him as incredibly hard on himself, lamenting his own sense of worthlessness and shame, and his utter trust in God to lead him, even from the depths of despair.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
The book was curated by a close aide, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, the Argentine theologian who heads the Vatican's doctrine office and writes that Francis wanted the papers published. Fernández is listed as the author, as his comments contextualize Francis' diary entries.
Written in a leather-bound calendar used as a notebook, it starts in 1992, when Jorge Mario Bergoglio was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. It continues through his time as cardinal in the Argentine capital and finally pope. The last entry is Aug. 18, 2024.
Francis tells of encounters with the devil
The most moving sections are Francis' revelations of his own spiritual torments and what he described as encounters with the devil — visceral, tangible and seemingly terrifying visions. Two occurred in Buenos Aires, and the third after his disastrous 2018 trip to Chile.
"A few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant possessing everything. 'Now I've gotten everything I wanted,'" Francis quoted the devil as saying in a Jan. 24, 2021, entry. "Just as I can't forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice."
During the 2018 Chile trip, Francis created an uproar by discrediting victims of Chile's most notorious abuser. After journalists, including from The Associated Press, challenged him during the in-flight news conference returning home, Francis commissioned an investigation and realized the victims were right, that he was wrong and had been misled by the Chilean hierarchy.
"Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane," Francis would write later. "I became aware of how serious the problem was. … It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Francis wrote on June 7, 2018, that in the Chile scandal, he "saw the entrance to hell. Pagan seduction in full force."
As he dealt with the fallout in the next two months, he wrote: "What shame and evil this has brought on the church!" and "Once more the gates of hell. … May holiness and conversion abound in the midst of so many scandals."
But Francis' spiritual crisis wouldn't come until 2021.
The diary reveals a spiritual crisis in 2021-22
The book dates the onset of the crisis to Jan. 24, 2021. The day before, Francis canceled several public appearances due to what the Vatican said was a bout of sciatica.
Fernández reveals, however, that Francis was suffering from "insupportable" pain from an intestinal problem that in July 2021 landed Francis in the hospital for 10 days for surgery to remove 33 centimeters (13 inches) of his colon.
In January 2021, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the Vatican was in utter upheaval over a massive financial investigation authorized by Francis.
In September 2020, he had fired a onetime close collaborator, Cardinal Angelo Becciu, convinced Becciu had embezzled money from the Holy See. The scandal — and Francis' belief that a web of corruption had engulfed the Vatican's secretariat of state — led to an unprecedented Vatican investigation and years of legal proceedings through which Francis sought to show his willingness to crack down on financial misconduct.
The trial resulted in some convictions, including against Becciu, but much of prosecutors' theory of a vast conspiracy of corruption was thrown out. The appeals process is ongoing, with Francis' own role in the investigation a key question for the defense.
There is no mention of the trial in Fernández's text, though he hints at it by revealing Francis' later musings that the 2021-22 spiritual crisis was "mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation."
Fernández writes that the crisis was primarily related to Francis' exercise of power, the temptation to omnipotence and belief that he was above the world. It's a vice Francis admitted to publicly in 2013, in his first interview as pope, when he acknowledged a tendency to wield power in an "authoritarian" way.
It is significant that Francis was tormented by something his critics often faulted him for: an authoritarian, go-it-alone governing style in an absolute monarch and supreme leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
For Francis, the temptation to omnipotence was the devil tempting him to "reductive curiosity," or believing he alone could solve everyone's problems, and essentially thinking of himself as God.
By Dec. 30, 2022, Francis had apparently overcome the crisis, by entrusting himself to God. Fernández writes that Francis realized that what began on Jan. 24, 2021, "was a powerful invitation from the Lord to become aware of an accumulation of interior darkness that he had to overcome so he could be free."
Fernández notes that the final two major teaching documents of Francis' life, a 2023 text on confidence in God's merciful love, and a 2024 encyclical on Christ's human and divine love, are deeply spiritual texts borne out of the crisis. They differ in tone and content fr

At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.
Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.
Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.
The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.
Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.
Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump saw little choice but to fight to reinstate Jensen Huang at AI behemoth Nvidia.
The president has staked the nation's economic growth on artificial intelligence, and worried Huang's ouster was not only tanking the stock market — but also risked putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for dominance in the field if Huang, widely seen by backers and critics as a generational talent in artificial intelligence, were to be poached by a Chinese firm.
And the president, a thrice-married man and real estate maven who has seen his own marital infidelity scrutinized in the press, bristled at Huang being ousted from the company he built because of extramarital affairs, including one with an executive at a Singapore-based company who U.S. officials suspect was a Chinese spy.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
So Trump engaged in an extraordinary level of behind-the-scenes maneuvering to reinstate Huang, starting almost immediately after the CEO's fall from grace when he resigned on Nov. 12 as reports trickled out about a trio of affairs.
The president stated plainly in a CNBC interview on Monday he used his considerable sway to get Huang his job back. "I spoke to them," Trump said of the company's board of directors. "Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them."
Monday's reinstatement was a remarkable turnaround by Nvidia's board, which had insisted days after Huang's ouster that it was not considering such a move, even as Trump pushed for it and thousands signed an online petition calling for Huang's return.
Trump urged Huang's reinstatement for days
Trump stayed loyal to the iconic CEO who was a trusted adviser to the White House on artificial intelligence and a big donor to the president's ballroom project, arguing the company and America would be best served with Huang in charge of Nvidia.
Trump is also a big personal believer, and investor, in Nvidia, a leader in the global artificial intelligence industry's boom. At the end of 2025, he had Nvidia holdings worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, according to his annual financial disclosure report filed in June 2026. That's up from the $615,000 to $1.3 million in Nvidia stock in his disclosed holdings at the end of 2024.
The White House has said the president's portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. "All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes," said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold."
Trump said that the walloping AI stocks had taken following Huang's sacking helped him make his case. Some of his closest advisers helped persuade the board: Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who as recently as last week had called for a "dramatic shake-up" at Nvidia.
Huang is far from the first CEO to fall from grace because of infidelity or inappropriate relationships. In recent years, prominent executives like McDonald's Steve Easterbrook, BP's Bernard Looney and Intel's Brian Krzanich were forced out of their jobs.
Trump downplayed the issue. "He's apologized for that to the company, to the country and to his family and his wife, who's a fantastic person," Trump said on CNBC. "People are realizing the job he's done."
Huang's scandal had additional complexity because one of the extramarital relationships was with a woman who U.S. officials suspect had been an asset of China's intelligence service. Beijing has denied it.
As part of his campaign for Huang's reinstatement, Trump said U.S. officials assured the company that Huang — who acknowledged his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — did not present a national security risk.
Trump said that the Nvidia situation was different from other corporate scandals because Huang is an unprecedented talent who is shaping a technology that could impact just about every facet of life in the years to come. Trump also said he was concerned Huang could have been scooped up by a Chinese firm.
"This is different because the vast amount of knowledge in his brain," Trump said.
Vance stepped up his involvement over the weekend in making Trump's case to the Nvidia board, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The person, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that the White House deemed Vance, who worked in Silicon Valley before jumping into politics, had the stature to serve as an effective emissary in helping Nvidia board members overcome their reservations.
Trump has long been influenced by stock market gyrations
Trump marveled during his CNBC interview at the impact Huang's reinstatement had on the stock market. The S&P 500 leaped 4.7% on Monday following Huang's return.
During his time in the White House, the president has looked at the market as the ultimate validator of his leadership. The ebbs and flows of the market have shaped some of his most significant policies, including decisions on his ongoing war against Iran as well as his administration's tariff policy.
Trump views the AI build out as a key driver of the economy. The biggest tech firms have spent roughly $800 billion this year building data centers and cramming them with the latest semiconductors from Nvidia as well as computing equipment, electrical components, HVAC gear, and copper wiring.
The investment is projected to only grow in coming years, and could total $10.3 trillion from 2025 through 2032, equal to about 3.6% of the nation's economy, according to research from Columbia University economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.

Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.
Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.
The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).
The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.
Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.
But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.
"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.
The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.
A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.
Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.
The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.
"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.
More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.
"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."
Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.
They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.
But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.
For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.
Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.
More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.
The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.
In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.
The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.
The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.
But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.
"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.
And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.
Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus

Two turkeys named Freedom and Feathers are set to get Thanksgiving pardons from President Donald Trump on Tuesday.
Watch in our video player above.
Both birds will get a reprieve from ending up on a Thanksgiving dinner table, but only one of them will get a ceremonial pardon at the White House. The public can vote online for which of the West Virginia native birds will get the in-person honor from Trump. Both will live out their days at Texas A&M University.
Tuesday's event will be the 79th turkey pardoning, according to the White House, but the tradition did not become annual until George H.W. Bush's administration in 1989.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Typically a light-hearted moment before the quintessential American holiday, the turkey pardoning can offer a brief departure from politics and policy.
An early story of presidential turkey pardoning dates to Abraham Lincoln's administration, according to the White House Historical Association, when he granted a reprieve to a bird that was to be served for Christmas dinner after his son Tad intervened on the gobbler's behalf.
Nearly a century later, a photographer captured the moment a smiling Dwight Eisenhower fed a cranberry to a speckled turkey in 1954. In 1963, John F. Kennedy, just days before he was fatally shot in Texas, pardoned a turkey that wore around its neck a sign that said, "Good Eating, Mr. President."
In 2024, Joe Biden relished wordplay while pardoning Peach and Blossom, who came from a farm in Minnesota. Peach, Biden said, "lives by the motto, 'Keep calm and gobble on.'" Blossom has a different motto: "No fowl play. Just Minnesota nice."
But politics isn't always absent.
In 2025, the first year of Trump's second term, he spared the turkeys but spent part of the ceremony attacking his political opponents. He said then that the birds should be named Chuck and Nancy — after Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi.
"I would never pardon those people," Trump said at the time.

Jane Collins had spent 30 years as an FBI agent, but there was one case that haunted her long after retirement.
Michael Donovan was a fraudster, former minister and multimillionaire she had pursued for years, and even in her retirement she could not escape him.
He was regularly featured in the news and on the radio, appearing as a spokesperson for a number of causes, from migrant rights to anti-racism and justice reform.
He and his husband, Richard Moore, lived about an hour's drive from her, in Augusta County, Virginia, on the edge of the Appalachian Mountains.
Together they owned a business, Libre by Nexus, which had made more than $200m (Â£152m) from migrants seeking release from US immigrant detention centres - but it was a scam, government regulators said.
To Collins, they were the ones who got away.
She had investigated Nexus from 2016 until her retirement from the FBI in 2021. But the only federal criminal charges either faced - after almost six years of her investigation - was a tax charge against Moore.
So when Collins left the bureau, there were still a few strands left of her investigation that she could not let go - like the case of Zach Cruz, the brother of the man who killed 17 people in Parkland, Florida.
They had fronted his $500,000 bail bond, personally picked him up from jail, given him somewhere to stay, and made media appearances on his behalf.
Investigators later found they also took $400,000 from him, proceeds from his late mother's life insurance. Last month, the pair were found guilty of stealing it - with Collins playing a key role as a witness during the trial.
Collins told the BBC in her only interview about the case that she saw it as her final chance to face them in court.
"It means something when people are held to account," she said.
A paper trail
Collins says she was still a young girl when she first thought about joining the FBI.
"I've always been very interested in justice, making things right, and I think all of those things just fell into place," the 64-year-old recalls from her home in Charlottesville, Virginia, where a picture of her late golden retriever named Yogi hangs on the wall and a vintage car is parked in the driveway.
She was accepted to Quantico, the FBI training academy, soon after finishing university, and began to climb the ladder at the bureau, conducting surveillance on suspected Russian spies and crack dealers. In the late 1990s, she began working more on white-collar crimes, which really excited her - "much to my surprise," she adds. What she liked about these cases was the paper trail, and the way they presented themselves as puzzles to solve.
"There's a lot more in those cases that are concrete. As we say, documents don't lie," she says. "It was more challenging."
It also changed her perspective on crime, and victims. Although there was no trail of blood, there was an undeniable ripple from the fraud to the people and families hurt by it.
"People getting defrauded of money, some people their life savings," she explains. "There's a lot of psychological issues that go with that for a victim. They have been duped, so they're very hard on themselves."
An opportune appearance
Weeks after his older brother gunned down 14 students and three staff members at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Zachary Cruz went to the campus to "reflect on the school shooting and soak it all in".
But when police found him there skateboarding, they arrested the then 18-year-old, charged him with trespassing and put him in jail. On the heels of his brother's massacre, a judge set his bail at $500,000.
His friend called Nexus, looking for help to get him out. But Donovan and Moore did more than that - not only did they pay his bail, but they picked Cruz up from jail and took him to a hotel room.
Cruz later told the court that when he met them for the first time, it felt "like a movie".
During dinner that first night, the couple asked Cruz if he wanted to move to Virginia and work for Nexus.
The Florida judge overseeing his probation called it a "wonderful opportunity".
Soon he was living with them, and sharing in their media spotlight. Donovan and Moore accompanied him on interviews where the young man spoke about trying to understand his brother's crimes.
The couple even helped produce a short-lived online reality show called "Being Zach Cruz", which chronicled what it's like to be the brother of a famous killer.
"It was not ordinary," he later said.
According to Moore and Donovan, in an interview with the BBC in 2022, Cruz had become part of their family. They called him their "son" and said they had spent lavishly on his pursuit of a skateboarding career.
But they were deeply in debt, fighting off creditors - and the IRS. And through it all, Collins was doggedly on their tail.
Donovan and Moore had spent their wealth extravagantly - a fleet of luxury vehicles, a $500,000 wedding and a million-dollar self-published book titled Not Free America: What Your Government Doesn't Want You to Know.
But they owed millions to several state insurance boards, which had fined them for operating an unlicensed bond company. They owed a former business partner, RLI Insurance, millions for their failure to pay back bail that was lost when clients skipped court. And Moore owed more than $3m to the IRS.
Prosecutors alleged it was this tax debt that spurred Moore and Donovan to dupe Cruz out of his inheritance. Donovan declined an interview, through his attorney.
Collins initially focused her investigation on Libre by Nexus, and whether the company had broken any laws.
But her case took a turn when she received a tip that Donovan and Moore may be personally exploiting Cruz.
Bank records showed that $428,000 - the insurance money Cruz was entitled to after his mother died of cancer - was transferred into a joint account held by Cruz and Moore, and then into Moore's personal account, in 2019, according to the county's search warrant.

Iowans are hunkering down as the US Army plans to blow up five tonnes of degraded explosives on Wednesday, with some fearing the controlled blast could be disastrous, even as others just want it over and done with.
The Army has argued a controlled detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly volatile compound used as a detonator, is necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion - something it said would become more likely as temperatures are due to fall in the coming days.
The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the city of Middletown is to go ahead after an appeals court overturned an earlier decision to stop the blast over concerns about theâ¯potential health and environmental hazards of lead exposure.
Officials have announced a five-mile (8km) optional evacuation zone and a 20-mile shelter-in-place advisory, with potential airborne lead dust reaching up to 100 miles, depending on weather and wind.
Those who have chosen to stay have been told to remain indoors around the blast time and to expect "temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead".
Many people in the area are from families who have been there for generations â working in farming, manufacturing or at the ammunition plant itself.
Margo Sprenger, 71, a farmer and landowner in Donnelson, about 20 miles south-west of the factory, said her land was in the direct path of the projected plume and that "it's going to change my life forever".
"Our grandparents started on these farms, and now we don't even know if they can produce food that we can trust," she said.
"Who's going to tell us if it is safe or not? How much money is that going to cost for us to even find if it's safe? We certainly know the dangers of lead, but we don't know the dangers of what they're doing to us."
Sprenger's neighbour, pie-maker Beth Howard, plans to head to Des Moines (about 150 miles away) where she will spend Thanksgiving while her partner, Doug, stays on their farm, which his family has run for more than 150 years.
"It's so upsetting because of the future," Howard said. "What does the future hold for us? Is this the end of times for our farm?"
"If you lived here, you'd be concerned too. That's a lot of ammunition, and we should have never been put in the situation in the first place."
But in Middletown itself, the epicentre of the blast, many residents the BBC spoke with were relatively unfazed.
"I actually want it to happen, because I'd rather it be controlled than just blow up," Middletown resident Trisha Klaus, 49, told the BBC.
She and her 99-year-old grandfather, Keith McNeil - who worked at the Iowa Army Ammunition plant for half a century â are among those who have not left, saying they will likely hunker down at the Army Reserve Center, bringing along their pets.
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson will have a camera watching his mobile home - monitoring it from his manufacturing job in a nearby town - when the detonation takes place half a mile from where he lives.
Johnson, who grew up 12 miles away, pointed out that people had been exposed to lead in fuel, fireworks and other common items. He himself survived lead poisoning as a child, although he can't be certain how he got it.
"Every two weeks, we have crop dusters flying over our homes," Johnson said. "There's a lot more dangerous stuff being put into the air."
He added that he doesn't believe those in Middletown, which has a population of around 360 residents, were as concerned about the detonation as those who live farther out.
In fact, Johnson believes many residents "will be very angry" if it is delayed again or cancelled.
Andrew Wiese, a pastor at Harmony Bible Church, which has a campus bordering the ammunition plant, agrees that "a lot of people are just kind of wishing it was over and done with".
But he believes people are worried.
"There's just a lot of uncertainty, and that's just been a breeding ground for a lot of ideasâ¦ I'd say there's fear in the community," said Wiese.
Some communities only found out recently about the detonation.
"We were blindsided," said Laura Leigois, the city manager of Fort Madison, which is roughly 20 miles from the ammunition plant. She told BBC the city was first notified on 17 November about the originally planned detonation three days later.
"We're just frustrated about the lack of information, and I think the general public is frustrated on how this is all turned around."
Leigois said locals were taking matters into their own hands "because we're going to take care of our people". This includes deciding to cover Fort Madison's water tower vents, which let air move in and out.
Jeff Kurtz, 72, a retired locomotive engineer and former state representative, who also lives in Fort Madison, is extremely worried about the aftermath of the detonation.
"There's no guarantee I'm still going to be alive after all this stuff happens," Kurtz said. "This could be apocalyptic."
After finding out about the detonation, he worked with a team of scientists who assessed the situation on the ground in support of a legal challenge that caused the detonation to be paused.
They believe there are other means for getting rid of the explosives and don't buy the Army's argument that the threat of self-explosion is imminent.
Kurtz said he would "work up until the last minute" trying to get the government to reverse course.
"I'm frantic trying to get this stopped," he said. "I don't see where anything good could come from this."

The Pentagon is in discussions with General Motors to turn over some of its auto assembly lines for the mass production of drones, The Wall Street Journal reported, as Washington reckons with persistent munitions shortfalls amid the nine-month conflict with Iran.
Even as the US downplays the shortages, it is increasingly turning to automakers â who offer proven industrial supply chains and manufacturing capacity â in efforts to ramp up production of cheaper weapons systems to counter Iranâs mass-produced drones.
US efforts echo those of Europe, where lucrative government contracts promise to compensate automakers pressured by Chinese imports: Germanyâs Rheinmetall recently converted two auto factories to build ammunition, mirroring similar initiatives in France and Slovakia.

It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.
He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.
In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.
During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.
Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.
One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.
"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.
Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.
One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.
Dark infatuation
Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.
After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.
But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.
On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.
Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.
He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.
'The beginning of the plan for murder'
His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".
He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.
In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.
While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.
But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.
On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.
Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".
By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."
Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.
Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, Â£12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.
He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.
But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.
The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".
Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.
Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.
The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.
Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.
US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.
His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.
Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.
The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.
Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.
They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.
"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning to travel to the United States in December for the G20 Leadersâ Summit, a US official confirmed to Semafor, a trip that would be his first to the US since the outbreak of the Iran war.
The summit, which US President Donald Trump will host on December 14-15 at his Trump National Doral resort in Miami, is expected to bring together leaders from the worldâs major economies.
MBSâ potential attendance is particularly notable given his limited international travel since the war began. The crown prince also skipped the 2024 and 2025 editions of the summit.
If he attends, the gathering could provide an opportunity for Trump and MBS to meet in person for the first time since the outbreak of the conflict.
Saudi Arabia has been pressing Washington for assistance in countering Yemenâs Houthis and strengthening the kingdomâs defenses. A face-to-face meeting could provide a forum to discuss those security concerns, particularly given the close relationship between Trump and the Saudi crown prince.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.
MBSâ last trip to the US, in November 2025, featured an elaborate White House reception and a series of high-profile announcements, with Washington and Riyadh pledging hundreds of billions of dollars in commercial agreements and investment commitments.
Shelby Talcott contributed to this report.

Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?
The likelihood is actually higher than you might imagine.
Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.
Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?
How do we define a white Christmas?
For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.
It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.
Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.
The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.
Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.
Are there signs we could have a white Christmas in the UK this year?
A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.
A major one is the record-breaking El NiÃ±o which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.
El NiÃ±o's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.
In the UK, the impacts tend to be subtle and unreliable.
Strong El NiÃ±o events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El NiÃ±os is decidedly mixed.
And this is far from the only factor driving our weather.
Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.
This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.
Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.
The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office, external, taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.
However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.
When will we know for sure if Christmas will be white?
It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.
Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.
It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.
You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app.

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.
Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump â potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.
Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal â one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy â the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?
Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.
