"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's goodlooking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.
They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing â and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
"Congress has much to investigate," he said.
While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.
"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.
The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.
The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.
Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.
Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.
The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.
Trump's decision to help save Huang â noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" â could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."
For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El NiÃ±o conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.
She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.
Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.
Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.
He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.
"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.
That decision would have devastating consequences.
She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.
They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.
"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.
Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.
Median initially thought she was dreaming.
"To my surprise, it was reality."
The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.
Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.
Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.
She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.
For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.
A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.
The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.
They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.
Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.
But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.
By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.
Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.
Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.
Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.
Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.
The violence has devastated communities and forced half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.
At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.
Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.
The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.
Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.
The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.
For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.
Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.
But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.
She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.
"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.
"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."
Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.
Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (Â£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.
The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.
Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.
Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.
"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.
Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.
The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.

Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez cautioned those listening about the spread of right-wing governments.
"What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?" he asked supporters, before invoking the administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
"If we don't want that for the world, why would we want it for our own country?" said SÃ¡nchez.
He issued his warning as Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) leads most of the polls and appears poised to form a governing coalition with the hard-right Vox. The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy.
In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, SÃ¡nchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister.
His strident rhetoric defending feminism, immigration and green energy, along with his condemnation of Israel's military action in Gaza and verbal clashes with Trump, has fostered this image.
Having overseen consistent economic growth in recent years, his stock is high among the international left.
Yet in Spain, SÃ¡nchez has become a hate figure for the right, who see him as an autocrat with little regard for the separation of state powers, obsessed with clinging on to power and surrounded by a corrupt cabal.
In a bullring in Valencia, the same day that SÃ¡nchez was staging his rally, PP leader Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o told supporters that the last few years of Socialist-led government had been "insulting and even humiliating for a lot of people". He added: "We know them, they are capable of anything."
A couple of days earlier, Ignacio Garriga, spokesman for Vox, had gone further, describing SÃ¡nchez as "a very dangerous psychopath".
Both the PP and Vox have cast doubt on the neutrality of postal votes and votes cast by Spaniards abroad ahead of the election, suggesting that government manipulation could sway them in its favour.
"This is a campaign that is overwhelmingly ideological," said Cristina Monge, a political scientist at the Complutense University. "That means that it is not so much about voters rewarding or punishing a government's performance or the proposals being made, but about belonging to one or other ideological bloc."
Much of the hostility to SÃ¡nchez stems from his reliance on hard-left and separatist parties.
Ahead of the 2023 general election, he faced fierce criticism from the right for his reliance on the pro-independence EH Bildu coalition, which had links to the defunct Basque armed group ETA.
After that vote, he was able to form a new administration with the support of another separatist party, Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for an amnesty for all Catalans facing legal action for their role in a failed 2017 bid for independence.
At the time, NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o accused SÃ¡nchez of being "a prime minister who has bought his investiture in exchange for the judicial impunity of his partners".
Guillermo FernÃ¡ndez VÃ¡zquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University, said those parliamentary partnerships "fed the rhetoric of the right and far right, which was that Pedro SÃ¡nchez is an amoral person without scruples â someone whose word can't be trusted and who just wants to remain in power".

At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
How we came to a figure near half a million
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian â unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll â ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.
The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.
I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.
"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.
It turned my world upside down.
Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.
We stopped speaking.
Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.
Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.
After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.
Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.
I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.
But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of Dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing Dad just as much as I was.
I told her I wanted to make a documentary about Dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.
I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month Dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.
Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.
This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.
In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.
Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.
It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.
"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.
With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.
"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only)
As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.
Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.
I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.
She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.
At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."
She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.
"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.
She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.
The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.
She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.
With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.
Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

The first thing renowned climatologist Daniel Swain did during his virtual office hours on Monday was set the record straight about California’s upcoming flood risk. This week, water levels along the state’s coast, bays and estuaries will be as high, if not higher, than they’ve ever been, he said.
“But this will not, I repeat, will not be because of extreme rainfall,” said Swain, a University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources weather and climate scientist who regularly hosts briefings to explain global warming’s effects on natural hazards.
Some news reports and government officials were blaming predicted record-breaking coastal flooding on extreme storms. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, for example, said the city would see rainfall “that this city had never seen before.” Others warned people living inland to prepare for severe flooding.
“None of that is accurate,” Swain said. “This is not being really driven by rain or a storm at all.”
These potentially record-high water levels are “almost exclusively” caused by the overlap between king tides “and the extreme thermal expansion from our extreme El Niño event,” he said.
King tides are naturally occurring, exceptionally high tides caused by the gravitational forces of the sun and moon. El Niño is also a natural phenomenon, happening roughly every two to seven years when warmer ocean waters spread across the central and eastern Pacific, affecting weather and climate patterns as stored heat escapes into the atmosphere.
But this El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, making coastal ocean temperatures 10 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than normal. It has increased the height of waters off California’s coast by at least a foot, and in some cases, nearly two feet, Swain explained. And it’s persisted across many high-tide cycles.
“I just want to be really clear about what is and is not happening in California this week,” Swain said. “We’re going to see overlap between water levels that have been consistently running 12 to 20 inches above usual levels, not because of storms, not because of tides, but because of El Niño and climate change, the extreme thermal expansion of the water column.”
Coastal water levels are higher because the upper several hundred feet of the ocean are as much as 10 to 15 degrees warmer, and below-surface waters are about five or six degrees warmer, he said. “The water molecules are literally taking up more volume and therefore more space.”
He predicted that Humboldt Bay, about 260 miles north of San Francisco, will likely get the worst of a storm projected to hit California on Tuesday. “The ocean will be potentially at record levels with storm surge, thermal expansion from El Niño, king tides and heavy rain, all stacking on top of each other.”
The storm is likely to lose most of its punch by the time it reaches the Bay Area, he said, stressing that the flood risk is along the coast, not inland. “There’s almost no risk of inundation at all this week anywhere that’s about more than three or four feet above sea level.”
San Francisco authorities are preparing for the worst, after unusually heavy downpours last week caused disastrous flooding across the city.
“It is critical that everyone stays far away from the water, at the bay and ocean,” Lurie said in a press conference Monday. Public works crews are clearing storm drains, city crews are using specialized trucks to remove debris and sediment and the port has installed flood barriers and pumps along the Embarcadero, Lurie said, referring to the city’s eastern waterfront boulevard.
The Bay Area’s largest airports have ramped up efforts to manage floodwaters, which could overtop the lowest points of seawalls at the San Francisco Airport.

Airport staff have deployed sandbags and portable flood barriers in addition to ensuring storm drains and pump stations are working. The Oakland airport recently raised its perimeter dike to adapt to sea level rise and expects “smooth and uninterrupted airport operations for Thanksgiving holiday travelers,” a release issued Monday said.
Researchers, community members and state agencies are concerned about how this unprecedented confluence of king tides and El Niño might affect thousands of toxic sites around the Bay Area, said Emma Lasky, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of California, Berkeley. Many researchers hope to use this opportunity to understand the potential for flood waters to move toxic chemicals offsite, said Lasky, who has started studying this possibility in historically contaminated low-lying areas of the East Bay.
By Tuesday morning, floodwaters had already inundated the Embarcadero pier and shut down several roads in Marin County, north of San Francisco.
Flooding hits hardest in communities like Marin County’s Canal District that have waited the longest for investment in protection, said Zoe Siegel, senior director of Climate Resilience at the nonprofit Greenbelt Alliance. “These communities need to be first in line for adaptation funding and they need to help design it.”

Nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders. The clues are in the fossilized insects’ legs and feet.
Special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The discovery suggests at least three insect groups evolved independently to move across water.
Paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber. Frozen in time were three pieces of amber containing wingless grasshoppers with short bodies and incredibly long, skinny legs. Due to their unorthodox body shape, Xu didn’t recognize them as grasshoppers at first and thought they might be harvestmen or stick insects.
“I was genuinely amazed,” says Xu, of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. “They are among the most bizarre insects.”
Under the microscope, two details stood out: Front legs with water repellant hairs and rear lower legs with leaf-shaped paddlelike structures. Estimates of the insects’ weight show they could have ridden on the water’s surface tension, with help from the repellant hairs on their legs and their spread-out footprint across the surface of the water. And the paddlelike lower legs would have propelled them forward.
The researchers named the insects Hydrelcana zhangi, placing them in the new family Hydrelcanidae.
“Walking on water is a pretty rare skill in nature,” Xu says. Until now, only two insect groups were known to have evolved to live on the water’s surface: water striders and their kin, and a similar looking but unrelated, long extinct family called Chresmodidae.
The grasshoppers had a different gait from other water-walking insects. The common pond skater (Gerris lacustris), by comparison, rows with its middle limbs.
And whereas modern water-walking insects are predators and scavengers, the ancient grasshoppers were also probably herbivorous, given their mouthparts and lack of claws. The researchers found nine of them preserved in the same amber chunk, suggesting the insects may have gathered in large numbers to feed. It’s possibly the earliest record of such swarming behavior in grasshoppers or crickets, the team says.

Bob Woodward:
Because they're -- they gave me permission, or they're deceased, so it's part of history. And there's a vast public record out there of a lot of these people turning over their papers and their records to various colleges and universities. So, a lot's there, but I wanted to add to it.
Amna Nawaz:
You write about during the Watergate coverage. You reveal that some of your sources were actually President Nixon's own lawyers. Why did they want to talk to you?

Yes.

Amna Nawaz:

Even with mitigation measures in place, such as blast containment walls and water misters, the controlled detonation of bomb-making materials in Middletown will release a toxic dust cloud that the Army projects will travel over 100 miles to the southwest.
There is no safe level of lead, which can damage the brain, nervous system and reproductive health and is particularly harmful to young children. Scientists and health professionals warn that lingering contamination after the detonation, particularly in the air and soil, could pose problems long after the blast for residents in the plume’s path and beyond.
“It’s important to take this seriously, and make sure that everybody’s watching and making sure that the kids are not being exposed,” said Mary Jean Brown, a public health expert and former chief of the lead poisoning prevention branch at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Following the planned 9 a.m. detonation Wednesday, airborne lead particles will likely travel southwest, over the Missouri River and across Iowa’s border into Missouri. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has advised residents in the plume’s path to shelter in place for 24 to 48 hours after the blast.
The Army is encouraging residents within an evacuation cone five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to leave the area for several days. The Federal Emergency Management Agency will help evacuate and shelter residents in that zone. They have offered lodging through Friday, Nov. 27, but say individuals can reach out if they need more flexibility.
The Sheriff’s Office for Lee County, south of Middletown, issued a public notice on Tuesday that Army soldiers will go door to door to notify residents of the recommended evacuation.
Evacuation is especially important for vulnerable residents, including pregnant people or families with children under 6, Brown said, adding that leaving the area would be “the very best thing.” Lead can contribute to preterm labor, low birth weight, preeclampsia, neurocognitive and developmental delays, heart and kidney issues and other problems.
Expert Advice to Stay Safe From the Lead Blast
The U.S. Army plans to detonate nearly 5 tons of degraded lead azide explosives on Wednesday in Middletown, Iowa, sending a cloud of toxic lead dust potentially more than 100 miles to the southwest. Here are tips for people within the plume’s path.
- Evacuate if advised.
- Stay inside for the first 24 to 48 hours.
- Wash hands and surfaces often in the weeks after the event, especially before eating.
- Wear an N95 mask outdoors, especially when washing surfaces like cars and sidewalks.
- Take off your shoes before entering your home to avoid bringing settled lead dust inside.
- Test your young children’s blood lead levels routinely.
In a Tuesday news release, Environmental Protection Agency officials wrote that “a controlled detonation during optimal weather conditions and incorporating robust mitigation measures, compared to an uncontrolled explosion, significantly reduces the potential reach and concentration of lead dust landing on surfaces, such as homes and windows.”
How far airborne lead particles travel after the explosion will depend on their size and weather conditions, factors that will become clearer after the detonation. Smaller particles may travel farther and remain airborne longer, while heavier ones may settle closer to the site within a couple of days.
Snow and rainfall can make lead settle more quickly, lowering the particles out of the atmosphere and onto the ground. Although lead could remain airborne for a week or two after the explosion, it will likely be diluted and spread out, said Nico Perdrial, associate professor of geoscience and faculty fellow at the University of Vermont’s Gund Institute for Environment.
For Perdrial, the biggest concern is that the explosion will add more lead to the environment, increasing risk of chronic exposure.
“Over the long term, it’s gonna end up in the soil,” Perdrial said. “Lead in the environment means accumulation of lead in the body.”
Low levels of lead can occur naturally in soil, but dust from the explosion and runoff from outdoor surfaces in the days afterward could significantly raise those levels, said Gabriel Filippelli, a biogeochemist and executive director of the Environmental Resilience Institute at Indiana University.

For the next few weeks, Perdrial suggested that people in the path of the plume and surrounding areas should keep dust out of their homes, wash hands and surfaces frequently, and store shoes outside the house.
“People should be trying to be less in contact with dust, less in contact with fine particles when they go outside,” he said.
Residents in and around the plume’s path should wipe down all surfaces inside their homes with a wet rag, even if they kept their windows closed and turned off any heating and cooling systems during the blast, said Filippelli.
Dr. Juanita Mora, a medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association and Chicago-based allergist and immunologist, suggested residents wear an N95 mask outdoors for the first 72 hours after the explosion and when cleaning cars, sidewalks or windowsills in the weeks that follow. Mora also advised filtering and recirculating air in their cars and avoiding the plume’s path while traveling over the Thanksgiving holiday.

Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.
She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.
So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor."
Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.
Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.
Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.
North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty.
"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds.
First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.
Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.
Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.
Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.
Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.
This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.
Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East."
Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.
The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".
North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.
All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says.
And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.
Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.
Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.
One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.

Program looks to build shipbuilding, defense manufacturing capability in Hawaii
One training initiative received a $7 million investment from DOD’s Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program.
HONOLULU—A Pentagon-funded workforce-development program at Honolulu Community College is aiming to forge the next generation of Hawaii manufacturing industry leaders—and grow the defense industrial base in the Pacific.
Inside a warehouse space less than 10 miles from Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard, students learn everything from how to read a blueprint to how to operate manual and automated machines. At the end of the course, they build parts for and then assemble a model submarine, the “USS Aloha,” to show that they’ve mastered every part of the process.
The program is a collaboration between the community college, the Pentagon’s Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program, and a Hawaii-wide workforce initiative called Ku’i Hao, with training provided by BG Workforce. IBAS invested $7 million in the project.
Master instructor Jake LaBonte is from New England, where there is a long-established culture of machinist training and factory work. It’s different in Hawaii, he said during a tour of the training facility.
“Our shop here is, in my professional opinion, one of the most advanced and well-rounded…training facilities out there, hands down,” LaBonte said. But “you can go to a guy’s garage in Connecticut, and you’ll see the same equipment in his garage, because it’s just so ingrained.”
When the first cohort of students arrived in August 2025, the curriculum didn’t quite fit the local need, LaBonte said.
“I think one of the things different about Hawaii is it’s a little bit further behind the industry…so we had to be a little bit more creative with how we kind of got people trained up.”
LaBonte and other instructors took the feedback from the students and local companies and “pretty much did a complete rewrite of the curriculum” between the first and second cohorts. Now, instead of 80 percent classroom time, the students spend 80 percent of their time in the shop.
Students start with a course on machining fundamentals. They can then choose to take one on machining with automated machines, and then progress into shorter bootcamp-style courses for specific skills, said LaBonte and Clint Hall, chief program officer for BG Workforce.
The students—eight per cohort—are military members, local students, or already employed by a local company. Two of the current students are trainers at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard.
“We understand that Pearl Harbor is looking to hire thousands of employees over the coming years,” said Kevin Beamish, BG Workforce’s chief operating officer, and the local companies’ individual in-house training capacity definitely can’t meet that need. The new program allows the Pentagon to invest in growing the ship repair and manufacturing base to support the force here. BG Workforce is also the implementing contractor for The Forge, U.S. Pacific Command’s expeditionary foundry on Oahu.
“It’s got to be closer to the fight, I think is what Adm. [Sam] Paparo would say,” Beamish said, referring to the PACOM commander.
The facility has already saved the military time and money, he said. A unit on the island needed parts that would cost $42,000 each and take two to three years to have built on the mainland. Instead, “we were able to get their engineer over here and make some parts.”
LaBonte and the team reverse-engineered the parts, “built them, gave them to the engineer from the unit who can quality them, and then they’ve given us license to work those into our machining curriculum. So now the students are making those parts…that goes to the unit now. They’ve got a shelf full of replacement parts that break often, and now they can fix them with local stock instead of having their assets down and not serviceable.”
And, LaBonte said, they cost only $100 or $200 to make here.
In September, Assistant Defense Secretary for Industrial Base Policy Mike Cadenazzi touted the program during a House Appropriations Committee hearing, saying the training capacity has not existed in Hawaii since the 1970s.
“We feel our workforce programs are best structured as tied directly to the needs of the community,” he said. “It’s definitely localized and tailored….We’re really thrilled wherever we can do it.”

Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania's governor have sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to families if any household member lacks eligible citizenship or immigration status.
The states say the rule could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing. States including California, New York, Arizona and Massachusetts joined the suit. HUD defends the rule, arguing illegal immigrants are taking advantage of the current eligibility requirements.
The rule takes effect on Dec. 14. It would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance.
"No child should lose their home over a parent's immigration status," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "This rule is cruel, and it's unlawful."
For over three decades, Congress has authorized prorated federal housing assistance for mixed-status families, whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. These families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status. The new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any assistance.
"Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home," Bonta said.
One in five children in California is part of a mixed-status family, said Bonta, estimating that the rule will affect 7,000 households in his state. The new rule would also require public housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
"Congress never gave HUD the power to throw mixed-status families out of their homes or turn private landlords into immigration enforcement. But that's exactly what this rule does," Bonta said.
The new rule is the latest in a series of moves by President Donald Trump's administration targeting legal immigrants. Those moves include restricting healthcare, nutrition benefits and other subsidies while stripping legal protections from some immigrant groups to make more people eligible for deportation.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner first announced the proposed rule in January, but the department finalized it only last week.
"HUD's final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist," said Turner in an emailed statement on Monday.
Earlier this year, HUD conducted an audit with DHS and identified 20,000 mixed-status households receiving federally funded housing assistance nationwide. The department said illegal immigrants were using "loopholes" to access benefits while the department struggled to provide housing for all who need it.
Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative.

A Florida politician whose teenage son was fatally shot during a camping trip with friends says the shooting was an act of "malicious intent", not a "freak hunting accident".
Joe Vinson, a newly elected county commissioner in Florida, said his son Carey Washington Vinson, 19, was inside his tent near the Blackwater River in Florida when a bullet struck him in the head.
"As we understand it, some person(s) stood on the opposite bank of the river and pointed a gun at the sandbar campground, knowing it was occupied," Vinson said in a post on Instagram.
The local sheriff's office has asked the public for help in identifying any suspicious activity at the campground.
Police said they responded to an emergency call about a shooting and found the victim at a campground in Holt, Florida, with a gunshot wound to the head. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Santa Rosa County Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told US media that a vehicle was parked on the other side of the river at the time of the shooting and that witnesses saw it leave after the gunfire.
Vinson, who was recently elected as commissioner in Escambia County, issued a statement saying he needed to "correct a misimpression" that the shooting was an accident.
"This was not a freak hunting accident â not someone firing carelessly in the dark," the teenager's father said in his social media post.
Vinson said those on the other side of the river were "close enough to see the campfire and hear people talking".
"They fired shot after shot with malicious intent, and after a pause when the panicked campers screamed 'stop,' they fired another volley, then laughed as they drove away," he said.
Vinson said his son was a "thoughtful young man" studying history at Florida State University.
"He was so outgoing and athletic, playing soccer, hiking mountains, and beating the rest of us to the top of Giotto's Tower and Mount Fuji," his father said. "Most of all, he had a tender and loving heart â for his friends and family, for his girlfriend, for animals, for the marginalized."
Vinson called on anyone with information about the shooting to come forward to the police.

DALLAS (AP) — Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is ending efforts to punish two doctors who were among the first in the U.S. to face accusations of violating bans on providing care to transgender youth, dropping the cases as the Republican prepares to leave office following a failed Senate run.
The lawsuits against the doctors, which were filed in 2024, were among a spate of high-profile cases that helped Paxton burnish his image as a conservative fighter but are now winding down as Democrats prepare to retake power in Texas for the first time in decades.
The state's lawsuits against May Lau and M. Brett Cooper were dismissed Friday, according to attorneys for the doctors. They were among three doctors who Paxton called "scofflaws" and "radical gender activists" in lawsuits that threatened to impose steep fines and revoke their medical licenses.
"Dr. Lau did nothing wrong, but she was a convenient scapegoat for the Attorney General's Office, which issued press release after press release about its case — a case that has now collapsed," Nicole LeBoeuf, an attorney for Lau, said in a statement.
LeBoeuf said the timing of the dismissal after Paxton's loss "validates that this case against Dr. Lau was political from beginning to end." Lau moved her medical practice from Dallas to Oregon during the lawsuit.
Paxton's office did not immediately return a request for comment Monday.
Texas was the first state to bring cases against doctors
Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump, dropped another lawsuit last year against a third doctor, Hector Granados, and his office later said the El Paso pediatric endocrinologist did not break the law.
Texas' ban on gender-affirming care for transgender youths took effect in 2023. And while other states have prohibitions on gender-affirming care for transgender youth, Texas was the first to bring cases against doctors, filing lawsuits against the three providers.
Trump launched a broad charge against transgender rights in his second term, moving to reverse years of legal and policy gains for transgender Americans. Even in states where the care is allowed under state law, major hospitals and hospital systems have said they were stopping or restricting the care.
Cooper, a Dallas physician, "has always maintained that he acted lawfully and in the best interests of his patients," his attorneys, Simona Agnolucci and Anika Holland, said in a statement.
Paxton and Republicans leaned into transgender attacks during midterms
In the final phase of this year's midterm elections, Republicans spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats, according to tallies provided to The Associated Press by data firm AdImpact. Texas' Senate contest between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico consumed the largest share of that spending, drawing an estimated $58 million for more than 50,000 airings before the election, according to AdImpact.
The GOP focus on transgender issues stood in stark contrast with what voters told pollsters they cared most about in the midterm season, which included the state of the economy.
Texas also dropping lawsuits over abortion pills and immigration
In January, Democrat Nathan Johnson will become Texas' next attorney general.
Other lawsuits Paxton's office has dropped since his Senate loss include those against out-of-state doctors for sending abortion pills to Texas and one seeking to stop the Council on American-Islamic Relations from operating in the state. The lawsuit against one of the largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy groups in the U.S. came after Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, declared it a "foreign terrorist organization."
Paxton's office has also dropped lawsuits against Jolt Initiative, a nonprofit that was accused of registering noncitizens to vote, and Annunciation House in El Paso, one of the oldest migrant shelters on the U.S.-Mexico border.

NEW YORK (AP) — A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge typically is used in organized crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from American companies.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which U.S. prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the U.S. and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
Lawyers for the company said U.S. investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei's more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn't actually exist.
Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
"That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together," and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict "repudiated the central government narrative in the case."
It's unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei's global fortunes. The company hasn't been allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
That hasn't stopped the company from doing a robust business elsewhere. Its smartphones and other telecom equipment are sold globally. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors, becoming an important alternative in China to chips made by companies such as Nvidia.
The U.S. announced its criminal charges against Huawei in early 2019 and later expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.
The indictment against Huawei accused it of a long pattern of outright technology thefts. Huawei, prosecutors said, once sold internet routers containing source code copied from a competitor. In another episode, a person working for Huawei slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade show to surreptitiously photograph the circuits inside another company's networking device, the indictment said. Prosecutors said that on another occasion, a Huawei worker removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
The victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to court records.
"The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating U.S. sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury at the trial.
In his closing argument to jurors, Huawei's lawyer said prosecutors leaned on "innuendo and facts ripped out of context," and testimony from ex-employees "with a bone to pick," to pursue a company that had relied on "hard work, innovation and competition" to succeed.
"Huawei didn't steal its way to success," Heberlig said, noting that much of the material the U.S. alleges was stolen was already public.
"You can't steal a secret that isn't a secret," he said.
He said Huawei paid billions of dollars in licensing fees over the years, with 75% of that money going to U.S. companies, and had reprimanded or fired employees found to have engaged in wrongdoing.
Heberlig noted that lines of Cisco source code turned up in Huawei software more than two decades ago. He said when the source-code copying was discovered, Huawei recalled routers sold in the U.S. and offered to replace them with Cisco routers and created a "compliance culture that permeates Huawei today."
U.S. prosecutors had originally also brought criminal charges against Huawei's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, accusing her of misleading HSBC bank about the company's business dealings in Iran. Meng, the daughter of Huawei's founder, was arrested in Canada in 2018, but ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its case against Meng.
The trial in New York overlapped with a summit meeting between President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin in the technology-centric city of Shenzhen, China.
Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed.

Watch: Trump pardons turkeys Freedom and Feathers
President Donald Trump continued a long-standing White House holiday tradition, pardoning two turkeys ahead of Thanksgiving Day. This year's turkeys, named Freedom and Feathers, were granted a "complete and total pardon".
The festivities mark the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation. The event dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first began presenting turkeys; however, the presidential pardon didn't become a tradition until 1989, under President George H. W. Bush.

- Published
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.
Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.
President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.
In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (Â£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.
They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.
