As if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.
Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.
Biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).
Researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as big cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.
“It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” says Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.
Three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.
While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter says.
“I found the evidence pretty compelling,” says Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.
The eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter says. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.
While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.
When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter says.
The eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter says. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.
The threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.
“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really important precursor [of language],” Hobaiter says.

Lizâs view
Fine, Jensen Huang can come back. Nvidiaâs board cannot.
In a truly Keystone Kopsian display of corporate governance, Nvidiaâs comically weak board reversed itself in six days. It either caved to a lame-duck US president â who, as Semafor scooped yesterday, called into Nvidiaâs board meeting Sunday to lobby for a ânational treasureâ â or gratefully took the air cover he provided them to bring back a CEO who appears to have lied to them repeatedly.
After firing Huang without all the facts, they rehired him still lacking those facts. The interim period encouraged a parade of Jensen School of Management stories, unimportant to the questions at hand but now an unflattering part of Nvidia canon. And Huang is unfireable now, even if the ongoing investigation turns up new bad facts, which it almost certainly will. Law firm Wachtell and its investigator, Joon Kim, might as well withdraw from what is now a no-win assignment.
Iâve written before that we should all be a little less puritanical about intraoffice relationships. But CEOs canât sleep with customers, for no other reason than that it makes other customers mad, and they canât sleep with spies, for reasons that donât require elaboration. Set aside the national-security breach: One of the most important people in the business world, on whose every move hang trillions of dollars, has been walking around with a giant âBlackmail Meâ sign taped to his back. Itâs now been replaced by an explicit debt to President Donald Trump, to whom Huang literally owes his job.
His comeback has repaired Nvidiaâs stock price, sort of: Even Mondayâs $1 trillion gain restored only about a third of the value lost since the AI trade began wobbling in September. But Huang cannot protect Nvidia, or the bull market that Trump appears determined to prop up, from the laws of gravity starting to assert themselves.
Money is getting prohibitively expensive as AIâs let-a-thousand-flowers-bloom era comes to a screeching halt. The data-center buildout is one construction delay or faulty grid hook-up from a calamitous and contagious flu. The AI labs have huge trust gaps with the customers they need to generate the revenue for all the Nvidia chips and GE turbines and Dell servers theyâve signed contracts to buy.
The hyperscalers burned through their cash and are now burning through other peopleâs cash â theyâre turning to Canada, one Wall Street executive told me yesterday, with a for-Peteâs-sake eye roll. Democrats are none too happy and Huangâs GOP allies are politically weakened.
Having bullied his board into submission, Jensen Huang is now the most powerful corporate executive in the world. Heâs still not powerful enough to outrun all of that. The question is whether, when he fails to do so, he retains Trumpâs loyaltyÂ or becomes his fall guy.
Notable
- âHuang has become the figurehead of the AI boom and one of the few people who can move the dial on sentiment across the sector,â an analyst told Reuters.
- Huangâs return was pushed by a faction of Silicon Valleyâs elite, but small traders piled in and reaped the rewards, Semaforâs Jake Angelo and Ellen DiMauro write.

Jensen Huangâs return was pushed by a faction of Silicon Valleyâs elite, but small traders piled in and reaped the rewards. Nvidia was the most-traded name across all of Robinhood on Nov. 12, when Huang resigned, and the retail brokerâs customers remained net buyers in the days that followed, a spokesman told Semafor.
Shares in Nvidia dropped 28% in the seven trading days following Huangâs resignation, only to rev back up and then some on Monday following the news of his return. Robinhood said it saw ârecord-breaking trafficâ yesterday after Nvidiaâs pre-market release announcing Huangâs return. âThe fundamentals of the company didnât change, but the company fundamentally changed,â Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told Semafor.

The youth of this era, both Gen Z and Gen Alpha, are often described as the “climate generation,” in part because climate change is already shaping how this generation (which also happens to be my generation) lives and what our futures will look like. Researchers have linked climate change to shifts in where Bangladeshi children live and learn, girls dropping out of school in Kenya during droughts or floods and declining the mental health of students.
But we are also the generation that has learned to push back: taking to the streets, as millions did worldwide during the global climate strikes inspired by Greta Thunberg’ in 2019, and to the courts, where 27 students from the University of the South Pacific launched the campaign that ultimately led to the International Court of Justice’s 2025 climate opinion. At this year’s COP31, the United Nations’ 31st climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, the climate generation was back.
The draft texts: The cover decision serves as the closest thing to a final summary of the agreements reached by nearly 200 countries in Antalya to advance the goals of the Paris Agreement. The first draft was released on Nov. 16, a week into the proceedings, and called for countries to treat climate impacts on children “as a primary consideration in national planning.” On Nov. 19, a shorter second draft was released. A paragraph recognizing the “meaningful participation of children and youth” in climate decision-making survived. Language on how climate change harms children, direct mentions of gender and education, a $120 billion target for adaptation finance and a reference to fossil fuels were cut. When I compared the two drafts, what stood out the most was that agriculture, the sector that employs 44 percent of working youth ages 15 to 24 worldwide, appeared in neither.
A third draft, released on Sunday, restored much of what had been cut, including language on the “disproportionate impacts of climate change on children” and their access to health and education. But the European Union, small island states, the U.K., Norway, and others rejected the cover decision due to a lack of mention of fossil fuels and no final decision was adopted in the end; you can read more on the breakdown from my colleague Bob Berwyn. This year’s talks were the longest COP in history and the first major breakdownin negotiations since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009.
Before the summit, the food and agriculture working group of YOUNGO, the official youth constituency in U.N. climate talks, called for grant-based adaptation finance that young farmers could access directly. The Nov. 19 draft does mention grant-based adaptation finance, but it reserves the “direct access” language for national development banks, not young people.
The one finance decision that appears to have survived the summit is on the loss and damage fund. It calls for the board to “enhance engagement” with the youth and to “take into account their perspectives, as appropriate.”
Did you also spend your free time reading the draft decisions? Email me at [email protected] to share what you noticed in the texts.
Inside the venue: The climate generation also had a dedicated physical space in Antalya. The Children and Youth Pavilion is in its fifth consecutive year as the only fully youth-led space at the official climate summit, opened with Sally Higgins, the COP31 Presidency Youth Climate Champion, in attendance. Higgins’ responsibility is to connect the voices of the global youth to the COP presidency. At the U.N. Secretary-General’s youth roundtable, Jayanti Bam, UNICEF Nepal’s youth advocate for climate action, asked that leaders “protect children. Listen to children. And act for children.”
On Nov. 19, Higgins said in a video published to the UN Climate Change Facebook account that “farming practices are really under threat from climate change,” the same concern YOUNGO expressed.
Outside the venue: One of the most prominent voices in the climate generation finally returned to the COP proceedings this year. On Nov. 10, Greta Thunberg, now 23, arrived at the Antalya Expo Center. It was her first U.N. climate summit since the 2021 COP in Glasgow, where she dismissed global leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.” She’s continued that thread. This year, she said that host governments use the summit to “whitewash themselves,” adding that the negotiations are full of lobbyists that are paid by industries profiting from fossil fuel dependence. Thunberg’s criticism of fossil fuel interests and lobbying proved prescient, as they contributed to the breakdown of the agreement.
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia will host the next COP next November. The climate generation, who came to Antalya asking for more support, now have a year to regroup and try again. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in a Facebook post describing their work in Turkey that “the activism of young people today is what gives [him] hope for the future.”

Last week, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, 62–33. The contentious permitting bill has the potential to lower energy costs for consumers, but as currently written, it weakens some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process.

The U.S. Army detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday.
Here's what to know about lead azide, and why local officials and scientists have some concerns about potential health and environmental effects from the planned explosion.
Lead azide, which typically appears as a white or colorless crystalline powder or needlelike crystals, is a highly sensitive chemical compound containing lead and nitrogen.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
The compound is used as an initiating explosive in munitions, and historically has been used in detonators to set off other explosives, such as TNT.
It is sensitive to shock, heat, impact and friction, and may explode when dry. With temperature changes and time, lead azide can form unstable, larger crystals that are even more sensitive.
The decades-old lead azide supply in Iowa was crystallizing, posing the risk of spontaneous detonation.
Broken down, lead is a toxic heavy metal that can harm the brain, nervous system, kidneys, heart and other organs. Lead exposure also causes developmental damage.
As lead exposure can pose both immediate risks and longer health and environmental hazards, officials and researchers are questioning the levels of lead that might be in the air and nearby land and water sources, impacting residents, crops, cattle and wildlife after the detonation.
The military stopped using lead azide in the 1980s because of its hazards.
The Army says Wednesday's planned detonation includes barriers around the blast zone to reduce the spread of the resulting plume, along with ballistic gels to absorb lead dust.

197f41c14b3e.text:
The U.S. Army has detonated the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa after warning that the degrading bomb-making chemicals could otherwise explode at any time. The controlled detonation of roughly 5 tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown has set off concerns about potential health and environmental effects.
Officials on Tuesday warned residents near Middletown to be ready to evacuate to avoid toxic dust in the air. The wind is expected to blow southwest — away from the nearby city of Burlington and the Mississippi River. The Army has also taken steps to limit the plume with barriers around the blast zone and ballistic gels to absorb the lead dust.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
The blast was originally planned for last Friday, but the Army rescheduled to allow more time for extra safety measures and more favorable wind conditions, according to court documents. It was the third time the Army had changed the date, winning approval from a federal appeals court after environmentalists sued to stop the detonation.
Here's the latest.
10:20 a.m. EST
2 plumes were seen overhead before dissipating
Video footage from several miles away showed two white plumes rolling over the detonation site before the clouds quickly dissipated. Journalists reported hearing a loud boom at the same time.
Despite warnings to stay inside, some residents pulled to the side of a road to watch the blast upwind of the ammunition plant.
10:13 a.m. EST
Army blows up bomb chemicals in Iowa despite fears a toxic plume could endanger residents
The U.S. Army intentionally blew up the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday after officials said the degraded materials were at risk of exploding uncontrollably as temperatures cooled.
Environmentalists voiced concerns about possible health and environmental effects from the controlled detonation of the bomb-making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.
Officials warned about the dangers of waiting too long, and a court ultimately cleared the way for the military to carry out the blast.
Officials advised people nearby to be ready to evacuate, but also sought to reassure them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume.
The Army set up blast barriers around the bunkers where the 5 tons of lead azide was detonated and used ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust. It said beforehand it also would douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water.
10:01 a.m. EST
The military is not livestreaming the Iowa detonation
The U.S. Army said it will film Wednesday morning's controlled detonation of lead azide and make the footage and photos available as soon as possible. It has been providing updates on its social media accounts.
The Army has kept media outlets and others more than 4 miles (6.4 km) away from the blast site.
"Please, do not put yourselves in harm's way," it warned in an advisory to news outlets.
The Associated Press is livestreaming from a location about 5 miles (8 km) away and upwind from the ammunition plant in Middletown.
9:53 a.m. EST
Decades-old lead azide came from across the country
The country's stockpile of lead azide was brought to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant from bases all around the country in 2009, according to Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The chemicals, used in munitions production, were stored in barrels in case the military needed to use them again.
In March, during a routine monitoring inspection, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found that the lead azide had partially crystallized, making it sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation.
The Army assembled experts to formulate a plan but found that alternative solutions like thermal treatment and neutralizing the drums' contents were not as safe as a controlled detonation.
Thousands of samples were collected ahead of detonation
The Environmental Protection Agency said it collected more than 1,200 air, land and water samples ahead of the controlled detonation to test for lead levels around the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
The EPA will also test lead levels during and after the detonation, it said Wednesday. The agency will monitor the air and report data every five minutes.
No lead was detected in the air before the detonation, and the EPA said it expects only a brief increase after the blast.
"It is the top priority of this agency to ensure impacted residents can swiftly be and feel safe and comfortable in their homes, at their schools, in recreational spaces, and in their community," said Tom Croci, the agency's associate administrator for national security and operations coordination.
9:43 a.m. EST
Farmers are concerned about effects of blast on their cattle, crops
Doug Seyb can't do much to protect his farm 18 miles (29 kilometers) southwest of the ammunition plant. His cows are out on a pasture, and there's no way he can get them indoors. Ponds also fill the farm's water tanks, and he can't change that.
"We can just cross our fingers," said the 71-year-old resident of Donnellson, Iowa.
Seyb is worried about the long-term effects the controlled detonation will have on his farm. He fears his calves could be born with deformities in the spring, and he is unsure how next year's soybean and corn crops will fare if the soil is contaminated with lead.
When the controlled detonation occurs, Seyb will head inside for a few hours until it's time to feed the cattle in the afternoon.
"Farm's been in the family over 150 years, and I've spent my whole life building it and making it what it is," he said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency issued the emergency alert about an hour before Wednesday's planned detonation at the Iowa ammunition plant.

Australia’s limbless geckos look a lot like snakes. It turns out they’ve evolved like snakes too.
Snakes are technically a highly modified group of legless lizards. Dozens of other lizard lineages have independently lost their legs, too. But the legless pygopod geckos aren’t quite like their slithering nonsnake kin. Pygopods have dietary pickiness and physical diversity patterns that are more reminiscent of those found in snakes than in other legless lizards, researchers report in a preprint posted at bioRxiv.org on October 23.
The 50 recognized species of pygopod geckos are found throughout Australia and New Guinea. Pygopods range from a meter long to the size of half a cooked spaghetti noodle. They have odd tails, which in some species can be fantastically long, exceeding 400 percent of their less-than-1-centimeter-long bodies. Some use their tails like a spring to leap.
“They create a little sine wave and they shoot themselves up in the air, and they can do successive jumps,” says Ian Brennan, an evolutionary biologist at the Queensland Museum Kurilpa in Brisbane, Australia.
But not much else is known about them, Brennan says.
“They’re real oddballs,” he says, noting that geckos are typically thought of as skilled climbers on walls or glass surfaces. “[Pygopods are] a group that’s gone the exact opposite direction.”
As part of a large project tackling the genetics of Australia’s lizards and snakes, Brennan and his colleagues gathered data on pygopods’ genes, diet and physical features. They analyzed DNA from all 50 species of pygopod and generated an evolutionary tree. The team also put together data from the literature on the ratio of their body and tail lengths and compared this with a dataset of similar information on over 3,100 lizard and snake species.
As they evolved, snakes got longer by lengthening their bodies. Limbed lizards tend to get longer by lengthening their tails. The team found that pygopods have done both, an unusual strategy among legless lizards. This dual strategy resulted in some unexpected physical diversity in tail and body ratio.
Next, the team tackled diet, comparing between 1,738 lizard and snake species. Snakes as a group have a broad diet with lots of specialization, which might be partly why they’ve been so successful at diversifying into so many ecological roles in so many habitats, Brennan says. There are pythons that eat only large mammals and sea snakes that eat only fish eggs, for instance.
This pattern is rare in lizards. Most geckos eat insects such as beetles and cockroaches, Brennan says. This is especially true of the legless groups, which mostly gobble down whatever insects they happen to slither past.
But the team found that the wide variety in what pygopods as a group will eat is exceeded among reptiles only by monitor lizards and colubrid snakes, a hyperdiverse group of over 2,000 snake species. Within that broad dietary range, particular pygopods flirt with snakelike pickiness. Some pygopods chiefly hunt spiders and scorpions. Another group targets ants and termites. One predatory pygopod — the Lialis genus — gulps down other lizards snake-style.
Pygopods’ evolutionary history may provide hints about how this heightened diversity developed. The team’s findings suggest they split off from other geckos in Australia 50 million years ago — much more recently than when the first snakes evolved around 160 million years ago, but before any modern snake groups reached Australia. Brennan thinks pygopods filled the roles of small snakes on the continent for millions of years in isolation.
“Pygopods were probably on a trajectory to do something spectacular, like snakes,” says Brennan. “But then all of these [snake] groups showed up in Australia and filled into those niches.”
Sonal Singhal — an evolutionary biologist at California State University, Dominguez Hills in Carson — would like to see this study’s data combined with data on pygopods’ skull shape, their habitat use and how their bodies move.
“For example, Lialis can swallow prey whole because their jaws are so flexible and kinetic and their teeth hinge back and forth, allowing them to trap prey.”
For Brennan, a lesson from the findings is that lacking limbs need not be an evolutionary constraint. Both snakes and pygopods “have diversified to do really interesting things, either due to or in spite of being limbless,” he says.

Even as they fervently push for the frictionless building of a new frigate, Congress can’t seem to fully stomach the idea of making Navy warships overseas. But despite their doubts, lawmakers want the Navy to develop “a full strategy and implementation plan” for “effective use of foreign partner capabilities.” The catch is that the administration can’t use appropriated funds for foreign shipyard work or foreign shipbuilding items, according to a draft funding bill.
If the bill is finalized, the plan must outline “concrete steps, resources, responsibilities, and timelines sufficient” to realize shipbuilding in different locations as part of its “distributed shipbuilding model along with foreign partner capabilities to transform domestic shipbuilding capability nationwide,” the Senate Appropriations Committee wrote in the explanatory statement for the 2027 defense spending bill.
Lawmakers criticized the Pentagon’s failure to implement 48 Government Accountability Office recommendations over the past decade that were aimed at improving shipbuilding performance. There’s also concern that the Navy’s push for distributed shipbuilding has “insufficient” scope, though they say “allies and partners may provide opportunities to expand shipbuilding capacity for the United States in certain circumstances.”
The bill text also seemed to reflect some ambivalence among Senate appropriators, which on one hand support “limited use of allied shipyards to address significant shortfalls in certain auxiliary vessels,” while being “unconvinced that foreign shipyards are an appropriate solution for combatant vessels.”
The proposed legislation comes as the Navy—with Congressional support—aims to build more ships, including a new frigate, faster.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who is nominated for the role, told senators during his confirmation hearing last week that the service needs to “look at other entrants” to speed up the shipbuilding process.
“We have to explore all avenues of building frigates,” Cao said. “For example, for the Koreans, the Chungnam, it takes them 15 months from the moment they lay a keel until they launch that vessel. So, we need to look at other entrants,” such as Hanwha, which bought Philly Shipyard in 2024 and has submitted a bid to acquire Austal USA.
In a separate confirmation hearing, Navy undersecretary nominee William Toti agreed, telling senators that a new, tech-forward, foreign-owned shipyard in the U.S. was the “quickest way” to build frigates.
But it’s still unclear how much a foreign-designed or built frigate could cost.
Tucked in a footnote of a recent report on the Navy’s shipbuilding plan, the Congressional Budget Office wrote: “[The] FFG-62 program was based on a foreign design, the Italian FREMM (Fregata Europea Multi-Missione). Adapting that design to U.S. Navy standards for construction and incorporating U.S. Navy combat systems and weapons played a significant part in the cost growth and delays that led to the cancelation of the FFG-62 program.”
The CBO did not analyze whether “foreign design would replace, complement, or augment the FF(X) Flight II program.”
The 2027 spending bill does not allow the use of the funds for “work in foreign shipyards or procurement of shipbuilding items from foreign sources…regardless of the potential enactment of authorizing provisions, such as section 1019 of S. 4784, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027.”

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.
Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.
Russia has not commented on the strikes.
The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.
The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.
Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line â the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.
"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.
Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.
Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.
"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.
Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.
But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.
Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since World War Two.
A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.
The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.
Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.
What is the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade?
The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.
The first event took place on Thanksgiving Day 1924. It has only been cancelled during the World War Two, when it was put on hiatus between 1942 and 1944. As a result, this year marks the 100th parade.
It is due to take place from 08:30 local time (13:30 GMT), ending at around 12:00 (17:00 GMT) , and involves marching bands, street performers and floats parading through the streets of New York City, as well as 100 brightly-coloured inflatable balloons.
However, due to city regulations full-size balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23mph (37km/h), or in gusts of more than 35mph (56km/h).
There is a risk that Thursday will bring winds approaching those strengths.
However, record wind gusts also made the 1997 route a no-fly zone and the balloons were still featured in the parade.
The giant character balloons were tethered to golf carts that year.
In 1989, when a major snowstorm stopped balloon handlers getting to the parade route, the cheer and dance teams stepped in to pull the giant balloons along.
What is the forecast?
Over the last few days, a cluster of showers and thunderstorms has been swarming in the Gulf of Mexico.
That area of disturbed weather is now moving northwards, close to the east coast, and deepening into a potent area of low pressure - a Nor'easter storm, so called because it delivers strong north-easterly winds which drive into the east coast.
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning for New York City, as well as Long Island and north-east New Jersey.
It comes into force part-way through the parade and warns of strong to damaging wind gusts, which could affect trees and power lines and bring significant travel disruption.
The winds are forecast to strengthen through the day peaking during the evening, meaning the very strongest gusts are likely to hit after the parade is over. However, there is a risk that they could approach the threshold that would ground the balloons.
Up to 3in (75mm) of rain could fall with the risk of flooding, which could be exacerbated along the coast as high tides arrive on Thursday evening.
Large waves and high sea levels are expected, bringing the threat of erosion and damage along the shoreline.
Other eastern parts of the USA will also receive heavy rain and strong winds, with snow in some inland parts adding to the Thanksgiving travel headaches.

MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (AP) — The U.S. Army plans to detonate the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide Wednesday morning in Iowa after warning that the dangerously degrading bomb-making chemicals could otherwise explode at any time.
Watch a live stream of the U.S. Army Reserve Center in Middletown, Iowa, in the video player above.
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the Army's leader of the operation.
The controlled detonation of roughly 5 tons of degraded lead azide is planned for 9 a.m. CST at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. It has set off concerns about potential health and environmental impacts from lead dust, and frustration over a lack of information.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
The blast originally was planned for last Friday. The Army changed the detonation date three times amid public backlash and to allow more time for safety measures and favorable wind, according to court documents.
Government officials encouraged residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) of the site to evacuate to avoid lead dust in the air, while also assuring them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume from the detonation.
Officials overseeing the detonation plan say the wind on Wednesday is expected to carry the plume southwest toward Missouri and away from nearby Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people that sits along the Mississippi River.
The Army will take steps to quash plume
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the public should not panic.
The Army has set up additional "blast barriers" around the bunkers where the 68 barrels of lead azide will be detonated. The materials will be surrounded by concrete and sand barriers two stories high.
Ballistic gels and foams will absorb the lead dust, and the Army plans to douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water to tamp down the plume.
Decades-old lead azide was crystallizing, risking spontaneous detonation
The country's stockpile of lead azide was brought to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant from bases around the country in 2009, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The chemicals, used in munitions production, were stored in barrels in case the military needed to use them again.
During a routine monitoring inspection in March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found that the lead azide had partially crystallized, making it sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation.
The Army assembled experts to formulate a plan, and they found that alternative solutions like thermal treatment and neutralizing the drums' contents were not as safe as a controlled detonation.
Court gives final approval amid pushback from environmental groups
Environmental groups filed a lawsuit in an effort to halt the plan, but a court ruling on Monday put the detonation back on track. A federal appeals court found the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.
Residents expressed a mix of concern about the planned blast. Some said the timing could be better given it is happening the day before Thanksgiving but acknowledged it needed to be dealt with now. Others expressed concern about the effect it will have on water, farms, animals and their own homes.
"I don't think lead danger goes away any time soon," said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. "It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this."
Ahead of the blast, schools near Middletown shut down, businesses closed and some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution.
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio, and Bauer from Madison, Wisconsin. Associated Press writers Susan Montoya Bryan in Albuquerque, New Mexico; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; Jessica Hill in Las Vegas; and Chris Weber in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

The first day of the United Nations’ COP31 climate talks in Turkey focused on the nexus of food, agriculture and health, setting a hopeful tone for negotiators and advocacy groups that have been pushing to make food systems a bigger priority at the annual gatherings.
Even before the talks wrapped up Sunday, those hopes had faded. Despite the increasing evidence that cutting emissions from agriculture and the land it occupies represents the most expedient path to lowering climate pollution in the short term—an emergency break on global warming—negotiators left the event with little action on the farming front.
Farmers in the world’s most vulnerable countries will pay the price, advocates and researchers warn, pointing to this year’s “super” El Niño as a case in point.
As the event got underway, a new report from the International Fund for Agricultural Development and Turkey’s Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry said the weather phenomenon could cost the global economy $11 trillion.
“The weather shock is becoming an economic shock, and it is arriving at the worst possible time,” said Jahan-Zeb Chowdhury, the fund’s lead technical specialist for the environment and climate. “Farmers are already vulnerable because of the two other shocks they have experienced—fertilizer and energy.”
The report noted fertilizer prices skyrocketed in 2026 as its main ingredients were stalled in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in Iran. Fuel prices also soared because of the blockage of the strait. These financial pressures, along with expected volatile weather over the next several months, could push tens of millions more people into acute food insecurity by the end of next year, the report said.
In its latest analysis, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization projected that the El Niño could cause major droughts across much of Africa, Central America and parts of South and Southeast Asia.
A separate FAO analysis submitted to the conference found that 86 percent of countries include food systems and agriculture in Nationally Determined Contributions, their roadmaps for meeting the goals of the 2015 Paris climate agreement. If those countries executed those contributions, emissions from agriculture could shrink more than 40 percent within four years and 76 percent by 2035, compared to 2019 levels.
Yet negotiators at the conference failed to produce any meaningful measures to address the climate crisis through agricultural practices. Governments did not reach any agreement on a cover decision, the concluding statement of the conference, which not only omitted any reference to fossil fuels, but also lacked any mention of food systems or agriculture.
“At a time when urgent and ambitious action is needed, commitments fall far short of what is required to protect our planet and support the hundreds of millions of smallholder farmers who are already bearing the brunt of unpredictable weather, declining harvests and increasing hardship,” said Surita Sandosham, president and CEO of Heifer International, in a written statement.
Countries first developed an agriculture-specific negotiating track at the conference held in Egypt in 2022. The intention was to bring a greater focus on agriculture and, ultimately, more financing for farmers to adapt to changing weather conditions.
But the FAO points out that financing for food and agriculture has fallen by 10 percent since 2024, and receives about 5 percent of climate-related development finance, despite needing nearly 20 percent.
“In their new climate plans countries clearly recognize the opportunities for actions that can build resilience while also reducing emissions significantly from the agricultural sector,” said Kaveh Zahedi, who directs the FAO’s Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment, in a statement. “But the urgency for action is not being matched by climate finance, nor reflected in the negotiated outcomes.”
Those negotiations likely will resume at COP32, which will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
Already, the leadership seems poised to tackle agriculture issues.
During the first week of this year’s conference, Ethiopia announced it would join the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation, a coalition of governments that are urging more robust negotiations around agriculture. Another group, the True Animal Protein Price Coalition, issued a declaration on low-emitting food systems, saying its members would explore “protein diversification”—a diplomatic term for the sensitive topic of reducing emissions from livestock through dietary shifts.
The U.N. has noted a lack of progress on reducing emissions from the livestock sector, which currently accounts for at least 15 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions and one-third of methane, the super-polluting greenhouse gas. Livestock industry lobbyists continue to show up in full force at each year’s conference, contributing to the collapsed efforts on food systems, critics said.

90e8391ed309.text: Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The U.S. economy grew substantially faster this summer than initially thought, the government said Wednesday — a blockbuster upgrade to its estimate of third-quarter GDP. By the numbers: The economy expanded at a 4.3% annualized rate, up from the 3.4% initially reported and nearly twice the rate of 2.2% in the second quarter. Why it matters: The economy has even more momentum than previously understood, a sign of remarkable resilience in the face of higher borrowing costs and stubborn inflation that could give the Fed more latitude to raise rates. Zoom in: The upward revision reflected stronger business investment fueled by the AI buildout and software investment, as well as consumer spending. A measure of underlying private-sector demand — which strips out trade, inventories and government spending — rose at a whopping 5.8% annual rate, up from the 4.9% initially reported. The backdrop: Separate data out Wednesday showed personal income jumped 0.7% in October while inflation-adjusted consumer spending stalled, pushing the saving rate up to 4.1% from 3.6% the prior month. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — climbed 3.8% from a year earlier, from 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, accelerated to 3.3% from 3.1%. On a monthly basis, both headline and core prices rose 0.3%. The bottom line: The U.S. economy was on remarkably strong footing heading into the end of the year, though inflation remains stubbornly high. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on China, the European Union, and more than a dozen other trading partners it says have distorted the global market by overproducing goods like automobiles, batteries and chemicals.
The so-called excess capacity tariffs, which conclude investigations begun in March, comply with existing trade deals and vary by country.
The administration is suggesting a 20% âacross the boardâ tariff on Chinese exports, a senior US official said, which would stack with 2018 tariffs (but not 2026 tariffs targeting forced labor) and exempt goods identified by the Board of Trade. That rate could rise as high as 40% should trade talks collapse, the official added.
The US, which previously notified the affected countries, does not expect China to retaliate with anything stronger than a statement: âThis is part of that process of establishing stability,â the official said.
As for other countries, the official shrugged off the suggestion that the announcement might foster tension: âWe actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 [summit next month] in the wake of these announcements,â the official said.
The announcement follows exit polling that found eight in 10 voters believe Trumpâs tariffs have harmed the economy. It also comes amid continued fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangâs affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has provoked bipartisan scrutiny of US-China policy.
The official predicted the proposed tariffs could take effect in January âat the earliest,â since the administration must first solicit comments and hold hearings. Similar investigations into Norway and Mexico, meanwhile, remain ongoing.
Also on Tuesday night, the administration proposed new tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft. The official attributed these levies to a âlack of progressâ on trade talks.

4abbf759f440.text: The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity. Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns. Post-election polling indicates voters overwhelmingly want tariffs to stay at current levels or decline. There's relatively little support — even among Trump's base — for them rising. Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs largely target specific goods, a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed. China is the exception: The proposed 20% tariff would apply to most Chinese imports, with that rate calibrated to preserve the nations' trade truce. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labor or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior U.S. official said. The official added that the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to live up to its commitments. Between the lines: The proposed tariff rates for other major trading partners are consistent with parameters set out in trade deals, the official said. Trade deals struck with the EU, Japan and South Korea last year established 15% tariff rates on most goods. Other economies targeted include Taiwan, India, Indonesia and Vietnam. On average, the proposals would raise existing tariff rates on targeted trading partners by roughly 5 percentage points, the official estimated. The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers. The proposed tariffs are subject to a public comment period and hearings, with the levies taking effect as early as January, the official said. What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations. The prospect of renewed tariffs weighed on global stocks, particularly Asian markets, overnight. U.S. futures were sharply lower early Wednesday as well. Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The administration proposes raising tariffs on sugar imports exceeding existing quotas (regardless of origin) and imposing a 10% levy on previously exempt Brazilian aircraft, a U.S. official said. The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

The Scoop
A pro-Palestinian group is stepping up its efforts against U.S. support for Israel, with new polling about the damage it did to Republicans this year and a new ad that will air during Saturday Night Live. The 30-second spot from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which shared it first with Semafor, contrasts an American girl saving up for a $400 bicycle with a girl in Gaza who lost a leg to Israeli bombs.
âEvery three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to do this,â says the adâs narrator. (The figure is close to the annual US military assistance to Israel.)
The ad directs viewers to a new campaign site to rally opposition for Israel funding. And the groupâs new polling is a temperature check on Republicans, whose argument about support for Israel has been inflamed since the administration first joined Israel in airstrikes on Iran last summer.
Conducted by YouGov from interviews with 636 respondents who voted for President Trump in 2024 but skipped the midterm election, the pollâs main finding was that Israel was a top factor in their change of mind.
Twenty-nine percent of the falloff voters said that the decision to attack Iran played a âsignificant roleâ in their decision to not vote, and 17% cited ârelations with Israel.â Among these 2024 Trump voters, 78% said that âwe should reduce U.S. support for Israel.â
This polling closes a loop for IMEUâs political arm, which last year interviewed voters whoâd voted for Joe Biden over Donald Trump, then sat out the 2024 election. The top issue cited by those non-voters was Gaza, with 29% of them saying they couldnât have supported Harris without a change in policy.
âWe are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going,â said Margaret DeReus, IMEUâs executive director. âThe vast majority of Americans are unaware that President Trump is reportedly on the verge of signing another long-term weapons giveaway to Israel. With this ad, weâre trying to change that.â
Trumpâs decision to join Israelâs strikes on Iran has divided the right, with some of its most prominent media personalities turning on the president, while most Republicans continue to support it.
The conversation about questioning funds for Israel was also changed by Abdul El-Sayedâs win in Michiganâs Senate race. There, Republicans and some Democrats complained about a Rebellion PAC ad that portrayed a couple cutting their grocery budget to pay more tax money to Israel. El-Sayedâs victory convinced many activists that the figures and organizations ruling some Israel criticism as âanti-semitismâ are badly out of touch with voters â as proved by the controversial ad.
âIt tested through the roof,â Rebellion PAC founder Cenk Uygur told Semafor. âMoved undecideds by double digits to Abdul. Probably the most popular ad in the online world. And was partially responsible for getting Trump to say heâd end funding on Election Day. Walk-off homer.â
Davidâs view
Support for Americaâs current relationship with Israel is lower now than itâs been in decades, with young voters driving the decline. Republicans worked this year to make this a problem for Democrats, who now roundly oppose military aid to Israel, to the extent that Chuck Schumerâs consistent support for it has become an issue for opponents of him leading their new Senate majority.
The math is different for Republicans, but the disagreement has been happening in public all year. It blew up with Vice President JD Vanceâs reaction to the midterm disaster. The GOP coalition is, obviously, nothing like the Democratic coalition; most support for Israel and for disarming Iran comes from evangelical Christians who vote overwhelmingly not Republican, not Jewish voters who still largely support Democrats.
Iâd be surprised if Republicans react to the IMEUâs polling as anything more than meddling by actors who want both parties to cut off the Jewish state. But we are in a moment of post-midterm, pre-presidential primary plasticity, where people with resources will try to influence what both parties are talking about.
Room for Disagreement
Sam Markstein, the political director of the Republican Jewish Coalition, told Semafor that the GOP was now the countryâs only âpro-Israel party,â and that any effort to turn it against the Jewish state was going to fail. If voters wanted a party with that agenda, he said, they now had the Democrats.
âMaking sure that Iran doesnât have a nuclear weapon will go down as one of the great decisions of any presidency,â he said.
Notable
- Last week, Axios reporter Marc Caputo published polling conducted for the Combat Antisemitism Movement, which found widespread support for Israel in early primary states, suggesting âa potential disconnect between GOP votersâ attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online.â
- U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told the Institute for National Security Studies that Republicans were now more supportive of Israel than Democrats, and that the presidentâs talk about halting aid may not pan out.

61ef52901630.text:
Lizâs view
The #SaveJensen punch wore off fast. The dopamine hit from Huangâs comeback that sent shares surging 31% on Monday has already faded as investors remember why theyâd been selling: AI money is too expensive, AI demand too tenuous, AI politics too uncertain. By Tuesday, Nvidiaâs shares had closed at their July 2025 levels.
Markets can be wrong, for a shockingly long time. But the laws of financial gravity are catching up to AI and its frontman at speeds that are hard to outrun. Over the past year, youâd have done better owning the largest landlord of American malls than Nvidia, which holds a near monopoly on the key component of the most transformative technology in human history.
Huang himself did little to help. A chastened CEO might have slipped back into headquarters, quietly mumbling something about getting to work and promising to address the corporate governance minefield he left behind. Instead he accepted a heroâs welcome and doubled down on the very things, like a lack of succession planning and dozens of direct reports, that precipitated one of the most acute and costly corporate crises in recent memory. In remarks to employees Tuesday, he said he has no plans to change any of the structural weaknesses that caused it. (He is, he noted, in therapy.)
Monday will go into the record books as the largest single-day value creation in market history: Nvidia added $1 trillion. But it will end up a reverse Groundhog Day â one we immediately forget as investors sober up and remember why they were discontent in the first place.
Notable
- Huangâs return to Nvidia will also be tough on China, Bloomberg columnist Catherine Thorbecke writes. âHis comeback puts both him and his arguments [about China] under an even harsher spotlight,â she argues. âAnd Chinese AIâs forced breakup with Nvidia is likely to only get uglier.â

The looming expiration of a blockbuster drug patent pushed Sanofi into the biggest M&A deal in its history this week (and the largest pharma deal in three years). It wonât be the last.
The French giantâs $41 billion takeover of respiratory drugmaker Insmed is in part a bid to replenish its pipeline ahead of the patent cliff facing Dupixent, the eczema drug whose $20-plus billion in annual sales will face generic competition starting in 2031. Across the industry, more than $500 billion of prescription-drug sales face patent expirations in the next six years, which could usher in a takeover wave.
The biggest of those is Merckâs Keytruda, the worldâs best-selling drug, which loses US patent in 2028. But all the big drugmakers are facing a similar crisis: Nearly half of Bristolâs sales are at risk by 2030 (which might help explain its merger flirtations with AstraZeneca earlier this year). Ozempic maker Novo Nordisk is regrouping after losing a bidding war over a new weight-loss drug last year to Pfizer.
Hoovering up promising molecules doesnât always pay off. Merckâs $12 billion purchase of Acceleron in 2021 brought it a new blockbuster blood-pressure drug whose sales have outperformed, but the jury is still out on Bristolâs $14 billion deal for schizophrenia drug Cobenfy.

IPO allocation gamesmanship strikes again, this time at Anthropic. Anthropic shares fell below their $83-a-share IPO price on Tuesday, careening toward the original target of $78 a share. The listing was reportedly six times oversubscribed, so where did those buyers go?
Investors in anticipated deals ask for more shares than they actually want, assuming theyâll be cut back.
âIf it sounds oversubscribed, they inflate their orders, and then it gets more oversubscribed, and so on,â said Jay Ritter, academiaâs godfather of IPO research. âItâs not the same as actual desire to own the stock.â He notes that pension funds, the classic buy-and-hold investors, tend to be cut out entirely of IPO allocations.
Investment banks tend to steer shares to favored hedge-fund clients likely to sell into an IPO pop (Anthropic shares opened last week above $111, a first-trade gain of 34%). Supply and demand are now fighting it out, which is harder for a $1 trillion-plus company with a murky path to profitability â just ask SpaceX, whose shares are down 22% since its IPO.
And Ritter? He put in an order in his Schwab account for 3,000 shares. He got 51.

Five baobabs have been replanted in a South African nature reserve after being uprooted and trucked to Durbanâs port, where they were going to be illegally exported. A landscaping company had sold the two-century-old trees, revered in many parts of Africa, to a customer in the Caucasus country of Georgia without seeking permission from the authorities, the South Africa-based conservation charity Baobab Foundation â instrumental in saving the trees â told Semafor.
After a three-day, 900 kilometer-journey on huge flatbed vehicles, the 7 meter to 9 meter high baobabs were returned to the soil. There is no systematic data collection on baobab smuggling, but others across the continent have told the Foundation of similar incidents targeting the trees, which for some serve as shrines and a connection with the spirit world, while also providing food, shade, and a meeting place.

Senegal were reinstated as the winners of Africaâs top football competition, after a court in Switzerland overturned a decision by the sportâs continental governing body that had declared Morocco the champions.
Januaryâs Africa Cup of Nations final in Rabat descended into chaos after Senegalese players walked off the pitch to protest refereeing decisions, only to return after some 15 minutes and go on to win the game. Eight weeks later, the Confederation of African Football annulled their victory over the walkout, handing Morocco the title. But the Lausanne-based Court of Arbitration for Sport disagreed, respecting the decision of the referee to continue the match. The extraordinary episode threatened to question the integrity of the CAF under the leadership of South African billionaire Patrice Motsepe.
Senegalâs football federation celebrated, declaring on Instagram: âAgain and always African champions.â But Morocco said it will look for ways to challenge the ruling.

South Africaâs biggest trade union federation backed workers angry at their exclusion from discussions over telecoms giant MTNâs potential takeover of partly state-owned Telkom, escalating political scrutiny of a proposed transaction that could reshape one of Africaâs largest mobile markets.
COSATU is supporting its affiliate, the Communications Workers Union, which said employees have not been consulted over the proposed $2 billion-plus deal and is demanding disclosure about its potential impact on jobs and collective agreements.
MTN, Africaâs largest mobile operator by subscribers, is in early talks to buy one-time monopoly Telkom in a purchase that will also test the stateâs willingness to relinquish its 40% shareholding and allow further consolidation in the sector. Nigeriaâs central bank held its benchmark interest rate at 23%, with its governor expressing confidence that West Africaâs largest economy was stable ahead of crunch elections in January. The bankâs rate-setting committee pointed to slowing inflation, which has eased for five consecutive months, but noted that continued tensions in the Middle East âcould sustain pressure on energy prices.â

94457aec61da.text:
Alexisâs view
The phrase âcash is kingâ remains true across Africa in a way that it doesnât in other parts of the world. In many African countries, the informal economy dominates and the flow of cash unites millions of entrepreneurs. But itâs also true that the continent has for years been at the vanguard of digital payments: That provides policymakers with more visibility into economic activity, expands the tax base, and improves the efficiency of revenue collection.
The small businesses that drive African economies are increasingly making use of cheaper mobile phone handsets to swap cash for digital payments, a new report suggests. Overall transactions using mobile phones in Africa last year were more than double the figure of 2021, according to digital payment research group AfricaNenda Foundation. The average amount spent on each mobile transfer nearly halved over the same period, suggesting digital systems are increasingly being used for everyday purchases, rather than larger one-off transactions.
These changing habits have far-reaching consequences. At an individual level, a digital transaction history can help to build a credit history. Some countries are even going further, linking payment systems to national digital IDs.
But at the same time, AI poses a raft of new challenges by making it easier, cheaper, and faster for criminals to set up scams, such as deepfakes, to trick people into authorizing payments. A recent Interpol report found AI was linked to more than half of cybercrime in Africa, with losses across 26 nations more than doubling in 2025 compared with the previous year.
Cash has remained popular because people trust money they can hold. Now that so many people in Africa have learned to trust digital payments, the next big challenge for policymakers and financial institutions is to protect users against the evolution of fraud.

0ace05fabf65.text:
- Published
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.
Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.
"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.
"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.
The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

0f7af8237d93.text:
- Published
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".
In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".
"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.
The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.
Political analyst Khanyi Magubane said the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility".
She made it clear that the ruling was not a criminal finding on possible improper conduct at the farm but rather an indictment at the independent panel's report.
"[So] he does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," Magubane said.
The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

af5fe33c0f02.text:
The News
Saudi Arabia can withstand the regional war without derailing its finances, Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan said, warning adversaries that missile attacks on civilian targets wonât force the kingdomâs hand.
The idea that Saudi Arabia âcan be blackmailedâ by missile attacks on civilian targets âis a total mistake,â Al Jadaan told reporters in Riyadh. âWeâre resilient enough to stand a prolonged conflict.â
The kingdom has only modestly increased its defense budget after nine months of war and can significantly boost military spending if required, the minister said. âWe have no price tag, we have no cap in terms of how much we can provide to our military if they need supplies.â
Saudi Arabiaâs finances have stood up to almost a year of unprecedented challenges from conflict in the region and disruptions to oil exports without dipping into reserves, Al Jadaan said.
Higher oil prices have offset lower export volumes this year, helping total government revenue beat earlier expectations. The non-oil economy is growing despite supply chain disruptions and strains on efforts to attract tourists. But higher oil prices havenât been enough to keep the economy running, and the government boosted spending to soften the impact, widening the deficit to 4.9% of GDP compared to forecast of a 3.3% deficit before the war.
The kingdom plans to cut spending next year as some investment projects are completed and the government seeks to contain the deficit, which it expects to narrow to 3.6% of GDP.
No âgood time to reformâ
Over the past year, Saudi Arabia has dropped some of its most expensive projects, including the 170-kilometer twin skyscrapers at NEOM, as it reins in runaway spending. Al Jadaan drew a distinction between projects used to achieve longer term economic goals and the overall vision for the kingdomâs economic development. âIf some of the tools are not right for the moment, weâll change them,â Jadaan said. âIf some need to be warehoused, weâll warehouse them â¦ Vision 2030 is way beyond just one program or one project.â
The economy is expected to contract 3.3% this year before bouncing back with 7.9% growth in 2027. Much of that is down to lower oil output. Corporate profits for listed companies rose around 15% in the first nine months of 2026, Al Jadaan said, indicating that the private sector growth is robust.
The government expects to keep running a deficit. Debt-to-GDP is forecast to hit 39% by 2029, with some economists expecting it could breach a self-imposed 40% ceiling sooner. Al Jadaan sees no reason to increase the limit in the next few years, saying it âserves us well, it brings more discipline.â
The kingdom is also pressing ahead with subsidy reforms such as measures to increase power prices from next year. The moves are unpopular and have received rare criticism of the government from Saudi citizens. âThere will never be a good time to reform,â Al Jadaan said. âYou go with the plan.â
Notable
- Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning to travel to the US in December for the G20 Leadersâ summit, Semafor reported.
- Nine months into the Iran war, Generation MBS are rallying behind the Crown Prince, who they credit for an era of new-found freedoms.

The Solomon Islands scrapped a security pact with China in favor of one with Australia, a reversal that dealt a major blow to Beijingâs efforts to expand its influence in the Pacific. The 2022 agreement allowed China to rotate police training teams through the Solomon Islands, sparking alarm in Washington and Canberra, which feared China was deepening a foothold in the region.
Australia has in recent years contested that effort, strengthening ties with Pacific nations including Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu with its own deals. âFrom Chinaâs closest friend in the Pacific to one of Australiaâs,â The Economistâs Asia diplomatic editor posted on X of the Solomon Islandsâ decision, âa big shift and an impressive piece of diplomacy.â

The head of the United Nationsâ agency for AIDS said infections worldwide were likely to rise as the worst-affected countries struggle to contain the fallout of Western aid cuts. A US court found Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of fraud, deepening antagonism between the superpowers as tech and trade tensions mount. The countriesâ leaders have built a strong rapport, but their policies are another matter.
