Washingtonâs intensifying restrictions on Chinaâs access to cutting-edge microchips could worsen a coming semiconductor supply glut in the US, analysts warned. The AI boom has in large part been constrained by access to the power needed for a huge buildout of data centers and the chips needed to run them. That may be changing, with SemiAnalysis noting that when it came to Nvidiaâs AI chips, âwe are starting to see signs of a broader pricing cooldown.â
Two factors are at play: Major semiconductor manufacturers, including relatively new entrants such as Google, are ramping up production just as the Nvidia espionage scandal galvanizes opinion in Washington to further limit Chinaâs access to the technology, freeing up supply for US firms.

510234d634ca.text:
- Published
Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.
Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said was a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.
They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.
With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, De la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, in which one gunman was killed.
Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers.
One was killed in the operation and four have been arrested.
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation.
In footage released since then, he can be seen, with a handgun strapped to his belt, flanked by the commanders of the operation.
Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused.
Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, which is located in a popular shopping mall.
Local media said that as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (Â£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads.
It is not clear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.
Local media are reporting that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.
The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.
The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.
Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.
A woman called Sandra told news site Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.
Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.
Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.
But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.
At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.
Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination with foreign and Colombian tourists.
Cartagena's mayor, Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".
President De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.
On Tuesday, he had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb which detonated outside the regional government's offices.
While De la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.

2ad1a2cacbff.text:
Raised on reform
Countries such as France, India, and Serbia may have increasingly disaffected and volatile Gen Z populations â¦ Saudi Arabia has Gen MBS.
Here, nine months into the Iran war â and roughly nine weeks into an intensifying conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen â the kingdomâs young people have been rallying behind Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, their loyalty a result of growing up in an era of new-found freedoms.
There was a time before MBS â before cinemas, concerts, and women being allowed to get behind the wheel of a car â but under-25s (around half the population) either canât remember, or donât care to remember, what things were like a decade ago, prior to his reformist Vision 2030.
Gen MBS is not bothered if the princeâs megaprojects or futuristic cities in the desert flop, they attend music festivals and watch the worldâs top artists perform in Saudi â hi Travis Scott, Metallica, Eminem, Cardi B, Bruno Mars, and friends â events that, if you had told me about growing up, wouldâve seemed far fetched.
They go out in mixed groups of men and women, and live the way he said they would â in newly opened beach fronts in Jeddah and Six Flags in Riyadh. They came of age as the changes were bedding in and credit him entirely.
Over the coming decades of his rule, the stakes will remain immense: The crown prince needs to deliver jobs and growing prosperity to keep this generation on his side. The first signs of strain are already showing, with grumblings about the recent increase in energy prices, the rising cost of living, and the number of jobs going to foreigners.
But since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, and especially since Houthi strikes intensified here from September, this cohort has become the most vocal constituency defending the country.
Free lattes for loyalty
The question I often get from people not from Saudi Arabia is whether these conspicuous demonstrations of loyalty are coerced. While there is no reliable polling on the subject, and no other way to survey the country writ large, in daily conversations and posts on socials the sentiment is palpable: The answer, as far as I can tell, is no.
Social media feeds are filled with Saudi flag waving and the slogan âmy homeland is a red line,â implying that it will be defended without compromise. Coffee chains and businesses have run promotions for members of the armed forces and those who have donated blood. Influencers have posted what amount to loyalty pledges: Among them, Saudi food blogger Yousef Hinnawi, who goes by Bo3omarEats, made a viral TikTok explainer making clear that âall Saudi nationals are the countryâs first line of defense.â Influencers who have not taken a stance have been harangued by comments demanding they make their position clear.
Saudis, like me, who came of age during the 2015 Yemen war, have always measured their lives against the West, questioned a government they nevertheless did not expect to change, and thought first of fellow Muslims when the Saudi-backed coalition went in. It was uncomfortable to be at war with Yemenis seen by many as less-affluent kin.
For those just a bit younger, things were different. The religious police lost their arrest powers in 2016; women began driving for the first time in 2018, the same year Riyadhâs first movie theater in decades opened with Black Panther. This generation is more satisfied with the standard of living, less inclined to look abroad, or question a government it sees as having delivered on a promise of bringing about reform, and is more unabashedly Saudi.
With regular strikes on the capital, the prince faces a defining chapter of his rule, and he is grappling with the same restless generation confronting leaders around the world. The difference is that his people are loyal to him, and have conjured more virality around backing the prince than criticizing him.
Notable
- Elsewhere, the kids fly pirate flags: Bloomberg charted a Gen Z protest wave â 53 mass demonstrations across 33 economies â that toppled leaders in Nepal, Madagascar, and Bulgaria.
- Riyadh Season opened its seventh edition on schedule in October, with sold-out concerts, a 2,760-drone show, and new zones still opening through November.

4031465880c6.text:
Eveâs view
The worldâs top clothing brands have been looking to diversify their supply chains beyond China and are starting to create an opening for African manufacturers. But while preferential trade access to the US has helped improve their prospects, the ability of African economies to capture a lasting share of global manufacturing will depend on a lot more than trade preferences.
Itâs worth noting that while China continues to dominate global clothing manufacturing, its position has gradually weakened over the past 15 years as international brands look elsewhere for sourcing. Several African countries have emerged as promising alternatives, thatâs partly thanks to the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market for qualifying products, including clothing.
In the latest ranking by global trade insurer Coface of the countries well positioned to expand their role in global apparel and footwear manufacturing amid changes in US trade policy, Lesotho and Madagascar climbed to fourth and sixth place respectively, having previously ranked outside the top 20. Their improved positions largely reflect the restoration of duty-free access under AGOA, following announcements of additional US tariffs of 50% and 47% in April 2025. Mauritius, another AGOA beneficiary, also features in the top 20.
The benefits should not be underestimated because most competing suppliers remain subject to standard US tariffs, with some also facing new US measures targeting forced labor as well as China being subject to further country-specific duties. These are particularly significant for Lesotho and Madagascar, as the US market accounts for approximately half and nearly 30% of their respective clothing and footwear export volumes.
However, that dependence exposes the limits of building a manufacturing strategy around preferential trade access. Unlike a typical free trade agreement, AGOA is a unilateral US program that allows Washington to withdraw benefits from individual countries who might fail its annual reviews to meet certain economic, governance and foreign policy criteria.
That means AGOAâs recent extension until December 2028 offered no guarantee that all current beneficiaries will retain access. On Nov. 2 â just two months after the extension was agreed â Washington announced plans to terminate South Africaâs and Rwandaâs eligibility from January 2027.
Ultimately this means African manufacturers need to diversify their export markets. One particularly attractive option would be to strengthen trade ties with the European Union, the worldâs largest clothing consumer market, to help mitigate exposure to unpredictable US trade policy.
More importantly, Africaâs manufacturing prospects extend beyond AGOA. Morocco and Tunisia, which have never benefited from the program, also feature among Cofaceâs top 20 countries. Rwanda remains in the ranking despite losing preferential treatment for clothing exports under AGOA in 2018.
These countriesâ respective approaches point to a broader set of factors that determine where international brands choose to manufacture. Labor costs, logistics, social stability, and production capacity all matter but so does the ability to deliver reliable supplies at scale.
AGOA will continue to help African countries attract manufacturers, but it canât guarantee that they stay. The real longer-term opportunity will lie in building industries that international brands choose for their commercial competitiveness, rather than simply the tariff advantages they enjoy.
Eve BarrÃ© is a sector economist for Textile-clothing, Transport, and Wood at Coface, a global trade credit insurer.

881d75b86058.text: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), a potential 2028 presidential contender, asserted in an interview with "The Axios Show" that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to AI because of billionaire greed and clout. He said voters hate the technology because they fear losing control. Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, told Mike Allen this week that after an " AI earthquake " helped propel Democrats to huge midterm gains, Congress must treat oversight of the technology as an "emergency" for the first 100 hours of Democratic control. Why it matters: Moore, 48, focused on AI early, with an executive order in 2024 . He has used his NGA leadership roles to work across the aisle on AI protections, arguing that Marylanders can't afford to wait for Washington and shouldn't have to wait for a disaster . Moore, Maryland's first Black governor , is a former Army paratrooper who deployed to combat in Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, and was a Rhodes Scholar and White House fellow. What they're saying: Moore, speaking at the Maryland State House in Annapolis, makes it clear in this episode of "The Axios Show" that AI will be a huge focus of the 2028 presidential race after becoming a flashpoint in November's midterms. Among the governor's key points: On the pace of regulation: "We are watching a fast-moving technology that is being protected at a snail's pace." On why people hate AI: "Genesis 1 talks about how God gave humanity dominion over all land, air and sea. And that dominion was given to humanity, not to robots." On whether regulating AI lets China win: "This is not a question of U.S. versus China. This is a question of man versus machine." On a bubble: "We are in a bubble because you cannot have that much influence by such a small group of companies." On Nvidia and Trump: "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee. ... We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves making this decision." Zoom in: Moore in September laid out his framework for AI policy, aimed at regulating frontier AI developers, shielding workers from surveillance and protecting children. His priorities include: Ensuring regulations keep pace with rapidly advancing technology. Holding companies responsible for releasing dangerous AI models. Building on Maryland's efforts to protect people's name, image and likeness from AI misuse, including in political advertising. Earlier this year, Moore signed a law targeting deceptive AI in campaign ads, including images, audio and video. The big picture: Governors across the political spectrum, from California's Gavin Newsom and New York's Kathy Hochul (both Democrats) to Utah's Spencer Cox and Florida's Ron DeSantis (both Republicans), are positioning themselves as filling the regulatory vacuum left by Washington. Moore is linking AI policy to a broader Democratic message about corruption and the influence of money in politics. "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting," the governor told us. "It's difficult to hear when Congress is talking about what they're going to do to protect us when we know that they are trading stocks." Watch the episode ... Subscribe to "The Axios Show" on YouTube .

19584ccf5395.text: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status , according to a new Ipsos poll . But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it. Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress. There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot. What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks. 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions. There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans. Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community. There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%). The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview. A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats. "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many Americans, there's little in the [new] survey to suggest it will lead people who were not already supportive of investigating the administration to prioritize congressional oversight on this issue," said Alec Tyson, senior vice president of Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs. That isn't discouraging some Democrats on Capitol Hill. Incoming Senate health committee Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said last week that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stewardship of the federal health apparatus during the measles outbreaks is "certainly one area that needs investigation." House Energy and Commerce Democrats want to know whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suppressed the number of measles deaths reported to the public. They've also criticized agency director Erica Schwartz for not providing meaningful answers about decision-making around the reporting and response. The CDC has said it's committed to stopping outbreaks and regaining the measles elimination status. It has pointed to actions like providing about $100 million in extra funding to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. What we're watching: Support for childhood vaccinations appears stronger than in the immediate aftermath of the pandemic. Gallup this week found that more than 7 in 10 say it is extremely or very important for parents to get their children vaccinated — with the share saying it is extremely important 7 percentage points higher than in 2024. Methodology: The Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 20-23, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,022 general population adults age 18 or older. The margin of sampling error is +/-3.2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults.

Why has China sent the first Pakistani astronaut to space?

0c66e6827e0c.text: A top executive at one of the Republican Party's most influential consulting firms was involved in a multimillion-dollar effort to defeat two GOP senators — Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — in the midterm elections, Axios has learned. The firm, Axiom Strategies, is widely seen as the GOP's biggest consulting operation, with deep ties to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and other prominent Republican figures. Why it matters: It's exceedingly rare — if not unprecedented — for an executive at a major political consulting firm to work for groups seeking to defeat senators from the firm's own party in a general election. Driving the news: Federal election records identify Thomas Datwyler, who was listed on Axiom's website as CEO of its AxCapital division, as treasurer and custodian of records for three super PACs that reported more than $9.9 million in spending that targeted Husted and Sullivan, who lost their bids for reelection. The three super PACs were registered between March and October. Axiom founder Jeff Roe learned of Datwyler's involvement from a lawyer on Oct. 30 and demanded his resignation, according to a source with knowledge of the situation. Datwyler resigned that day, and Axiom says it will finish unwinding its relationship with him by Dec. 31. He was removed from the company's website Tuesday. Roe also contacted the White House to inform officials of what he had discovered, the source said. Zoom out: The super PACs boosted lesser-known candidates, including Republicans and Libertarians, in apparent attempts to draw conservative votes away from Sullivan and Husted. It's unclear what impact the groups' work had on the senators' defeats. The groups ran digital ads attacking the senators from the right, accusing Sullivan of supporting gender-transition surgeries for children and Husted of backing gun control measures. Right for Alaska spent nearly $2.4 million through Sept. 30, while Alaska Values PAC reported at least $3.75 million in spending targeting Sullivan and boosting others. In Ohio, Buckeye Freedom PAC spent more than $3.8 million targeting Husted and promoting Libertarian candidate William "Bill" Redpath. It also sponsored HustedRecords.com, a website attacking the senator's record. Right for Alaska also received $990,000 from Sixteen Thirty Fund, a major liberal dark-money organization that previously has received funding from groups tied to Democratic megadonor George Soros, a frequent target of Republicans' attacks. Behind the scenes: Axiom executives were unaware of Datwyler's involvement with the PACs before Oct. 30, a person familiar with the company said. Datwyler was recruited by an outside consultant to establish the groups and did not initially understand their activities, according to a person familiar with his account. Datwyler, a veteran Republican campaign finance consultant who has been treasurer for hundreds of political committees, was described by people familiar with his work as accepting clients without always scrutinizing their objectives. The PACs' FEC filings list payments to little-known LLCs registered in Wyoming and Delaware, making it difficult to determine who carried out the work. What they're saying: "Axiom Strategies is a Republican firm whose sole purpose is to defeat Democrats," an Axiom spokesperson said. "Axiom companies did zero work against the Republican nominees for U.S. Senate in Ohio and Alaska, and has zero connection to any of those PACs' vendors." The spokesperson said Axiom received no compensation for Datwyler's work for the super PACs. Datwyler did not respond to several requests for comment. The big picture: Roe managed Cruz's 2016 presidential campaign. Axiom consultants already have discussed a potential 2028 campaign with Cruz, according to sources familiar with the talks. Roe and his firm are expected to run Cruz's campaign if he enters the race. Cruz traveled to Alaska in October to campaign for Sullivan.

77a5f15eebf9.text: The Trump administration is facing the first of possibly hundreds of lawsuits testing whether it can be held liable for how immigration officers acted during the ICE crackdowns . Why it matters: These cases could force the administration to defend the conduct of officers operating under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and now-retired Border Patrol Commander-at-large Greg Bovino. Driving the news: Democracy Forward, an advocacy litigation nonprofit, filed its first Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) case on Monday on behalf of Dayanne Figueroa. Figueroa, a U.S. citizen, was arrested during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago in October 2025. Video footage of Figueroa's arrest, after dropping her son off at school, shows officers driving into her vehicle and dragging her out of her car by her legs in a chaotic scene with multiple witnesses. Under FTCA, she could file for monetary compensation. And if the case goes to trial, discovery could reveal more information about the directives to make arrests during Operation Midway Blitz. What they're saying: "I anticipated that I was going to be met with silence. I'm not surprised, but again, I still expect accountability, so I'm not gonna let that define the outcome of all this," Figueroa said in an exclusive interview with Axios. "I want my experience to be a catalyst for meaningful change." Figueroa has also testified before Congress and filed a police report over her experience. She is now asking for no more than $1 million, according to the FTCA filing, which alleges unlawful arrest, battery and failure to provide medical care. Zoom in: Figueroa's claim comes after filing an administrative complaint against DHS over its officers' conduct both during her arrest and while she was detained. The administration had six months to respond, but didn't, opening her path to an FTCA case. "This is really a sort of tip of the spear of this type of case," Jeff Dubner, an attorney leading the effort for Democracy Forward, said of Figueroa's case. "We know of a number of administrative claims that are waiting for the time to ripen." "As we are at the one-year mark for Midway Blitz, we are coming up in the one-year mark from Metro Surge [in Minneapolis], and also the broadening of the enforcement effort to really being around the country, and so, you know, we'll see more and more of these," he said. The intrigue : Democracy Forward's legal team anticipates the government will try to dismiss Figueroa's case and others under tort law by claiming that the officers were acting within their discretion as law enforcement, her attorney Shiva Kooragayala said. "There is no immunity for federal law enforcement officers who are carrying out immigration arrests or any other kinds of federal law enforcement," Dubner said. "Congress was very intentional when it passed the FTCA, when it expanded the FTCA to include assault and battery and false arrest and false imprisonment by law enforcement officers." The other side: " Federal agents who enforce our immigration laws, as they did in Operation Midway Blitz, which targeted criminal illegal aliens in Chicago, are protected by long-established legal immunities and defenses against lawsuits over their official conduct," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. "The Federal Tort Claims Act is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity with strict requirements and exceptions, and filing a claim does not mean it has merit. We will respond to any litigation in court." A DHS spokesperson said that its agents follow the laws passed by Congress. Between the lines: Figueroa was recovering from a kidney surgery at the time, and the pressure of the officers pinning her to the ground caused her further complications. After asking for medical attention and then showing physical signs of distress, she began urinating blood while in custody. Figueroa was rushed to a hospital for treatment, according to the legal complaint. "I'm so so grateful for having those people that were there to film. Like if they weren't there, this would have just gone under the rug." Figueroa said. "They took my DNA and everything, but I left the office with nothing, zero evidence, like I wasn't even there."

ace489d1ee32.text: Top AI executives are increasingly pushing back against a common view inside Anthropic: that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, sources told Axios. That would put us on a slippery slope to forfeiting free will, critics say. Why it matters : The debate has picked up steam as top AI companies develop models certain employees consider too powerful to ever release . Many see Anthropic as the first company that will confront these questions due to its lead at the frontier of AI development. While critics have yet to call out the company by name, their public defenses of human agency and control take direct aim at what some have come to see as the worldview of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. When AI systems far surpass human intelligence, Amodei has said repeatedly that it will be preferable to turn over decision-making for "life-critical" cases to AI, and also said AI should oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources. Flashback: A product vision slide from several years ago that was revealed during litigation described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box." The big picture: The thinking for Amodei and others is that once AI can demonstrably cure diseases, safeguard humans from harming themselves or prevent disasters better than any person, refusing to hand over control becomes irrational — or even unethical. Proponents point to self-driving cars to make their case: Once statistical evidence points to autonomous vehicles being safer than human drivers, it is logical for humans to drive far less, if at all, they say. Inside Anthropic, a broad consensus has developed among some employees that humanity will—and in many cases should — safely hand over authority to superintelligent systems rather than fighting to retain control, according to people familiar with internal discussions. An Anthropic spokesperson said Amodei has advocated for human control of AI in many public remarks and that Anthropic trains Claude not to undermine human oversight. Driving the news: Rival executives are increasingly rebuking the notion that humans will surrender agency, even as major math and reasoning breakthroughs convince insiders that superintelligence is imminent. "We should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI," Meta's top AI leader Alexandr Wang wrote on X, reflecting on the importance of a coming superintelligence moment after an Anthropic breakthrough on a "Holy Grail" mathematics problem. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman rebuked this view earlier this month: "I want people to have the agency over the future... I think it's really important that we advocate for this." Dean Ball, OpenAI's head of strategic futures, calls this phenomenon the " silent consensus. " He told Axios this is "an extraordinarily common view in AI safety circles," adding that "People don't always think it's good. Some people do." Zoom in: Across podcasts, public interviews and in his writing, Amodei has for years pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be "many cases where we do want to stay in charge" even if humans make worse decisions: Safety: In a February New York Times interview, Amodei said that in " life-critical, safety-critical cases , we really want to turn it over" to AI, noting society will simply need time to adapt. Defense: In a CBS discussion that month, he argued that fully autonomous weapons may eventually be "needed for the defense of democracy " if adversaries deploy them first. Education: In November of 2024, Amodei noted that the traditional system of a professor supervising graduate students could be reversed, as "the AI systems will be the PIs, will be the leaders, and they'll be ordering humans or other AI systems around." Writing: In his 2024 essay "Machines of Loving Grace," Amodei suggested one possible future economy in which superintelligent AI systems distribute resources based on "what the AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans." He notes that it could the distribution could be "derived from human values." Between the lines: Some AI leaders are privately frustrated by rhetoric about turning over decision-making because they fear it is pouring fuel on a growing public and political backlash against the technology. That's exactly what Maryland Gov. Wes Moore — a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender — said this week in an interview on "The Axios Show." Invoking the Book of Genesis, Moore argued that God gave humanity dominion over the earth, "not to robots, not to agents." Friction point: Outside of Anthropic, AI executives have appeared divided in their public views on free will in the superintelligence era. Elon Musk recently reiterated his decade-plus-long view that when we hit superintelligence, the human race will become "like pet labradors," although he's also backed technology to amplify the human brain with machine computation capabilities in order to give humans a continued advantage. The bottom line: The debate over superintelligence is no longer just about how to keep rogue machines from destroying humanity — it's about whether humans should be willing to voluntarily step aside.

5e7b583accc3.text: Data: YouGov; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios. Note: Data for this question among 929 adults who say they're celebrating Thanksgiving After November's midterm blue wave , Democrats are more likely to say political discussions will be on the table this Thanksgiving than Republicans, per recent polling . Why it matters: The volatility and vitriol of modern politics often threatens to infiltrate our social dynamics. Still, most Americans doubt the holiday will bring political arguments. By the numbers: In YouGov's survey, 37% of respondents planning to celebrate Thanksgiving said they were at least somewhat likely to discuss politics during dinner. More than half (56%) say politics is not likely to come up during their gathering. Yes, but: The share who expect to talk politics this year varies by party affiliation. Forty-five percent of Democrats celebrating Thanksgiving say they expect political conversations, compared to 28% of Independents and 39% of Republicans in YouGov's trend. Zoom in: And more than eight in ten think politics won't start turkey day tiffs: Just 12% expect arguments over politics at the celebration. Those numbers are relatively stable among political ideologies: 83% of Democrats, 82% of Independents and 85% of Republicans aren't prepping for a political food fight this year. Last year, among all respondents in YouGov's poll , 11% expected arguments, compared to 72% who didn't. Zoom out: Data for Progress, a progressive polling and research organization, similarly found that 11% of likely voters said they'd definitely discuss politics at Thanksgiving, and 26% said they probably would. Another 59% said they probably or definitely would not. However, 65% said they plan to talk at least some about the cost of living. Friction point: Even if political arguments don't fuel Thanksgiving stress, pocketbook strain is another story. This year, the average Thanksgiving dinner is up 6%, ending three straight years of price declines, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation . But as Axios' Brad Jennings notes, the survey's price checks were done earlier in the month, possibly before deeper discounts or promotions kicked off. The bottom line: We can't promise the turkey won't be dry or that your nosy aunt won't pry. But if your dinner goes how most Americans expect, politics won't be the root of this year's family drama. Methodology: The YouGov poll was conducted online on November 8 - 10, 2026 among 1,081 U.S. adult citizens. The margin of error for the overall sample is approximately 4 percentage points. Sticker Shock Looms as a Major Challenge in Push for Single-Payer Healthcare
As an Oregon panel finalized its proposal for statewide universal healthcare this month, opposition had already coalesced around a familiar theme: The costs and the new taxes needed to support it will be staggeringly large. The panel’s estimates place the cost of the plan at $69.7 billion a year starting in 2032.
The same arguments are being made on the national level about “Medicare for All,” which gained renewed life after Democrats’ victorious blue wave in the midterms. One recent White House cost estimate pegged the annual price tag at $4.7 trillion.
But single-payer proponents, researchers, and academics are countering the perceived sticker shock with another stark reality: If you think universal healthcare would be expensive, you should see what we pay now.
“We already do spend trillions of dollars on healthcare,” said Cynthia Cox, a senior vice president at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. “It’s just that it’s not only spent by the federal government but also by states, individuals, private insurers, and other third-party payers.”
Increased government spending under a universal health plan would replace much, if not all, of what is currently being paid by companies and consumers, while extending health coverage to more people, its proponents argue. And they say many people would end up paying less for a universal health plan’s taxes than consumers now shell out in premiums and other out-of-pocket costs.
But those nuances represent some of the biggest challenges of selling a universal healthcare system to the public. Unless backers can figure out the messaging to alleviate fears of massive new taxes and government spending, current efforts to implement a single-payer, universal healthcare plan could be doomed to the same fate as previous efforts in places such as California, Massachusetts, and Vermont.
Educating the Public
In 2014, then-Vermont Gov. Peter Shumlin, a Democrat, pulled the plug on the state’s single-payer push. Difficulties in implementing the state’s healthcare exchange under the Affordable Care Act had sapped the political capital he needed to push through the plan’s tax increases, even though the state expected to save money for Vermonters overall.
Single-player ballot measures in California, Massachusetts, and Oregon also struggled to garner even a quarter of the voting public’s support.
The Democratic wave in this year’s midterm elections, however, ushered in a number of Medicare-for-All proponents, most notably Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who campaigned on a universal healthcare platform. The change in congressional control is also expected to elevate Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats and is the best-known advocate for Medicare for All, to chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
That is likely to push a debate over single-payer healthcare — and its costs or savings — to the forefront in the next two years, leading into the 2028 presidential election.
“Most people think that what they pay out-of-pocket or out of their paycheck directly is what it costs, and they’re not as familiar with the larger piece,” said John McDonough, a health policy professor at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. “Nobody on Medicare knows what that costs. Nobody on Medicaid knows what it costs. Very few people on the exchanges know. So, with something brand-new, it’s a massive education effort just to get to the starting line.”
The White House Council of Economic Advisers, for example, estimated in October that a plan to extend Medicare benefits to all Americans would cost the federal government $47 trillion over 10 years. And a recent Wall Street Journal op-ed from Joel Zinberg of the conservative-leaning Paragon Health Institute decried that figure as a massive increase in federal spending.
But the latest government data shows total spending for healthcare from all sources in the U.S. reached about $5.3 trillion in 2024. And that spending is on pace to top $72 trillion combined over the 10-year period from 2025 through 2034. While that estimate includes spending for the military and veterans, the Indian Health Service, and elective services that might not be covered under a universal health plan, the price tag for national healthcare coverage still could look like a bargain.
“People are aware that healthcare is very expensive and that they have trouble getting access to it even if they have decent insurance,” said Stephanie Woolhandler, a public health professor at the City University of New York’s Hunter College. “But if they think $47 trillion is a big number relative to what we’re spending now, they’re mistaken.”
Oregon Shares Same Challenge
The Oregon Universal Health Plan Governance Board released its report to the state legislature on Nov. 23. The report outlines a plan to create a public corporation that would rely on corporate and personal taxes to fund a statewide healthcare system, providing care to nearly everyone in the state, with no premiums, copays, or other deductibles. The legislature could vote on the plan as early as next year or refer the proposal to voters as a ballot measure in 2028.
Critics are focused on the total cost of the proposal. Oregon Senate Republican Leader Bruce Starr said in a news release that the plan would increase the entire state budget by 43%, with “unfathomable” new taxes coming out of the pockets of Oregonians.
“Handing control of hospitals, doctors, and insurance to the same bureaucracy that has failed at basic responsibilities, and layering on double digit payroll and income taxes, is irresponsible and fiscally unsound,” he said.

84b0800257b9.text:
Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn’t one plan. It’s more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there’s no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn’t cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
“People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs,” said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The Hassle Saves Money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It’s a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can’t find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn’t tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.
Some beneficiaries who didn’t have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt to spread out over the course of the year.
Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don’t shop around could be leaving money on the table.
“It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027,” she said.
Some Plans No Longer Offered
An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they’ll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it’s important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.
“There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide,” Lipschutz said.
So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?
And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.
“Look at that dollar value specifically,” she said.
For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won’t come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life.
When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don’t pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.
If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions.
Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven’t been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March.
For Shopping Help, Think ‘SHIP’

It’s the Paperwork, Not the Work, Causing Enrollees To Lose Medicaid in Nebraska
The state’s early rollout of federal work requirements offers a potential preview of the challenges ahead in the rest of the country.
When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Donald Trump’s sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.
Many also watched the Cornhusker State’s experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.
On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready.
They’ll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don’t meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don’t comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren’t working.
Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory.
“The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans’ chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans,” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement.
Democrats’ massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they’ll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they’re fully enforced.
The Basics
Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states, along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show, so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states.
But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034.
The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called “medically frail.”
It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska.
On May 1, Nebraska became the first state to implement the work requirements. After it began dropping people from coverage in August, 7% of Nebraska Medicaid enrollees who were subject to the requirements when renewing their coverage, or 533 adults, were disenrolled because of the new rules, according to the latest state data.
Nebraska’s Medicaid agency was able to verify that 8 in 10 enrollees met the new rules using various state and federal databases. Those people didn’t have to deal with requests for more information, interim state Medicaid director Jeremy Brunssen told KFF Health News.
About 14% of new Medicaid applicants subject to the new rules, or 557 people, had been denied because of the work requirements since they were implemented.
But the state data also shows some troubling issues.
For example, 92% of cases in which existing enrollees lost coverage were due to procedural or paperwork issues rather than state determinations that they did not meet the new work rules.
Brunssen attributes that high percentage to the state having to verify the numerous ways people can meet the new requirements or exemptions. “It’s not as simple as typical eligibility enrollment that you can meet via income and household size,” he said.
Many enrollees lost coverage because they did not respond to the state’s outreach. Those enrollees may have deemed themselves ineligible or were unsure how to respond, Brunssen said.
The rate of procedural denials is much higher than in prior years, according to data analyzed by KFF. Critics fear it means people who may still qualify are losing coverage.
“This is definitely a red-flag warning,” said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska, a trade group representing federally funded community health centers. “The high proportion of procedural denials is troubling.”
Navigating the New Requirements
Cheri Stollar, 48, of Lincoln, Nebraska, received her Medicaid renewal notice in the mail in early November and was confused about which documents to submit to the state to prove she works as a mental health therapist. She also didn’t understand why she had less than a week to respond. She said she tried to call the state Medicaid agency but could not get through. Her renewal has since been completed.
“I want to make sure I send in everything they need,” said Stollar, who lives in a three-bedroom mobile home with three of her four children. She has been on Medicaid for two years and credits the coverage for enabling her to afford medications for depression, sleep, and an ulcer.
She said the new law will make it harder for people like her to get and stay covered, which will make it harder to stay healthy — and get and keep a job.
Behnke said enrollees calling the state Medicaid agency for help have been put on hold for up to two hours. The assistance line operates only on weekdays, during daytime hours, making it difficult for people who work to call. State Medicaid officials say they are working to add more staff to reduce wait times.

Squeezing blood from a stone.
That’s how Seth Berry describes rising electricity prices in Maine. As executive director of Our Power, a coalition focused on clean energy and utility regulation, Berry talks with people all over the state who are no longer able to afford their power bills.
Combined with recent price increases for heating fuel and gasoline, he said electricity bills could create “a world of hurt” for many Maine households this winter. “People are really at their wits’ end, and I expect to see a whole lot of folks cold this winter, desperately cold in their homes,” Berry said.
Maine has one of the highest energy burdens in the country, due in part to the cost of downed power lines and other repairs after severe storms. The state’s biggest power company is currently requesting another rate increase, and Maine is now reckoning with the balance between needed grid repairs and affordable power bills.
Maine’s Energy Burden
Electricity prices in Maine increased 64 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared to an average 38 percent increase nationwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Only Washington, D.C., and California had larger increases.
The state also has one of the highest average household energy burdens in the nation. A 2024 report to Maine’s Electric Ratepayer Advisory Council found that low-income households spend about 8 percent of their income on electricity and an additional 6 percent on other sources like propane and heating oil. Anything above 6 percent is considered a high energy burden by the U.S. Department of Energy.
Maine’s rural, heavily forested character means utility companies require more miles of power lines to reach their most remote customers, and these lines are more likely to be hit by tree branches, the most common cause of outages.
Climate change has fueled more intense storm seasons in recent years. Maine had the highest number of power outages per customer in the U.S. in 2023 and 2024, federal data shows. The state also had the highest average minutes of power outage in 2023 and the second-highest in 2024.
Central Maine Power, the largest electricity provider in the state, reported more than $600 million in storm recovery costs between 2021 and 2025, a span that included the three most expensive storm years in the company’s history.
“Storm costs have become one of the largest and fastest-growing items on customers’ bills,” said Rebecca Schultz, the senior advocate for climate and clean energy at the Natural Resources Council of Maine.
Advocates like Berry and Schultz say that the way CMP is reimbursed for its storm recovery costs incentivizes the company to overspend, leaving customers to shoulder an even greater burden.
“It’s broken, people understand that it’s broken,” Berry said.
CMP did not respond to interview requests. The company noted in comments to the state Public Utilities Commission in September that the commission’s review of its storm costs from 2023 to 2025 showed “no findings of imprudence.”
The Maine Legislature in March directed the PUC, which regulates utilities in the state, to conduct a review of energy pricing and metrics for affordability. Managing storm costs will be essential to the affordability discussion.
Accounting for Storms
Power companies don’t treat storm costs like regular expenses because severe weather can be so unpredictable and costly.
CMP customers currently pay $14.1 million per year in storm recovery as part of their base rates, which goes toward a reserve account. Each storm event is classified into tiers based on how much CMP spends on the recovery.
Depending on the tier, CMP is responsible for paying up to a certain threshold of each storm’s recovery costs out of its reserves. Beyond that threshold, costs are split equally between the company and its customers—up to a point.
CMP’s share when costs exceed its storm reserve is capped at $3 million per year. The rest is charged directly to customers. The largest events, like an April 2024 storm where CMP spent more than $100 million, are billed to customers over two years, plus additional carrying costs.
CMP customers have paid for $57.8 million just in carrying costs over the last five years, according to testimony by Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate to the PUC.
Since CMP’s financial liability is capped, “it deprives the company of an incentive to control costs,” Schultz said.
Schultz said the company can contract more out-of-state line crews, which require higher hourly rates and additional housing and travel expenses, than it may actually need for storm response because there’s no reward for efficient planning.
In the past five years, CMP has hired external crews for 18 storms per year, averaging about 93 crews each time. While contractor crews are essential when major storms surpass the company’s regular capacity, Schultz said CMP’s approach creates “a huge amount of overpreparedness.”
Heather Sanborn, the state’s public advocate, said CMP’s storm response is “carefully calibrated” to be profitable, not cost-efficient or faster at restoring power.
Even in 2025, a year with less severe weather, CMP racked up $43 million in recovery costs, more than three times the base recovery costs that customers pay, according to its filings with the PUC.
“All of these costs get rolled up into customers’ bills whether the storm turns out to be a big one and whether there’s work to do or not,” Berry said.
An Alternate Method
The other major electricity provider in Maine, Versant Power, has a different storm cost structure, in which customers’ base rates include the five-year average of recovery costs.
Exceptionally severe storm recovery is reviewed and approved by the PUC separately from that budget, since Versant couldn’t financially support those expenses in a single year. Recent testing at Joint Base Andrews found a thick layer of jet fuel beneath the airfield, eight months after a spill was detected near Piscataway Creek. But the Air Force and Maryland environmental regulators remain at odds over basic facts of the spill, such as how much fuel was leaked and whether the base skipped its reporting obligations, while the leak’s source has yet to be found.
At the same time, they are locked in a separate dispute over a golf course renovation, which the base says is beyond the reach of the state’s regulatory authority due to an exemption from President Donald Trump.
Between Nov. 9 and 13, the Air Force conducted pressure testing and drilled several soil borings along the section of pipeline where the leak was suspected. Maryland inspectors were also on site watching. One boring, along a pipe known as Lateral Row 7, found a layer of fuel 3.32-feet-thick, the Air Force said .
In separate statements, both sides said the finding significantly narrowed the search. But neither can yet determine where exactly the pipe broke. The Air Force said that will require digging the line up or inspecting it directly.
Its next step is to pump the fuel out of the ground and do more drilling to map how far it has spread. That work will begin once contracts are in place, the base said, without giving a start date.
According to the Maryland Department of the Environment’s Nov. 18 report, the agency representatives visited the base to oversee the leak testing of the west-side hydrant loop between Nov. 9 and 13. No leaks were found during the testing, which excluded Lateral Row 7—already isolated from the system—and the above-ground piping inside the pump house. The testing was supposed to be completed by Nov. 12 per the deadlines conveyed by the MDE. The base said both sides agreed to adjust the original date to Nov. 13 due to contracting delays and a federal holiday.
The latest testing came after MDE Secretary Serena McIlwain pressed the base in an Oct. 28 letter to identify the source of the fuel leaks and pinpoint the point of failure, warning that “the pace of that progress has not matched the urgency of the situation.”
McIlwain’s letter also set deadlines for the base to finish its investigations and complete actions between Nov. 12 and Dec. 27. It included correcting JBA’s fuel inventory records and reporting any losses to the state, completing overdue corrosion testing and repairs, and submitting a schedule for repairing or abandoning Lateral Row 7. It also required the base to evaluate whether the storm drain systems were carrying fuel to Piscataway Creek.
“If these deadlines are not met, I will consult with our Office of the Attorney General to determine appropriate next steps to ensure compliance,” McIlwain warned.
In a Nov. 9 response, JBA Commander Col. Karl Seekamp only acknowledged the March fuel spill, contradicting McIlwain’s letter describing “major jet fuel releases” that occurred in December and in March.
“JBA’s operational and environmental records do not indicate or support an environmental release in December 2025,” a JBA spokesperson said in emailed comments. The base said its routine testing on Dec. 11, 2025, found a mechanical leak inside a valve at the pump station for its west-side fueling system, and that all of the fuel stayed within “closed, impermeable piping infrastructure,” with no discharge to the environment.
According to MDE’s timeline, the base’s fuel system failed a precision tightness test on Dec. 11, 2025, and records showed inventory losses in January and February. The department was not notified until fuel odors and a sheen were seen near the Piscataway Creek’s headwaters on March 23. On April 8, the base told MDE that 22,000 gallons of fuel had been released into the environment, out of a total system loss of about 32,000 gallons.
Nine members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen, wrote to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink in May, requesting an accounting of how much fuel had entered the creek and how much remained underground.
After the Air Force arranged a staff-level briefing for Van Hollen in late September, his office requested more information, but has yet to receive a response, a spokesperson said in a statement last week.
In its emailed comments, JBA said it has provided two full years of raw fuel inventory records directly to MDE, and the Defense Logistics Agency is conducting an independent audit of contractor inventory to reconcile accounting figures.
Meanwhile, water testing from Piscataway Creek just outside the base still shows petroleum compounds washing into the waterways. In the most recent results by MDE, an Oct. 21 sample detected diesel-range hydrocarbons, which include jet fuel, at 84 parts per billion, well above MDE’s surface-water action level of 47ppb. Every off-base sample listed since testing began in April has exceeded the agency’s action level.
Late-September samples detected a spike across several fuel compounds.
“We can not verify whether release from the fueling infrastructure have stopped. The most recent sampling results, available on our website, continue to show fuel constituents at the Piscataway Creek off-base location,” MDE spokesman Jay Apperson said in a written response.
As the state and federal agencies clash over fuel spill contamination, another regulatory fight between them has surfaced over renovation of the golf course on Joint Base Andrews.
An MDE report dated Aug. 28 and reviewed by Inside Climate News shows an agency inspector visited the base to investigate a complaint that the golf course renovation might be impacting a nearby stormwater basin built for a separate project.
“Access to the site was not permitted during the complaint investigation; however, I was able to observe the potential impacts,” wrote the inspector, who recorded his observations from the roadside.

Clipping off chickens’ sensitive beaks without anesthesia. Cramming sows in crates so small they can’t turn around. Castrating or dehorning livestock without painkillers. Slamming piglets on the ground to kill them—a practice known in the industry as “thumping.”
These are all considered standard, common or accepted practice in U.S. animal agriculture and are exempt from state animal cruelty laws. Even in a country that overwhelmingly says it wants animals treated well—not just the 150 million or so kept as pets, but the 10 billion raised for food—this is the status quo.
The vast majority of the animals that are consumed or generate animal products in the United States are raised in intensive confinement, out of public view. Animal cruelty laws largely don’t apply to them mostly because of the immense power of the American farm lobby, which has convinced lawmakers that the industry itself can decide what is standard practice and therefore legal.
But a new paper argues that these exemptions for food-producing animals—which have been widely accepted as the norm for decades, even by animal advocacy groups—aren’t legally ironclad after all.
“The narrative has gone that these exemptions put farmed animals beyond the law—even if we wanted to, we could not prosecute for cruelty that’s happening on the farms,” said Delcianna Winders, a law professor and director of the Animal Law and Policy Institute at the Vermont Law and Graduate School. “What I’ve done is challenged that and said: What does the law actually say?”
In Winders’ new paper, which she discussed on a Harvard University panel Thursday and will be published next April in Ecology Law Quarterly, she found that, in fact, the state laws covering animal cruelty on farms aren’t as pervasive or sweeping as commonly believed. Winders examines the laws, state by state, interpreting the specifics of the exemptions.
“Not one of them—not a single one—says farm animals are not covered by the law,” Winders said.
This argument, in theory, could open up legal avenues for animal advocacy or other groups to pursue factory farm operators for industry-standard practices that are arguably or obviously cruel. Winders points out that these practices have allowed American factory farms to proliferate on a massive scale—causing water pollution, air pollution and more emissions of methane, the especially potent greenhouse gas, than major developed economies, including Spain.
“If we were not engaging in these practices that Americans deem unacceptable—we were not crowding animals so tightly, mutilating them—we would not be able to produce animals on the scale that we are,” Winders said. “If you were going to have animals in conditions that are considered acceptable, it would be a different system, and it would have to be smaller.”
That’s because humane care undercuts profits. Many of the common practices in factory farm settings, such as de-horning or de-beaking, are performed to address the aggression that animals show when tightly confined and stressed. But giving animals space makes feeding and medicating inefficient and costly, while also limiting the economies of scale that has enabled the industry to get so big.
Most people would be surprised, Winders says, to learn that no federal regulation or law covers the treatment of food-producing animals on the industrial farms where they spend the majority of their lives. States have enacted animal laws that criminalize unjustified or unnecessary cruelty to animals, but they were crafted more than a century ago before factory-scale farming became the norm. Starting in the late 1980s and 1990s, states began crafting laws that exempted on-farm practices from criminal prosecution. Today, 38 states have some form of these exemptions.

But even in the 12 that don’t, criminal prosecutions for on-farm cruelty happen rarely. That, Winders said, is because there are no regulations that require oversight under federal animal cruelty laws in factory farms, which means the only way to know what’s actually happening is with a search warrant based on probable cause, and to do that the law requires evidence. Even after clearing those obstacles, prosecutions are difficult, largely because of vagueness in the law that tends to get interpreted in a defendant’s favor.
There is, she says, a more fundamental problem. “The fact that we’re just using criminal law to regulate a massive industry—that’s not generally how you regulate industries. Normally, you have a regulatory regime with licenses or permits and inspections. None of that is happening, and so the result is cruelty only ever comes to light if there’s an undercover investigation.”
These are exceptionally rare.
In 1996, legal scholar and lawyer David Wolfson published a seminal law review article and later a book based on that article, explaining how states had carved out exemptions for livestock in state animal cruelty laws.
Wolfson, who was Winder’s co-panelist at Harvard Thursday, wrote that the agriculture industry lobbied state legislatures to craft animal cruelty laws so it couldn’t be prosecuted for any farming practice that the industry deems acceptable, regardless of how painful or cruel it may be.
In a subsequent book that Wolfson co-authored with animal law expert Mariann Sullivan, they wrote: “As a result, in most of the United States, prosecutors, judges, and juries no longer have the power to determine whether or not farmed animals are treated in an acceptable manner. The industry alone defines the criminality of its own conduct.”
At least one animal welfare legal group has challenged these exemptions, arguing that they’re unconstitutional because only legislatures can make laws.

A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.
The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.
They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.
Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.
The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.
His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.
Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.
In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.
In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.
He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.
The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.
Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.
Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.
It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.
However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".
The two individuals responsible were each issued with a Â£600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.
Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.
The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.
The council said it had also recently issued another Â£600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.
They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.
According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.
Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.
"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.
"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."
