Pictures will be released later of damage to an asteroid that was deliberately hit with a spacecraft four years ago as part of a test of Earth's defences.
In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it slightly off course.
The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Now, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.
The asteroid poses no threat. Instead, this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock were heading for our planet.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.
The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m wide.
The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km/h (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out upon impact.
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists answer many more questions.
"Dart exploded in the asteroid and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.
"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."
The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos and will look at Didymos too.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments and has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.
The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.
"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted and none are heading to Earth.
"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.
"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."
Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.
A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.
There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including one called Apophis, which is about 450m long.
Apophis was discovered in 2004 and was initially thought to have the potential to hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.
But now scientists understand its orbit better and say it will not hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km above our surface.
This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.
Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

e6a1d6f65a88.text:
- Published
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.
Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.
Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

43221454ebb8.text:
Moment Chinese space mission lifts off with first Pakistan astronaut aboard
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday to bring three astronauts to its Tiangong space station.
It was a landmark moment as astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first foreign national to board the Tiangong space station.
The mission is expected to last for several days before he returns to Earth.

a27486344dcf.text:
- Published
The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.
At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.
There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.
On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.
Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.
He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".
"Those days are done, gone," Wale said.
Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.
"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."
"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."
On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.
"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.
The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.
It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.
Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.
"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.
William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".
Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.
Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.
The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.
Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (Â£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.
Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

d55f2bd937d7.text:
- Published
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.
Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.
On Wednesday evening, the Army said that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.
President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".
"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.
Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.
"Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete," the Army added.
Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin also said on social media that in the hours after the detonation "all EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead".
The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.
He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.
"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.
Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.
The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.
"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.
"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."
Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.
"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.
Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said on X that his state was "seeing little to no impact" from the blast. In a press release, he said he was directing state agencies to remain on standby for any "unanticipated impact".
The Iowa site is only 10 miles (16 km) from the Illinois border.
But there is also caution from some.
Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".
Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".
Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.
In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.
It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.
The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.
But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.
Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

bc5fdc9d3370.text:
What UK season changes mean for you
In collaboration with Met Office

d192dc670f52.text:
- Published
The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.
Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost â when the air temperature falls to 0C or below â was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.
In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.
The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.
"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.
"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.
"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."
The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.
Where have winters changed most?
Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.
Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.
On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.
Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.
Where are summers getting hotter?
Summer days reaching 25C have become more common across the UK.
Some of the biggest increases have been in southern England, where the average number of summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled, from just over eight to more than 16.
In Essex and Suffolk, they have risen by almost 13 days in both counties.
The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.
Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.
The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.
Summer 2026 was the hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data.
There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.
What's the impact on food?
"Humans, animals and crops are encountering extremes of temperature that we've not seen before and this is a physiological challenge to all three," says Thomas Crocker, science manager with the Met Office's climate security team.
This has led to water challenges, he says, with wet winters causing problems with planting, pests and diseases.
Dry summers have meant there has not been enough water to grow crops.
"The impact on horticulture is seismic, it's affected all crops," says John Walgate, CEO of British Growers, which represents most British horticultural organisations growing vegetable and fruit.
Walgate says this year's weather has been particularly tough for brassicas like cauliflowers, cabbages and broccoli, with yields down by about 50%.
Irrigated crops such as onions, potatoes and carrots also suffered from a lack of water due to low rainfall and hot temperatures.
It's not all been bad though. Walgate says soft fruit such as strawberries have had a "good year".
Tim Young and his family have been farming in Norfolk since the 1960s.
But his arable crops - onions, wheat and sugar beet - have been struggling because of the hotter, drier summers and fewer cold days in winter which kill bugs.
With some crop yields decreasing, Young has been looking at ways to diversify the farm's income and planted a vineyard three years ago.
Last year he harvested double the expected amount of grapes.
"With climate change, the frontier is moving further north of where we can grow grapes," he says.
Despite annual variations in weather, he is confident it can be profitable.
What's the impact on wildlife?
Changing weather patterns are shifting where species live and when they migrate, breed and feed, says Zoe Quiroz Cullen, head of climate and international policy at The Wildlife Trusts charity.
Warmer winters mean bats are waking from hibernation when there are too few insects to feed, she says, while amphibians emerging and spawning earlier can be caught out by cold snaps.
Meanwhile, warmer springs mean oak trees are coming into leaf earlier than usual, and caterpillars are hatching earlier.
The UK's bird population has fallen in recent decades, largely because of habitat loss and climate change, external.
Starlings and swifts have declined significantly, although milder winters and conservation work have helped some species thrive.
Kevin Anderson, visitor experience officer at Somerset Wildlife Trust, has worked at Avalon Marshes for 15 years and has seen its bird life change first-hand.
Thirty to 40 years ago, he says, it would have been rare to see an egret north of the Mediterranean.
Now the reserve is home to a growing population of great white egrets taking advantage of warmer winters which allow them to fish all year round.
The birds first bred in Somerset in 2012, with just two nests. Last year, about 73 chicks were born in Avalon Marshes with the population thought to be around 200 now.
What could the future look like?
Climate change - mainly the result of the burning of fossil fuels - is raising average temperatures in the UK.
The current global warming level is 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, climate scientists estimate.
The Met Office says changes to the UK's seasons are expected to continue as temperatures rise.
If global warming reaches 2C above pre-industrial levels, the UK could experience an average of about 24 winter air frost days, compared with 38 during the period from 1961 to 1990.
Summers could also become hotter.

1266bb9606f6.text:
- Published
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.
Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisationâone that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

d3f9ecd871f2.text:
Authorities are investigating why a small plane carrying six members of a Florida family crashed off the Mississippi coast on Tuesday. They were returning home from a fishing trip, relatives say.
The plane's pilot was Brent Stokes, the 50-year-old president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. Stokes' company's website described him as an "avid fisherman and life time boater."
The other victims were Stokes' 16-year-old son, Hunter Stokes; Stokes' sister, Arlyn Knox, 43; her husband, Michael Knox, 43; and their two sons, 12-year-old Charles Holden Knox and 10-year-old Truett Knox.
Arlyn and Michael Knox ran Knox Technologies, a Fort Myers-based IT company they founded in 2012, according to the company's website.
The Knox and Stokes families confirmed their deaths in an emailed statement provided to The Associated Press.
"They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family," the statement said. "In the middle of our grief, we are holding on to that, and to how much love they gave us and how much love surrounds us now. We will carry them with us always."
Lynd said that autopsies are being performed on Brent Stokes and Michael Knox, who was also a licensed pilot.
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported at about 3:45 p.m. that it had lost contact with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. The closest National Weather Service station, in Pascagoula, shows there were light winds, no precipitation and clouds blanketing the sky in the area at the time of the crash.
The pilot doesn't appear to have reported any problems when the plane took off from an airport in New Orleans or made a distress call during the flight, according to air traffic recordings publicly available on the website LiveATC.net.
Shortly before losing contact with the plane, an air traffic controller at Gulfport–Biloxi International Airport advised the pilot of precipitation and adverse weather in the area.
Todd Curtis, an aviation expert and former Boeing safety engineer, said that nothing appeared out of the ordinary based on the publicly available audio recordings. But he noted that precipitation in below-freezing temperatures can cause dangerous icing, potentially leading to inaccurate instrument readings or loss of lift. It is unclear whether the plane had a de-icing system.
The plane had been flying at around 9,000 feet (2,743 meters), above the bottom of the cloud layers, when it began descending rapidly in a right-hand turn. That's according to FlightAware tracking data analyzed by Steven Arroyo, a retired airline captain with 50 years of flying experience.
"It's highly, highly irregular," Arroyo said. "I think it's safe to say this aircraft had some serious problems."
Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, according to Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Divers found their bodies in the fuselage after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to FlightAware.
Both Stokes and Knox had received private pilot certificates in 2023, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The Page Field airport in Fort Myers said in a statement that its community is "shocked and devastated."
"We have lost great friends and outstanding aviators," the airport added.
Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard coordinator for search and rescue in the Mobile area, called the situation heartbreaking.
"While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families," he said in a statement.
The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash.
Earlier this month, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in South Florida, killing all nine people on board. People inside their cars captured the crash on video.
Associated Press reporter Hallie Golden in Seattle, Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire and Philip Marcelo in New York City contributed to this report.

e3f7fcad0ff4.text:
- Published
Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.
Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.
The last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.
A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.
The potent nor'easter storm is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.
Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.
"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.
Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.
Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.
"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."
Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".
Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.
During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.
The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade was due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern US as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow, BBC Weather reports.
The governor of the neighbouring state of New Jersey on Wednesday declared a state of emergency across the state's 21 counties, beginning at 18:00 local time (23:00 GMT).
Governor Mikie Sherrill's office said the powerful coastal storm is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall, and severe tidal flooding through Friday, with coastal and bayside communities facing the greatest risk. Sherrill urged residents to stay off the roads as much as possible once the storm arrives.
Originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade, the celebration, which also features live performers, debuted in 1924 as a way to boost holiday sales. It was founded by Macy's employees and their families.
From 1942 to 1944 New York went without the parade as the US directed materials like rubber and helium toward the country's war effort.
The 2.5mi (4km) procession route begins at Macy's Herald Square flagship store and concludes in Manhattan's Upper West Side, with performers and spectators lining the streets to greet Santa Claus and ring in the holiday season.
Country artist Megan Moroney and Grammy nominee Teddy Swims were slated to perform at the flagship store, but it is unclear whether they, along with the dozens of celebrities and float performers on the roster, would be returning on Saturday.

b071a8c91c54.text:
WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children visited Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday, serving a Thanksgiving meal to troops and joining them for lunch in what Vance called an "amazing opportunity" to have "unfiltered, off-the-record" conversations with service members.
Watch Vance's remarks in the video player above.
The family is spending the holiday in the state, and the base in southwest Ohio is about 60 miles (97 kilometers) from their home in Cincinnati and close to where Vance was born. In tow for the trip: Ewan, 9; Vivek, 6; Mirabel, 4; and four-month-old Alec.
Along a cafeteria-style food line, Vance asked civilians and uniformed active-duty service members for their home state and whether they wanted roast turkey, prime rib or baked ham. The Republican vice president then passed plates along to his son Ewan, who spooned out sides including sweet potatoes, green beans, cornbread, corn calico and mashed potatoes.
"Ewan, this is an Ohioan, you want to ask?" Vance asked his son, whom he called a "dedicated Ohio sports fan." Ewan then quizzed the man about his status as an Ohio State fan.
"Better a Bulldogs fan than the Buckeyes this year," the vice president told one man who said he was from Georgia, whose football team has been highly ranked all season.
Usha Vance, with baby Alec in her arms and Mirabel nearby, chatted with attendees as they waited in line.
Later, the couple sat with troops at a long table to eat lunch, where Vance was overheard on a hot mic telling a story related to the 2011 escape of dozens of lions, tigers, bears and mountain lions from a private animal farm in the state after the owner opened the cages and took his own life.
Vance told a tale about a friend who had worked for former Ohio Gov. John Kasich and, after taking Ambien to help fall asleep, woke up to a call from celebrity zookeeper Jack Hanna, who said, "'We have (expletive) bears running wild in Zanesville, Ohio,'" according to Vance's retelling. Groggy from the sleeping aid, the man went back to sleep, Vance said.
Ohio lawmakers hope this base becomes home to Space Academy
The visit comes just days after Ohio's congressional delegation, led by Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, a friend and former Senate colleague of Vance, made a push for the Trump administration to locate the U.S. Space Academy close to the technologically advanced Wright-Patterson complex.
"What West Point is to the Army and Annapolis is to the Navy, Wright Field should be to the United States Space Force," Moreno wrote in a letter co-signed by GOP Sen. Jon Husted and all 15 of Ohio's U.S. representatives.
Asked after lunch about locating the academy in the state, Vance told reporters there were "a lot of good options" in other places as well, mentioning Florida and Texas and adding that his visit to Wright-Patterson "has had nothing to do with those plans."
Spending time with family in Ohio for the next few days, Vance said they would do "what most Americans are going to do, which is hang out with people, eat a lot and hopefully not drink too much."
Associated Press writers Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report.

2fd7466eccb9.text:
The Trump administration announced plans for a new round of tariffs on China, the European Union and 12 other major trading partners. China would face the highest rate with a new 20% tariff on most products. To discuss how this will impact Americans and the economy, Lisa Desjardins spoke with Gavin Bade of The Wall Street Journal.
How Trump's newest tariffs could impact Americans and the economy
Read the Full Transcript
Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.
Lisa Desjardins:
Now our other major story tonight.
The Trump administration announced plans for a new round of tariffs on China, the European Union, and 12 other major trading partners. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argues, this is to protect manufacturing in the U.S.
Jamieson Greer, U.S. Trade Representative:
We have a very consumption-driven economy, and we should be producing more of that here in the United States, but it makes it really hard when these other countries are producing or creating capacity that are not really justified by the economics of the situation.
And so we're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them. And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries. We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it.
Lisa Desjardins:
China would face the highest rate with a new 20 percent tariff on most products. That would top existing levels, setting up a potential 40 percent tariff if negotiations fall apart. Other countries would face 10 to 20 percent in additional tariffs. Those could go into effect as soon as January.

Airborne lead, when breathed in, can harm the brain, nervous system, and other organs, especially in young children, leading to developmental damage.

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.
"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.
They bought a controlling interest in ChÃ¢teau Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.
In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.
The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.
"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.
Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".
The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.
It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.
Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.
Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.
Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.
Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.
They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.
It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.
At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.
They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.
The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston.
It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.
Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.
In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.
The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.
Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.
Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections said she has ended an agreement under which the state shared its voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for possible removal.
No voters were removed as a result of the agreement signed last December, and the Justice Department since then had not identified "any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska's voter registration records," the office of outgoing Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said.
Dahlstrom said she notified the Justice Department that Alaska was terminating the agreement, effective Monday. That's also when Alaska officials announced that the results of the Nov. 3 general election, in which Democrats flipped a U.S. Senate seat and the governor's office, had been certified.
The Alaska Division of Elections directed the department to destroy the confidential voter information the state provided, Dahlstrom's office said in a statement released late Monday. A Justice Department spokesperson on Tuesday said the agency would send a formal response to the state.
The federal government's demand for detailed state voter information was part of a broader effort throughout the midterm election cycle to promote the idea that scores of noncitizens were on state voter rolls and potentially casting ballots illegally. In fact, years of research, state investigations and the Justice Department's own record of arrests showed the issue to be extremely rare.
The Justice Department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for not complying with its demands to provide detailed voter registration data or other election-related records, with 28 of those lawsuits dismissed by courts, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. The department entered a settlement agreement with Oklahoma and dismissed its case with that state, the group said.
Alaska was one of at least 16 states to provide voter lists that included information such as driver's license and partial Social Security numbers, dates of birth and addresses. Alaska and Texas also signed data-sharing agreements with the Justice Department, in which it outlined plans for its own analysis of voter files, its plans to flag voter list issues and directions for removing voters deemed ineligible.
Voting and civil rights groups sued Alaska elections officials earlier this year, alleging that sharing the state's full voter registration list violated the Alaska Constitution and that terms of the agreement violated due process rights. That case is still pending.
ACLU Voting Rights Project, one of the organizations involved in representing the groups, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Dahlstrom said the Division of Elections "entered the agreement in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners as permitted under Alaska law. The circumstances have now changed, the election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose."
She said Alaska "has strong list-maintenance procedures and will continue to protect both the accuracy of its voter rolls and the rights of eligible Alaska voters." Her office said terminating the agreement "does not constitute an acknowledgment of wrongdoing by the Division of Elections."
Alaska state Sen. Bill Wielechowski, a Democrat and critic of the state's decision to hand over voter information, said Tuesday he believed the motivation for ending the agreement was to try to "make the lawsuit go away" before the administration of Alaska's new governor, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, "could settle or produce discovery."
He said he wants Kreiss-Tomkins' administration to look into the circumstances surrounding the decision. Wielechowski also questioned the impact of the demand to delete the records.
Kreiss-Tomkins and his lieutenant governor, independent Zac Johnson, take office Dec. 7.

ATLANTA (AP) — A judge on Tuesday ordered Georgia's Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of ballots and other election records seized by the FBI earlier this year to the State Election Board, which had been trying for more than two years to obtain certain records from the 2020 election in the state's most populous county.
Fulton County Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe ordered that the records be delivered to the state board by 5 p.m. Wednesday. She also put in place a protective order that limits who can see the unredacted records.
A Fulton County spokesperson declined to comment on a pending legal matter. The State Election Board did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
The FBI served a search warrant at the Fulton County elections hub on Jan. 28 seeking records related to the 2020 election, leaving with hundreds of boxes containing ballots and other records. The county unsuccessfully sought to have a judge order the return of the records, but the federal government did provide the county with what it said was a digital copy of the records that were taken.
The overwhelmingly Democratic county, which includes most of the city of Atlanta, has been a target of President Donald Trump and his allies since he narrowly lost the presidential election in Georgia to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. Trump has consistently insisted without evidence that widespread voter fraud in the county cost him victory in the state. Multiple courts and state and federal officials have found no evidence of fraud that would have altered the outcome.
A statement from an FBI agent supporting the search warrant used to take the records said the agency was examining possible "deficiencies or defects" in Fulton County's 2020 vote count. More than six years after that election and 10 months after the records seizure, no charges have been filed.
The FBI in July instructed field offices across the country to dedicate more than 200 staffers to its investigation of the 2020 election in Fulton County, describing it as a "priority investigation," and The New York Times reported that the FBI and federal prosecutors last week interviewed the man who served as the county's election director in 2020.
A Trump-aligned majority on the State Election Board has repeatedly sought to reopen a case alleging wrongdoing by Fulton County during the 2020 election. The board in November 2024 served subpoenas on the county seeking records related to the 2020 election. County election officials asked a judge to quash the subpoenas.
Fulton County Superior Court Judge Robert McBurney in December 2025 declined to quash the subpoenas, finding that the State Election Board's inquiries "fell squarely within the SEB's authority." He ruled that the state board would have to bear the costs of producing the records it was seeking and a hearing on that matter was pending when the FBI seized the county's records. As a result, McBurney put the case on hold.
Ellerbe, who took over the case this year, held a hearing on the matter in October before issuing her order Tuesday. Her protective order says the State Election Board can use the records for its investigations but says the records cannot be disclosed to anyone other than people identified in the order, which includes the board members and staff, as well as experts they may consult.

MADRID (AP) — Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after what his lawyer described as a temporary departure, with hopes of returning to his family's home in Maryland after President Donald Trump leaves office.
Ábrego García, who has an American wife and child, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and was deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official called an "administrative error." A judge later ordered his return to the U.S., where he fought the Trump administration's efforts to deport him again, this time to Africa.
After receiving officials' permission to leave the U.S., Ábrego García voluntarily departed on Tuesday from Washington Dulles International Airport, accompanied by his wife.
"The government does not decide where my story continues," the 31-year-old said during a virtual news conference Wednesday after he arrived in Spain. "My family and I will decide our future."
Ábrego García's lawyer anticipates a temporary absence
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, called the move "a temporary departure," though he declined to say what his client's immediate plans are, including where he will live.
"Mr. Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen spouse and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
David Leopold, an Ohio immigration attorney and past president of the American Immigration Lawyers Association, said such a return would require government permission and a Department of Homeland Security waiver. He said Ábrego García would need to demonstrate that his continued absence would cause his wife extreme hardship, including financial and psychological harm.
"My guess is he can do it because he has a family he was supporting," Leopold said.
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Ábrego García in El Salvador last year, a visit that put the national spotlight on Ábrego García's predicament, celebrated Ábrego García's decision to leave the U.S. on his own terms.
"They wanted to leave him to rot there, to rot there for the rest of his life," Van Hollen said of the Trump administration and its decision to send Ábrego García to the notorious CECOT mega-prison. The Democrat said he was grateful Ábrego García would be a free man "living in dignity."
Ábrego García migrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
Ábrego García would decide where to settle for the next two years to wait out the remainder of the Trump administration, Sandoval-Moshenberg said. Ábrego García's immigration status in Spain wasn't immediately clear.
A judge cleared the way for his departure
U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who presided over Ábrego García's long-running immigration proceedings in Maryland, ordered the case's dismissal on Wednesday after receiving confirmation that he had left the U.S.
The court also unsealed an order that Xinis signed last Friday to spell out the terms of his "unimpeded" departure. In the order, Xinis said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to go "to any country that is willing to accept him."
The judge, in turn, set Tuesday as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.
The order didn't address why the government had changed its position on him leaving the U.S. to a country of his choice.
Sandoval-Moshenberg, the attorney, declined to elaborate on how the agreement came together for Ábrego García to leave the U.S., citing confidential settlement negotiations with the government.
Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security and the Justice Department didn't immediately respond on Wednesday to messages seeking more information about the resolution of Ábrego García's immigration proceedings and the agreement leading to his departure from the U.S.
Questions remain over his criminal case
It was unclear how Ábrego García's departure would affect prosecutors' efforts to revive a criminal case against him in Tennessee. After a judge ordered U.S. officials to arrange Ábrego García's return from El Salvador, prosecutors charged him with human smuggling in a case stemming from a 2022 traffic stop. Officials alleged he had been paid to transport people who were in the U.S. illegally.
Ábrego García pleaded not guilty, and his attorneys decried the prosecution as politically motivated. A federal judge dismissed the case in May, calling it an abuse of prosecutorial power and noting the time that had elapsed between the traffic stop and the charges. Prosecutors appealed the ruling, and a three-judge panel of the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals is scheduled to hear the case in February.
Sandoval-Moshenberg said a successful appeal would leave the government with a choice: drop the charges that it fought to reinstate or seek Ábrego García's return to the U.S. to face a trial. "That will be up to them," he said. "I don't think it will happen, but if it does, it will be interesting to see which of those two options they choose."
Federal officials say he won't be allowed back
DHS said Tuesday night that Ábrego García left for Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn't receive any incentives and won't be allowed back into the U.S.

Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.
Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.
Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.
Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.
A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

FORT WORTH, Texas (AP) — Three weeks after midterm elections that devastated the Republican Party, several dozen of its more youthful members gathered at a brewery to sort through the pieces.
The Monday meeting was organized by the Tarrant County Young Republicans, a local organization on the front lines of a national reckoning. Their last leader resigned shortly before the midterms because she couldn't bring herself to vote for some of her party's candidates. Then their county, once a conservative stronghold, flipped blue.
"Everyone has someone to blame, and that finger is never pointed at ourself," said Derrick Wilson, who heads the Texas Young Republican Federation, a coalition that includes the Tarrant County chapter. "So we're going to have to get past that and figure out, what did we do wrong?"
Democrats won the U.S. Senate race and the governor's office in Texas, their first statewide victories in over three decades. There's no consensus about the path forward, but several people at this week's meeting gave similar answers.
Some are bored with "owning the libs" and put off by meme-driven political messaging that they see as flippant in the face of real challenges. Many felt President Donald Trump didn't follow through on his promises. And others gave similar advice to their party leaders: "grow up," "take themselves seriously" and "be humble."
Some Republicans saw no progress on affordability
The event opened with someone introduced by Wilson as a "survivor" of the midterms. State Appeals Court Judge Brian Walker, a Republican who won reelection, gave a withering assessment of how the party had stumbled down the wrong path with Trump-style belligerent politics led by the "loudest" and "craziest" voices.
Robert Coe, a mustachioed 29-year-old in a black cowboy hat, murmured in agreement as Walker spoke.
Coe voted for Trump three times, and now gives the Republican Party an approval of 4 out of 10 after seeing little progress on affordability.
"Me and millions of other Americans are just tired of that, and we're not seeing any viable solution to it," he said. "It's almost as if the people in power don't even want to try and solve it."
Coe, who still voted for Republicans in the midterms and was the one who wanted party leaders to "grow up," has been put off by "the high school level name-calling, the infighting on an almost childish level." Citing Trump's screeds against talk show hosts, Coe said "there is no decency."
Another attendee who nodded through Walker's remarks was Andrew Gochis, a 29-year-old coach and teacher who has worked in politics. He voted for a mix of candidates rather than just Republicans.
He said Republicans had conflated being respectful and being weak. The party has to "do better," he said, at standing on their principles of deportations or opposition to abortion while also treating people such as immigrants or women who get abortions as "a human being that has value."
Leaders say they're in 'listening mode'
Others had a far more extreme view.
"The Republican Party needs to get meaner," said Stephen Nesbitt, a 26-year-old former U.S. Marine. "We need to get stricter, we need to triple down." He listed non-Christians, immigrants and communists as the "enemy."
His view meshes with some who believe the Make America Great Again movement didn't go far enough, but he was an outlier among those interviewed at Monday's meeting.
Wilson, the chair of the state organization, wants the party to "return to its roots" of "fiscal and social conservatism." He and the organization are currently in "listening mode" to be better prepared ahead of 2028, a strategy that he felt was missed before the midterms.
"Young people wanted to buy homes and start families," he said, "then they look on the news and they see Trump say, 'I don't want housing prices to go down, I want them to go up.'"
Trevor Carr, 25, attended the meeting for the first time because he saw the midterm elections as a repudiation of the party's old guard and he wanted to have a role in its future.
Carr didn't vote in the midterms because he doubted Trump was going to fulfill his promises, and he wants to see a party less focused on loyalty to one man and one that clings more closely to an ideologically sound platform.
While Carr said Trump's approach was once helpful for shaking up the system 10 years ago, "it's served its purpose, and it's time to move on to be a serious political movement."

North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.
It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.
The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.
Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.
Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".
It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."
Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

The holidays are all about food, family — and financial pitfalls.
Though the season has barely started, the best time to plan for those upcoming purchases to avoid overspending was a couple of months ago, according to NerdWallet credit card expert Sara Rathner.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
Spending beyond your means during the holidays is common, a recent NerdWallet survey found. About 76% of people who said they would throw down money this holiday season identified at least one reason they might overspend, including fear of missing out or not spending enough time planning.
The good news, according to Rathner, is that the second-best time to make a plan is right now.
"It's OK to spend money on the things you care about that make you happy, and make other people happy," Rathner said. "It's just helpful to plan for it."
NerdWallet found that Americans who plan to spend during the season will devote more than $2,500, on average, to holiday expenses like gifts, travel and parties.
And holiday spenders are likely to rely on credit, whether in the form of credit cards or "buy now, pay later" options.
Credit card balances are up across the country, but that's not surprising, said Aaron Klein, senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution. As the economy grows, the total amount of money on credit cards also rises, he said.
On the other hand, prices have increased faster than wages over the last year, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet, he added.
"Often, running up a credit card balance is the first thing people do when they're trying to make it through until prices go back down or they're able to earn a little more money," Klein said.
Here are some tips for staying financially healthy during the holiday season.
Reconsider how you gift
Americans may find their money doesn't go as far this holiday season, and many may be cutting back. NerdWallet found that among those planning to spend, Americans expect to buy nearly $880 worth of gifts on average. That's down from $1,107 last year, despite inflation likely raising the cost of presents.
Whether Americans plan to spend more or less this year depends on income, found the Conference Board, an economic think tank. Americans with incomes of $200,000 or more plan on spending 14% more on the holidays this year than last, according to the Conference Board, while those with incomes under that overall said they will spend less than last year.
If you're feeling the strain, talk with the people in your gift-giving circle about alternatives to buying everyone one gift.
"I promise you, you're not the only person in your circle feeling this way," Rathner said. "By opening up about it, you might make a friend or family member feel complete relief."
Set a budget for exchanging gifts, pull a name out of a hat instead of buying a gift for everyone or pool your money to buy one big gift instead of multiple small ones.
Parents in particular might choose to limit gifting. A third of parents with children under 18 surveyed by NerdWallet said they would buy gifts for children in the family but not adults, compared with 18% of those without children. And more than a quarter said they'd use secret Santa or a similar game to limit gifts, compared with only 11% of people without children.
Avoid spending more than you can pay off in full
Almost two-thirds of Gen Z Americans who plan to spend money this holiday season will use "buy now, pay later" plans, NerdWallet said. And 22% of Gen Z spenders said they would use "buy now, pay later," but don't expect to make all the payments in full when they're due. Meanwhile, 19% of total holiday spenders planned to pay with a credit card but didn't expect to pay the balance in full when it's due.
Part of the reason Americans' record-high credit card debt isn't a total red flag is that it may actually be balances carried by people Klein calls "transactors." Those are people who put the majority of their regular spending on credit cards, often to take advantage of cash back or reward points, and then pay the balance off monthly. They contrast with "revolvers," who tend to pay in cash or with debit and maintain a continuous balance on credit cards.
If the growth in outstanding balance "is made up of transactors, who are paying off in full, then you really haven't increased debt. You've increased usage," Klein said.
This could be a function of the K-shaped economy, with credit card usage high among all sectors, but being paid off in full by those at the top, while those at the bottom are racking up debt and defaulting more.
Though transitions into delinquency and serious delinquency have remained relatively flat since 2024, they're higher than pre-pandemic levels. And a greater percentage of people with lower incomes are delinquent than people with higher incomes, according to recent research by the New York Federal Reserve.
Many holiday spenders still owe money a year later, Rathner said.
"All of those New Year's resolutions you're going to be setting in a month or so — they're really hard to accomplish if you also are paying hundreds of dollars a month on your credit card bill left over from holiday-related purchases," Rathner said.
"I always say: The best gift you can give to yourself is a holiday season where you don't overdo it," she added.
Change up how you celebrate
Many cities have free holiday activities, Rathner said. In Richmond, where she lives with her family, their local newspaper The Times-Dispatch compiles a "Tacky Light Tour," which includes stops with 40,000 or more lights.
"For the cost of however many miles you drive in your car, you get to have this fun holiday experience with your friends and family," she said.
If you're hosting a holiday dinner this year, throwing it potluck style can help spread the labor and costs.

Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.
The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.
The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.
The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs.
But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.
"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.
Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

NEW YORK (AP) — Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed to Saturday as a storm bearing powerful winds is expected to bear down on New York during the holiday event, organizers announced Wednesday.
The 100th annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, has been moved "out of an abundance of caution" and following consultation with city officials, Macy's said in a statement.
"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the company said.
The postponement came as New York City is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised concerns throughout the week about how the parade's massive, helium-filled balloons would fare while floating in the windswept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers.
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday. The city's emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty tractor-trailers from bridges Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether the event's expansive lineup of performers would also shift to the new date.
The parade's iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy's representatives had repeatedly put off interviews with media on-site, raising additional concerns before the official postponement.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma. Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy's said in a statement.

76cbbc419810.text: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in the event's history, the retailer confirmed Wednesday. Why it matters: Macy's was expected to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables — but an impending nor'easter will keep its iconic giant balloons from flying on the holiday. What they're saying: "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's told NBC on Wednesday. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year," Macy's said. The parade has been pushed back to Saturday. NBC will air last year's parade during the allocated Thanksgiving time slot. What we're watching: It's unclear if any scheduled performers will be unable to participate following the postponement, but thousands are involved in the parade each year. Saturday's forecast currently shows mostly sunny conditions and a high of 55 degrees, according to the National Weather Service . Driving the news: A large storm bringing mostly rain and wind to the East Coast could disrupt travel plans, holiday parades and more this Thanksgiving, per projections from AccuWeather. High winds could also cause widespread sporadic power outages across the region, disrupting holiday meal preparations. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for Manhattan on Wednesday morning, with sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph and gusts of up to 55 mph forecast for Thursday. How it works: Large balloons can't fly when sustained winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts exceed 34 mph, per rules announced by former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani in 1998. The NYPD has ultimate authority over whether balloons should fly. Worth noting: The parade set an all-time viewership record in 2025, with an estimated 34.3 million people watching across NBC and the company's Peacock streaming service. Flashback: Officials have only grounded all the giant character balloons in the parade once before, in 1971, because of the weather. In 1997, strong winds pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, critically injuring a spectator. That incident prompted the overhaul of the city's safety regulations. In 2019, the parade's giant balloons flew close to the ground because of the weather. Balloonfest at MetLife Stadium on November 07, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey.
