The U.S. Army detonated five tons of degraded lead azide explosives in southeast Iowa this morning, following delays and legal challenges over concerns about toxic dust generated by the blast.
Shortly after 9 a.m. local time, a series of explosions ignited the bomb-making material, sending two plumes into the air that were visible for miles. Cars passed along the north end of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown a minute before the detonation, with more traffic passing soon afterward.
After the blast, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin said initial air samples collected downwind of the explosion showed no detectable lead. “It looks like it caved inward perfectly,” he told CNN. At an 11 a.m. briefing, Army officials also said initial air monitoring had detected no airborne lead.
But some scientists cautioned against drawing broad conclusions from the initial results, questioning whether the Army’s monitoring could totally rule out lead exposure from a blast of this scale.
Measuring airborne lead is more complicated than a single reading might suggest, said Bruce Lanphear, an expert on lead exposure and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia. The monitoring methods used, the size of the particles being measured and the height and location of monitoring equipment can all affect the results.
“The failure to detect an increase in airborne lead from preliminary samples does not establish that no lead was released or that no one was exposed,” Lanphear said in an email exchange with Inside Climate News on Wednesday. Lanphear submitted an expert witness statement in support of an emergency lawsuit filed last week on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter.
“We need to know how lead was measured and the detection limits of the sampling methods. We should also await the results of other environmental samples before drawing conclusions.”
After the blast, wind gusts traveled southwest.
The force of the blast could be felt at least four miles away, according to a KWQC-TV reporter observing the detonation from a field north of the ammunition plant. The haze from the plumes dissipated quickly, but officials are tracking air quality into Missouri.
The Army says that extensive mitigation reduced the release of lead.
“I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” said Major General Eric Shirley. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa.”
The EPA’s air monitoring results are being rounded to one decimal place, said Alexander More, a professor of urban public health at the University of Massachusetts Boston and a researcher at Harvard University’s Initiative for the Science of the Human Past. In an email to Inside Climate News, More said the website’s code shows values less than 0.05 micrograms per cubic meter, one third of the federal air quality standard for lead, are rounded down to 0.0.

More added that seven non-zero readings registered in the EPA’s website code as of noon on Wednesday after the blast. There were three non-zero readings before the detonation.
Soil monitoring in the days ahead will reveal how much lead dust settled in the environment, and where. Blood lead levels in children will also be important to monitor.
The EPA and Army will continue monitoring the blast site and surrounding communities.
After delaying the detonation by five days while a court weighed a challenge to the military’s plan, the Army and EPA say they used the extra time to collect more than 1,000 soil, dust, water and air samples and take additional mitigation measures.
In a post early Wednesday morning, the Army wrote that personnel in Middletown implemented measures including “a water wall filled with more than 100,000 gallons of water, earth berms, sand filled blocks, expert dispersion modeling, and temperature-regulating tarps.”
The Army also used a PFAS-free retardant foam to contain the blast. General Shirley attributed the plumes visible for miles following the explosion to the 3,600 gallons of liquid foam they’d applied to the site.
The Army believes these actions limited the spread of lead after the detonation.
Lanphear said detecting little or no lead is a sign that the delay and additional safeguards the Army took ahead of the operation were necessary and successful. “The public outcry prompted additional safeguards, and we should commend the Army, EPA and other agencies for taking steps to better protect surrounding communities,” he said.
Lanphear hopes the situation in Iowa will help draw more attention to other sources of lead exposure for Americans, such as the use of leaded aviation fuel by small aircraft.
Ahead of Wednesday’s detonation, the Army encouraged residents up to five miles southwest of the site to evacuate with support from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, a change from earlier plans.
While Middletown residents learned of the planned explosion at an October town hall, most Iowa residents, including state agencies and Gov. Kim Reynolds, weren’t notified until just five days before the operation was set to take place. The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20.
At the time, the Army advised members of the public in the plume’s projected path to “consider avoiding the affected area” and keep windows and doors closed. It also suggested cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces after the air exposure period ends.

Holiday shopping season is officially here, and the National Retail Federation forecasts that this year's sales could top a record $1 trillion, even as many Americans report feeling the pain of rising prices and inflation.
"Despite the fact that Americans are struggling to make ends meet, they are not willing to give up the holiday season," said Andrea Woroch, a consumer saving and spending expert.
Online holiday sales will hit $275 billion, according to Adobe's holiday sales forecast, which also predicts a record 63% of sales will happen on mobile devices. And a new trend is emerging, says Adobe's lead insight analyst Vivek Pandya: using Cyber Week to stock up on everyday essentials. Personal hygiene product sales are expected to jump 150% this year, Adobe's data shows.
Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News
With the ever-changing landscape of holiday shopping, how do you know you're getting the best deal?
Woroch and Pandya offered these three tips.
1. Black Friday and Cyber Monday are still the best times to get deep discounts, but not for every item on your list
This year, "we won't see as wide a selection of doorbusters like we have in the past," Woroch said.
What are some of the best deals to find on Black Friday? "Products that have plugs, so small personal gadgets, small kitchen appliances, smart home devices, even beauty tools like blow dryers, and then household cleaning products like vacuums," she said.
Deep discounts on electronics and apparel peak during Cyber Week, but this year, so will sales on everyday items.
Consumers will "see these different types of categories being marked down, especially personal care products, cosmetics, and they're really using these moments as an opportunity to stock up for the year ahead."
2. The best way to avoid overspending during cyber week? Make a plan
To stay on track, Woroch says, list the people you need to buy for and specific gift ideas. Then, set a realistic budget that doesn't rely on credit cards or taking cash from essential bills.
This guide means "you're not shopping aimlessly and then leading to impulse purchases or overbuying. So that's gonna be a really important tool as you approach sales events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday."
You can also research current prices and historical pricing data from the last six months before the big shopping days arrive.
"See what things cost before the deal drops. This will just give you better information to make better buying decisions so that you can spot the really good deals when they do become available."
Woroch also has a pretty reliable rule of thumb: If something you've been searching for is 30% off, you should buy it.
"Chances are it's not going to get much cheaper than that."
3. Love it or hate it, AI can help you find the best deal
Pandya expects traffic from AI platforms to retail sites to be up 140% from last year.
This is in part because AI-powered chat and browser services can supercharge your hunt for deals.
Not sure where to start? Woroch suggests entering a product name, along with some prompts like "compare prices across every retailer selling this item, apply any working coupon codes or free shipping offers to get me the lowest possible deal."
You can also ask: "Can you find me a cheaper option for a similar item?"
These strategies helped Woroch save $20 on a gift from her own list this year.
"Imagine you multiply that across all the gifts on your list, that can add up to big savings."

WASHINGTON (AP) — First lady Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families, bringing the total number of kids in these wartime reunifications to 43, the White House announced Wednesday.
It's the latest example of the first lady taking modest yet tangible interventions to address Russia's war in Ukraine, which started nearly five years ago. Her husband, President Donald Trump, had vowed to broker a quick end to the conflict but has said it's been harder than he expected.
"Children in this region of the world, like children everywhere, cannot possibly understand why geography and government have put them into the horrors of war," the first lady said in a statement shared first with The Associated Press.
"As adults, it is our moral imperative to elevate our children above the divisions that power war in order to restore the simple joys of life, immediately," she said.
Melania Trump said the reunification of these nine children with their families took place with the "full cooperation" of Russian and Ukrainian leaders. No additional information about the children was made available.
The first lady has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband's second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
The work began in August 2025, when she had the Republican president hand-deliver a letter that called for peace in Ukraine to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a summit in Alaska.
After a year, she had helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives after they had been separated because of the war, and she has said she has a "direct channel" with the leaders of the warring countries.
Then in October, she helped negotiate a six-day ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Earlier this month, she hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House to mark that milestone.
The local ceasefire in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. During the pause in the war, some 800 people were able to leave the city while food, water and other humanitarian aid were delivered to help those who stayed.

NEW YORK (AP) — One of the stars of this year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade should be very easy to spot. Just look in the sky for a gigantic blue hippo with a goofy smile.
Blue Hippo is one of 100 inflatables included in the 100th parade set to float — weather permitting — through Manhattan on Thursday, lovingly reconstructed by hand from old photos and video because the original balloon disappeared in 1931.
The long-lost hippo — also part of the store's holiday window displays this year — will take its rightful place in the show along with such musical celebrities as Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, JoJo and Jimmy Fallon & The Roots.
This year will include a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer and Holly Robinson Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus. Nine Broadway shows will be featured as part of a 10-minute medley, replacing the traditional sprinkling of full show numbers.
"It's all about celebrating the tradition of the parade," says Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production at Macy's Studios. "It's got so much weight behind it, and we're just trying to inflate it with some air and fly it down the street."
Forecasters say an impending storm may try to foul the party, with AccuWeather forecasting winds of 12 to 25 mph (19 to 40 kph) and rain later in the day. Under guidelines, large balloons must stay grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 kph). The parade balloons have been grounded only once, in 1971.
Bluey, Mickey Mouse and Underdog
Will Coss, vice president and executive producer of Macy's Studios, wanted each decade represented in this year's parade. Joining Blue Hippo will be balloons of Bluey, Petula Pig, Hello Kitty, Snoopy's alter ego Joe Cool, Mickey Mouse, a Minion riding a banana and Underdog. There will also be a 101-foot-long (31-meter-long) Doodlebug caterpillar snaking along the streets and 1,000 clowns.
"The parade every year is a snapshot. It's a time capsule of that specific year. And, in this case, this is going to be a representation of our larger history," he says.
The parade began in 1924 as a way of creating buzz for the holiday windows — which that year had 27 fairy tales acted out with marionettes — at Macy's Herald Square flagship store.
Puppeteer and illustrator Tony Sarg created the windows, as well as the floats and costume characters, and Macy's borrowed animals from the Central Park Zoo for the first parades. In subsequent years, they even brought in tigers and lions.
In 1927, Macy's put an end to the animals after children were getting scared, and Sarg — believed to have been inspired by Indonesian shadow puppets — replaced the real animals with air-filled balloons. The next year, he partnered with the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company to create balloons that could be filled with helium.
"With each year, the balloons got a little bit bigger and more sophisticated. And in many years, they would take a character and then the next year they would repaint the balloon to be another character," says Darin Johnson, founder and CEO of the American Theater for Puppetry Arts.
A float on Thursday will honor Sarg, the creative force behind the parade through 1941 and a man considered the father of modern American puppetry.
The balloons actually floated away
In the parade's early years, the helium-filled balloons weren't packed up and stored for next year. Instead, they were released into the sky, with an attached envelope promising a finder's fee for anyone who returned them to Macy's.
Blue Hippo was among those set loose 95 years ago and unfortunately never returned, a mystery that prompted Kennedy to go digging into newspaper archives to look for clues.
He and his team found footage of the hippo flying past the newly finished Empire State Building in 1931 and read accounts that it was likely missing at sea. All the images they found were black and white, of course. But what was the real color of the balloon?
"What we decided was that, of course, it was the color of the sky because how else do you lose a flying hippo?" he says. His team added age spots for the 2026 version: "It's had some time out there, and we're really excited to bring it back."
Blue Hippo will also honor beloved real hippo Fiona from the Cincinnati Zoo, who died this month after ingesting a knit hat. Handlers walking Blue Hippo will wear purple patches with Fiona's face inside a heart and the words "Celebrating Fiona."
Building a balloon uses old and new technology
Parade balloons begin with a sketch that gets turned into a 3D rendering, then into a physical model thanks to digital printing technology.
Technology is embraced: Converted lawn mowers under the floats have given way to today's self-driving electric vehicles, and the "Harry Potter" float this year will have an animatronic Sorting Hat. But the old ways also persist.
"The art of building a balloon is still very much a sacred art for our Macy's and Macy's Studios team. Every piece of fabric is cut and sealed together by hand. Every balloon that you see is assembled, painted, and brought to life by hand," says Coss, who heads a team of 75 full-time staff members.
The parade has marched every year — except from 1942 to 1944 when the balloons were donated to the World War II effort — and has inspired awe for generations. "These giant balloons turn you into a child," Kennedy says. "I feel like we're all kind of kids for a day."
For the 100th parade, Johnson won't be watching — he'll be in it. He's been asked to be a handler for a recreation of one of the first-ever character balloons, Felix the Cat.
"It will be a dream come true," he says.
Thursday also marks a milestone anniversary for a newer Thanksgiving TV tradition: the National Dog Show, which is turning 25 this year. NBC broadcasts the canine spectacle right after the parade.

a8b01bc4ee4c.text: Prominent Democrats are calling for new restrictions on AI development following Axios reporting that employees at OpenAI and Anthropic increasingly fear their most powerful models cannot be safely released. Why it matters: The political debate over AI is expanding beyond the economic consequences of the technology to a more existential question: whether companies should be allowed to build systems they may not be able to control. The issue is gaining traction among Democratic leaders ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.), a potential 2028 contender, outlined a playbook for AI regulations in an interview with "The Axios Show," noting that voters hate the technology because they fear losing control . Driving the news: Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for immediate action: "The people inside AI companies are sounding the alarm ," Kelly said. "We built protections for nuclear weapons and other dangerous technologies, so why are we waiting with AI? We need safeguards and independent examiners in these companies, now." "It is absolutely indefensible to say 'we will take this up next year' when the risks are imminent and the alarm is nearly universal," Schatz said. "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter, and yet big tech refuses stop," Van Hollen said. "Inaction is not an option. Congress must step up." Sanders went further, calling for a halt to advanced AI development : "The humans who are creating AI fear it could soon escape their own control," Sanders said. "Congress must act and pause advanced AI development NOW." Catch up quick: More than two dozen sources familiar with internal debates at OpenAI and Anthropic told Axios that recent breakthroughs in AI capabilities have raised questions about whether future frontier models can be safely released. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some believe the problem is a technical one that's fixable. Others believe companies should go a step further and stop training new models entirely. The intrigue: As politicians debate how to ensure humanity retains control over AI, top industry executives are embroiled in a separate debate over how much autonomy humans should voluntarily cede to the technology as these systems become increasingly capable. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei personally pushed back Wednesday on a separate Axios story about views within the company that humanity will inevitably surrender some autonomy to superintelligent AI systems. "No, I do not believe that we should 'surrender human free will' to AI systems, and it's absurd to suggest that I do," Amodei said on X . Amodei argued that AI must be governed by legitimate democratic processes. Between the lines: Amodei's essay acknowledged room for nuance, highlighting that his views on human agency are mixed in specific instances where it could make sense for highly powerful AI systems to step in, like AI driving a car or designing a cancer drug. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have acknowledged safety challenges and indicated a willingness to slow aspects of AI development or deployment. What to watch: Whether concerns about losing control of AI become a defining issue in the Democratic presidential primary — and whether more lawmakers embrace restrictions on AI development itself, rather than just its deployment. The bottom line: A debate that has consumed the people building the world's most powerful AI systems is spilling into national politics.

ae08f2517070.text:
Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.
Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.
Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
The BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle explains.

Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low â to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case â concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 â met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

46ac3b65de55.text: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems. The big picture: The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans."

9f3c068b5d47.text: Presidential envoy Jared Kushner urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday to make good on commitments he made to Donald Trump to implement a Gaza peace plan , according to three sources with knowledge of a call between them. Why it matters: The White House and Trump's Board of Peace have been increasingly exasperated by what they viewed as Netanyahu's obstinacy on Gaza, convinced that he's been prioritizing his political survival above all else. "I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status," Kushner said in a New York Magazine interview published Monday. But two sources with knowledge of the call said it was "positive and constructive." One of them said Netanyahu signaled again that he's ready to move forward with the steps in Gaza that the White House wants. A third source confirmed that Netanyahu said he's committed to the Gaza plan. The Israeli prime minister's office confirmed that the call took place but declined to comment further. The big picture: The Gaza roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election and now wants the prime minister to reciprocate. But many of the Gaza measures are loathed by Netanyahu's base. Netanyahu's opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, currently has a window to form a new government. He's making progress, and if he succeeds, Netanyahu could be ousted as early as next week. Eisenkot promised during the campaign to implement Trump's Gaza plan with the goal of ensuring that Hamas no longer controls the territory within 18 months. Catch up quick: In July, the Board of Peace agreed with Hamas on a 15-point plan to disarm Gaza's armed groups and transfer civilian and security control to a new Palestinian technocratic government. Since then, Netanyahu's government has largely refused to move forward with implementing it. Netanyahu was and still is extremely skeptical that Hamas would ever demilitarize. He says the group is reconstituting and rearming in Gaza. Driving the news: President Trump spoke to Netanyahu two weeks ago and asked him to move ahead with implementing the Gaza plan. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said Netanyahu told Trump he would approve measures that are needed to implement the plan. But since then, nothing has happened. Behind the scenes: During his call with Trump, Netanyahu said that he couldn't approve the steps in Gaza the U.S. wants because he's heading a caretaker government. But the Netanyahu government accepted the Gaza plan and committed to taking those steps long before the election. "Bibi claimed he can't do small things in Gaza he already agreed to because he is a caretaker prime minister, but at the same time he claimed there is no problem for him to go to war with Iran. This wasn't a serious argument," a source with direct knowledge said. Zoom in: The sources said that implementing the Gaza plan hinges on the Israeli government's green light. They said the White House and Board of Peace have been asking Netanyahu to approve these steps: Allowing the International Stabilization Force (ISF) to deploy in Gaza. Permitting 4,000 Palestinians who were vetted by the Israeli security services and accepted to be part of a future Gaza police force to leave the enclave for training in Egypt and then be allowed to return. Approving materials for water and sanitation projects in Gaza. Allowing temporary mobile homes to enter Gaza to provide shelter in the winter. Allow construction materials into Gaza for building the ISF bases. Permitting a Palestinian technocratic government to begin operating in one area in southern Gaza as part of a pilot project. What to watch: A source with knowledge of the matter said that there's a sense that the Trump administration's private and public pressure — as well as the results of the midterm elections — has made Israel more receptive to implementing the Gaza plan. The source added that while the call with Netanyahu was positive, it remains to be seen whether Israel will actually take the steps the U.S. wants.

a4e095697f8d.text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras' Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.
But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. "Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department," says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.
The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% during President Donald Trump's second term.
The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that don't stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.
They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.
The reports have been "reverse-engineered," said Elliot Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college's Migration and Asylum Lab.
"They're trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places," said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.
In a statement, the State Department said that in line with U.S. laws and regulations it "may provide information about conditions in foreign countries" to immigration courts and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.
A system in turmoil – and targeted
Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of Trump's immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the U.S. as "not legitimate asylum-seekers."
Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.
"Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status," he said in a 2018 White House appearance.
Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.
But he had a point about poverty.
Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.
Even during President Joe Biden's years, most asylum claims were rejected.
But denials have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Democratic administration to 94% in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.
Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.
The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.
A sanitized view of troubled countries
Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, "membership in a particular social group." They also have to show that their government can't or won't protect them and that they can't move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.
The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.
They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that "the availability of services" can vary across each country.
Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.
The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government approach to rights abuses "is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself," and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.
"In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power," it says.
For Honduras' Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates "compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States," says the report.
Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.
"These shorter reports clearly don't address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed," said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.
They are "especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued," he said.

Export controls on chips and other technology shouldnât aim to cut China off completely â a strategy that will only backfire, warns Christophe Fouquet, CEO of ASML, the sole maker of the lithography machines needed to produce the worldâs most advanced AI chips.
âYou need [export controls] to protect very advanced technology, but you also have to use export control in such a way that you donât completely frustrate a country and invite that country to basically double down or triple down on development,â Fouquet said on Semaforâs Future Proof.
The debate over Chinese access to Western technology has intensified in Washington after revelations of Jensen Huangâs affair with a suspected Chinese spy left lawmakers divided on how aggressively to tighten curbs.
As a $520 billion de facto monopoly in chipmaking equipment, ASML sits at the center of that fight. Fouquet argued that continuing to sell China older equipment â ASMLâs shipments there are more than a decade behind the cutting edge â maintains a strategic âgeneration gapâ that keeps Beijing hooked on Western hardware rather than racing to build its own.
âFor almost 30 years, we have been able to keep an extremely high market share in China â very high means close to 100% â which means that they have accepted to rely on our technology with the idea that they had access to it,â Fouquet said.

Washington will provide an Nvidia split-screen next week, as CEO Jensen Huang faces questioning on Capitol Hill while the company touts new products at its DC conference less than two miles away.
Nvidia has reportedly assembled a team of top Washington lawyers and lobbyists ahead of Huangâs closed-door interview with three House committees on Tuesday, the same day he was scheduled to give a keynote at its annual tech showcase for developers, industry partners, and government officials.
Huangâs appearance was scrubbed from the schedule after he resigned as CEO, and thereâs no word yet on whether heâll make a grand return to the stage now that heâs been reinstated and reassured staffers that itâs mostly business as usual.
A tech-focused address in front of adoring fans could serve as effective counterprogramming to the lashing heâs likely to receive at the Capitol, and underscore the gulf between how the scandal is playing in Washington and in Silicon Valley.
Lawmakers still have plenty of legitimate questions for Huang and Nvidia, while to much of the tech world, the hearings are little more than political theater.

52f91f349def.text:
Reedâs view
A new ripple of consternation recently made its way out of AI labs to Axios, which reported internal concern that models have become too unsafe to release publicly.
But âsafetyâ can mean different things in different contexts. What this concern really means is that AI labs are having trouble creating ever more capable models that they can both understand and control.
These models are not actually a threat â so long as nobody uses them to do any important work, or gives them access to important things. The industry has internalized this framework. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella treats AI as an âinsider risk.â
This is bad news for AI labs. They wanted to build AI models that were so good they could take over all knowledge work. At closed-door conferences in Silicon Valley, people talked about Anthropic being nationalized because it became the entire economy.
But the failure to build anything remotely like that is good news for the rest of society. An AI model that is powerful but completely unpredictable is a very expensive and very useless tool.
The company that builds such a thing would have no customers.
Notable
- Anthropicâs share price has dropped below its $83 IPO price, as investors rethink the AI trade.

US President Donald Trump pushed for Jensen Huangâs reinstatement to the top of Nvidia because of his support for US open-weight models, which offer an alternative to Chinese versions.
But Huangâs return could also spur Beijing to speed up its own push to build homegrown chips.
Tech executives have waxed on about how bad a Jensen-less Nvidia would have been for the sector, given his role as both industry cheerleader and central banker, as well as Nvidiaâs promotion of the computing platforms developers use to train and run open models.
Still, the open-source world âis bigger than one man, even if that man is Jensen,â one AI startup founder told me.
If a newly emboldened Washington intensifies scrutiny of chip sales to China and curbs Beijingâs access to advanced computing power, that could slow down Chinaâs AI labs and Western companiesâ obsession with staying ahead.
